lessons.title: Track every possible computation
lessons.description: Ordered stacks, midpoint guesses, trees, and full-input acceptance.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

PDA branching: one stack per candidate explanation · chap2_PDA2.pdf, pages 1–7

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–5: union of count checks and configuration branching
  • PDF pages 6–7: even palindromes, reverse and midpoint guess

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The problem: the input may not announce the right plan

Consider {aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}\{a^ib^jc^k:i,j,k\ge0,\ i=j\text{ or }i=k\}{aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}. Read it carefully: there are three blocks in order, and either the a-count matches the b-count or it matches the c-count. Both equalities may hold, but both are not required.

A nondeterministic PDA can branch into two plans. Both store the a-count on the stack. One matches it against b's, then scans c's. The other scans b's without spending the stored markers, then matches against c's. Each branch has its own stack history. There is no shared pile that the first branch can damage for the second.

Two branches can stand in the same state with different stacks. Same room, different backpacks. If you merge them by room number, you lose the exact obligations they carry, and your trace starts accepting nonsense. Keep the state, unread input and ordered stack together as one whole situation.

Round 1 — OR means one full check can succeed · pages 1–5

The language {aⁱbʲcᵏ:i=j or i=k} requires block order a's, then b's, then c's. The equality is an OR, so either equality suffices; both may hold. The PDA stores one a marker per leading a and nondeterministically chooses which equality to verify.

In the upper branch it pops an a for each b, demands all a markers be exhausted, then reads any c suffix. In the lower branch it reads b's without changing the stored a count, then pops an a per c. States enforce block order in both branches. Arbitrarily matching any later symbols would solve a different language.

The slide's a²bc² is aabcc: i=2,j=1,k=2. The upper branch matches its one b against one a and still owes one a match; it cannot complete the i=j check. The lower branch keeps two a markers while reading b, then pops one for each c and reaches acceptance. One failed branch and one successful branch means accept.

A PDA's branch identity must include the entire stack as well as the state and input position. Two branches at q with stacks a$ and aa$ are not equivalent. Merging them into just {q} loses the count that future input needs. This is why the finite-state subset trick does not directly turn every PDA into a DPDA: the number of possible stacks is unbounded.

The ε moves choose phases without consuming symbols. A branch may guess too early or too late and die. Wrong guesses are permitted; a successful path still has to consume the whole input and meet the actual stack requirements.

Round 2 — Reverse comes from stack order · pages 6–7

wᴿ means the symbols of w in reverse order. For w=01, wᴿ=10, so wwᴿ=0110. For w=001, wwᴿ=001100. This language contains even-length palindromes, including ε; it does not include odd-length 010 in this particular construction.

Push each first-half symbol, then guess the midpoint using an ε move. After the switch, read each input symbol only if it matches the top and pop it. If the first half was 01, the stack top-to-bottom is 10$: the reversal is already supplied by last-in-first-out storage. You do not separately reverse the input.

Trace the successful branch of 0110: install $, push 0 giving 0$, push 1 giving 10$, switch without input, read 1 and pop 1, read 0 and pop 0, remove $, finish in accept with no unread input. A branch switching after the first 0 tries to match the next 1 against top 0 and dies. A branch never switching cannot finish the required matching phase.

Round 3 — Why a delimiter changes the design problem

With a promised midpoint marker, such as language {w#wᴿ}, the input itself tells the machine when to switch from pushing to popping. Without it, this NFA-style PDA guesses. This comparison explains what nondeterminism contributes; it is not by itself a proof that no deterministic PDA can recognize the unmarked language. Claims about all possible machines need a separate impossibility argument.

Both examples combine finite phase memory with unbounded structured memory. The stack handles the obligation; the state says what kind of work is currently legal. Keeping those roles separate makes the arrows far less arbitrary.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Follow a concrete case

For aabcc, the counts are i=2, j=1, k=2. The a=b branch spends one of its two markers on the sole b and still owes a b when c begins, so that branch fails. The a=c branch ignores the b, spends two markers on the two c's, and succeeds at the end of input. Therefore the NFA-style acceptance rule—at least one complete successful run—accepts the string.

A single rejecting branch does not reject the whole input. A branch that reaches an accepting state with unread input also does not accept the whole input. Keep the complete condition intact.

Another missing boundary: the midpoint of a palindrome

For {wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}\{ww^R:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}{wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}, wRw^RwR means w reversed. The first half must be matched against its reverse, so a stack's last-in-first-out behavior fits perfectly. Push the first half. At a guessed midpoint, switch by ε to popping and comparing.

Trace 0110. Push 0, then 1, giving stack 10$ top-first. Guess the midpoint. Read the next 1 and pop 1; read the last 0 and pop 0; finish at $ with no input left. The successful guess consumed exactly two symbols before switching.

Why not switch after just the first 0? The next symbol would be 1, but the stack expects 0, so that branch dies. Why not push all four symbols? Then no input remains to discharge the four markers. A bad guess failing is fine; a correct complete path is enough.

What a node in your trace must contain

A PDA configuration needs three pieces: current state, unread input, and entire stack. Two branches at the same state with different stacks are not the same configuration. Merging them as if this were NFA subset construction loses information.

A tree is useful: each node is a full configuration; each edge is one allowed transition. A table is useful too, provided each row retains all three fields. The representation is a tool, not the algorithm's definition. For an exam, label enough that a reader can check the pop condition and input consumption at every step.

Why this connects to grammars

A grammar also chooses among alternatives, some of which cannot generate the desired terminal string. A PDA can store the grammar's pending work and guess which production to use. That's the next deck: not an unrelated trick, but these same branching obligations applied to derivations.

Keep: a PDA branch carries its own state, remaining input, and stack. Nondeterminism guesses a plan; acceptance still demands that the whole plan works.

One connected check: If two branches have the same state and unread input but stacks 01$ and 10$, why can't you combine them into one stack set {0,1,$}?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

A branch is a whole situation: state, unread input and ordered stack. Keep those three fields together or the trace starts lying about what can happen next.

A PDA's live situation is state + unread input + full ordered stack. Two branches at the same state can have different stacks and futures. Combining them into one state-only set throws away the very memory the machine uses.

One path versus the whole tree

For an NFA or PDA, one complete accepting path proves acceptance. To prove rejection by tracing, every possible path must fail. When the question specifically requests a simulation tree, draw the branching even if you already see a winning path. The 2020 and 2022 solutions explicitly penalize replacing the requested tree with a single path. The 2025 comment-parser question, in contrast, explicitly asks only for an accepting path. Read the deliverable.

Worked branching example: even palindromes

Target: {wwR∣w∈{0,1}∗}\{ww^R\mid w\in\{0,1\}^*\}{wwR∣w∈{0,1}∗}, where wᴿ is w reversed. Use start s, push state p, compare state r, accept f. Initialize $; in p, read 0 or 1 and push that same symbol. At any point take ε,ε→ε to r. In r read 0 only while popping 0, or read 1 only while popping 1. Pop $ with ε to reach f.

The guess is the middle. For input 0110, the useful guesses are:

Symbols pushed before switching Stack just after switch What happens
0 $ Can't consume the first 0 in r; an early f has unread input
1 0$ Next input is 1, but top is 0; branch dies
2 10$ Read 1, then 0, then pop $; accepts
3 110$ Next input is 0, top is 1; branch dies
4 0110$ Input is exhausted with working symbols still stacked; cannot reach f

The stack 10$ means 1 on top of 0. It is not the integer ten and not a set. The accepting branch is

(s,0110,ε) → (p,0110,$) → (p,110,0$)
→ (p,10,10$) → (r,10,10$)
→ (r,0,0$) → (r,ε,$) → (f,ε,ε).

Turn this into a tree on paper

Write the initial configuration. Add every applicable ε move at that input position, each as its own child. For each current branch, consume the next symbol along every compatible transition, including its stack update. Continue its ε moves. Mark dead ends where no compatible move exists. Keep input position explicit so ε moves don't accidentally consume a character.

For this particular machine, pushing then guessing creates a finite tree with at most one switch point per prefix. General PDAs may have ε loops or unbounded ε pushes; blind “keep taking ε until done” may not terminate. A finite simulator cutoff then means inconclusive, not rejection.

Reading a language from a diagram

Explain phases, not just nodes. Which input block is read before the transition to the next phase? What is pushed? What later pops it? Does a mandatory arrow require at least one symbol? What must be on top to reach the final state? Then combine the resulting count and order constraints.

For example, if a zero pushes two markers and each later one nondeterministically pops one, two, or three, successful emptying says 2m=c₁+⋯+cₙ with cᵢ∈{1,2,3}. Hence n≤2m≤3n. To prove the reverse direction, you must also show that every integer in that range can be expressed by n choices. The 2022 paper asks for that proof separately; don't skip it.

Fresh practice

Trace all midpoint guesses for 010 in the palindrome machine. Then explain why changing the target to all palindromes needs a new option.

Show the answer

Switching after 0 pushed symbols cannot consume the first 0; after 1, the next 1 mismatches top 0; after 2, the next 0 mismatches top 1; after 3, the input ends with working stack symbols remaining. No accepting run exists. This machine recognizes even palindromes only. To include odd palindromes, add p→r moves that consume one middle symbol without changing the stack (0,ε→ε and 1,ε→ε). The central symbol has no partner. The original ε switch handles the even case.

Keep: acceptance is existential, a requested tree is still a tree, and an accepting state reached before the input ends is not yet acceptance of the full string.

the state says what kind of work is currently legal. keeping those roles separate makes the arrows far less arbitrary. ## reconnect the pieces in the worked model now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct. ## follow a concrete case for `aabcc`, the counts are i=2, j=1, k=2. the a=b branch spends one of its two markers on the sole b and still owes a b when c begins, so that branch fails. the a=c branch ignores the b, spends two markers on the two c's, and succeeds at the end of input. therefore the nfa-style acceptance rule—**at least one complete successful run**—accepts the string. a single rejecting branch does not reject the whole input. a branch that reaches an accepting state with unread input also does not accept the whole input. keep the complete condition intact. ## another missing boundary: the midpoint of a palindrome for \(\{ww^r:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}\), \(w^r\) means w reversed. the first half must be matched against its reverse, so a stack's last-in-first-out behavior fits perfectly. push the first half. at a guessed midpoint, switch by ε to popping and comparing. trace `0110`. push `0`, then `1`, giving stack `10$` top-first. guess the midpoint. read the next `1` and pop `1`; read the last `0` and pop `0`; finish at `$` with no input left. the successful guess consumed exactly two symbols before switching. why not switch after just the first `0`? the next symbol would be `1`, but the stack expects `0`, so that branch dies. why not push all four symbols? then no input remains to discharge the four markers. a bad guess failing is fine; a correct complete path is enough. ## what a node in your trace must contain a pda configuration needs three pieces: current state, unread input, and **entire stack**. two branches at the same state with different stacks are not the same configuration. merging them as if this were nfa subset construction loses information. a tree is useful: each node is a full configuration; each edge is one allowed transition. a table is useful too, provided each row retains all three fields. the representation is a tool, not the algorithm's definition. for an exam, label enough that a reader can check the pop condition and input consumption at every step. ## why this connects to grammars a grammar also chooses among alternatives, some of which cannot generate the desired terminal string. a pda can store the grammar's pending work and guess which production to use. that's the next deck: not an unrelated trick, but these same branching obligations applied to derivations. **keep:** a pda branch carries its own state, remaining input, and stack. nondeterminism guesses a plan; acceptance still demands that the whole plan works. **one connected check:** if two branches have the same state and unread input but stacks `01$` and `10$`, why can't you combine them into one stack set `{0,1,$}`?

lessons.title: Turn a grammar into a machine
lessons.description: A stack of unfinished work, reversed pushes, and terminal matching.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

CFG to PDA: run the grammar as a stack of pending output · chap2_PDA3.pdf, pages 1–10

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: equivalence direction and grammar language
  • PDF pages 3–7: reverse push, helper states and matching
  • PDF pages 8–10: complete source trace and both-direction invariant

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The bridge: generating a string and checking a string can cooperate

A grammar chooses how to build output. A PDA can guess those grammar choices while checking them against the supplied input. Its stack means: this is the sequence still owed by the current derivation. The next owed symbol belongs on top, so we can deal with it first.

The deck's grammar is S→aTb∣bS\to aTb\mid bS→aTb∣b, T→Ta∣εT\to Ta\mid\varepsilonT→Ta∣ε. S either produces a single b, or an a, then T's output, then b. T can produce any number of a's. So the language consists of b and all strings of one or more a's followed by one b.

The stack is the machine's to-do list, with the next job on top. Expanding a variable breaks a job into smaller jobs. Matching a terminal checks off finished output against the actual input. Don't let the notation blur those actions together: planning an a and reading an a are two different damn steps.

The stack changes jobs here. Instead of unpaid IOUs from earlier input, it stores the grammar’s future to-do list. The next job has to sit on top. That is why push order matters: shove the list on backward and the machine tries to print the sentence backward. Let’s make that ordering explicit.

Round 1 — The stack becomes a to-do list for a derivation · pages 1–2

The theorem says a language is context-free exactly when some PDA recognizes it. This deck proves CFG→PDA. Start with a grammar and build a machine that guesses a derivation while checking its terminal output against the supplied input.

The source grammar is S→aTb|b and T→Ta|ε. T can make any number of a's: each use of T→Ta adds a pending a, and T→ε stops. Therefore S makes b, or one initial a followed by any number of additional a's and a final b. In compact notation its language is a*b. Recognizing that language directly is easier than the general conversion, but the slide deliberately demonstrates the conversion procedure.

Round 2 — Why the right side gets pushed backward · pages 3–7

For S→aTb, the next input to check is a, then whatever T generates, then b. The stack must therefore have a on top, T underneath, and b underneath T. Push b first, then T, then a. If you push a first, b ends up on top and the machine tries to read the output backward. That ain't a harmless implementation detail.

Initialize with $ and then S. At the main loop, if the top is a variable, nondeterministically choose one of its productions and replace it by the right side. If the top is a terminal t, consume exactly input t and pop it. If only $ remains, remove it and go to the accepting state.

A course PDA transition pushes at most one symbol, so pushing a whole right side is shorthand for a chain through fresh helper states. Those helper states must have only the intended continuation; otherwise another rule could interrupt halfway through the push. Rule expansion consumes ε input. Terminal matching consumes real input. If you include only expansion arrows, you can generate a stack forever while never checking a single input symbol.

Round 3 — Read the slide's aaaab trace as unfinished output · pages 8–9

After initializing S$, choose S→aTb and obtain top-left aTb$. Match the first a: unread input becomes aaab, stack Tb$. Expand T→Ta three times: Tab$, Taab$, Taaab$. Then choose T→ε, leaving aaab$. Match the remaining three a's and b one by one; only $ remains. Remove it, with no input left, and accept.

Notice the subtlety: while T keeps expanding, those extra a's wait below it. They are not consumed until T is removed. The stack represents future required output, not a bag of characters already seen. The old “stack counts previous zeros” example used the same data structure for a different purpose.

Round 4 — Why guessing can't fabricate a wrong string · page 10

At main-loop checkpoints, the already-consumed input prefix followed by the pending stack string above $ is a sentential form derivable from S. A variable expansion applies a genuine production, preserving that statement. A terminal match shifts the first pending terminal into the consumed prefix without changing their concatenation.

If the machine accepts after consuming all input and exhausting pending work, the complete input was generated by the grammar. Conversely, choose a leftmost derivation of any grammar-generated string; the machine can choose the same productions and match its terminals, reaching acceptance. These are the two correctness directions.

A branch that reaches the accepting state with unread input does not accept that input. A branch that expands forever produces no finite accepting run. Neither invalidates the construction; the existence of a correct finite branch is what matters. Nonaccepting branches are not allowed to vote down the successful one.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

There are only two kinds of work

If the stack top is a variable, replace it using a grammar production. This consumes no input, because choosing how to produce a symbol is not the same as matching an actual symbol.

If the top is a terminal, it must equal the next input symbol. Consume that input symbol and pop the matching terminal. If they disagree, that branch has no matching move. A terminal cannot be expanded into something more convenient.

Initialize with S above a fresh bottom marker $. Finish when the pending work is exhausted, by removing $ and entering accept. Input must also be fully consumed.

A complete trace of aaab

Write the stack top first; omit $ in this table only to make the pending work visible.

Move Unread input Pending stack
initialize aaab S
choose S→aTb aaab aTb
match a aab Tb
choose T→Ta aab Tab
choose T→Ta aab Taab
choose T→ε aab aab
match a ab ab
match a b b
match b ε empty

Now $ can be removed and the run can accept. Notice how T→Ta adds a pending a after T. Expanding the variable repeatedly builds more work without consuming input; terminal matching pays it off afterward.

Why pushes appear reversed on the diagram

To leave aTb top-first, physically push b first, then T, then a. The last pushed symbol is on top. That is a consequence of stack order, not a rule that reverses the generated language. If a diagram abbreviates a multi-symbol push, expand it into single pushes in that order using fresh intermediate states.

With a wrong production choice, the machine may get stuck. It can also keep choosing T→Ta forever. Such a branch does not accept. A finite successful derivation supplies a finite successful branch; existence of other bad branches doesn't invalidate it.

Why the conversion is correct

After matching a prefix of the input, the stack records the ungenerated/unmatched remainder of a chosen leftmost derivation. Variable expansion changes that remainder exactly as a grammar step would. Terminal matching removes the next symbol only when it agrees with the input.

Thus a successful run describes a grammar derivation of the entire input. Conversely, a derivation of the input tells the PDA which productions to choose, giving a successful run. This is the two-way language-equality proof; tracing aaab alone is only an illustration.

Keep: expand variables without input; match terminals with input. Next we reverse the bridge: describe a PDA's balanced stack behavior with grammar variables.

One connected check: Why would consuming an a while applying S→aTb, and then consuming another when popping that terminal a, be wrong?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

The grammar hands the machine a to-do list. The stack keeps its next job on top, so pushing in reverse order is what preserves the intended output order.

A CFG-to-PDA conversion makes the stack a to-do list for generating the input. The top item is what must be dealt with next. A variable means “expand this using a grammar rule.” A terminal means “match this against the next input symbol.”

Use the exact slide example

PDA 3 gives S→aTb|b and T→Ta|ε. The grammar generates b, ab, aab, aaab, and so on. We'll convert its actual productions rather than inventing a replacement language.

Initialize by pushing $ and then S. In the main state q, the stack starts S$, top at left. To use S→aTb, replace the top S with aTb, so the resulting stack is aTb$.

But if each transition pushes only one symbol, the push order is b, then T, then a. Last pushed becomes top. Pushing a,T,b would put b on top and force the wrong input order. That's the entire reason for “reverse the right side.”

Every transition, including the boring ones

States: s (start), d (after bottom marker), q (main), u,v (long S rule), t (T rule), f (accept). F={f}. Stack alphabet Γ={a,b,S,T,$}; input alphabet Σ={a,b}.

From Label To Job
s ε,ε→$ d Bottom marker
d ε,ε→S q Start variable
q ε,S→b u Begin S→aTb
u ε,ε→T v Push middle T
v ε,ε→a q Push first terminal a
q ε,S→b q S→b alternative
q ε,T→a t Begin T→Ta
t ε,ε→T q Put T above a
q ε,T→ε q T→ε
q a,a→ε q Match terminal a
q b,b→ε q Match terminal b
q ε,$→ε f Finish

The two moves from q labeled ε,S→b have different destinations and represent different grammar choices. This is allowed in a PDA. Intermediate states force a long production to finish its pushes before returning to q; they prevent arbitrary interleaving of unfinished replacements.

Follow aab all the way

After initialization, stack S$. Choose S→aTb, yielding aTb$. Match the first a, leaving Tb$ and unread input ab. Expand T→Ta, yielding Tab$. Now choose T→ε, leaving ab$. Match a then b, leaving $. Pop $ and reach f with no unread input: accept.

Written as macro steps, this used two-symbol pushes; the table above expands each macro into legal single-symbol transitions. On an exam asking for the procedure's diagram, show those intermediate nodes unless the question explicitly permits a string-push abbreviation.

Why conversion preserves the language

At q, the stack records the remaining symbols of a guessed leftmost derivation, above $. Expanding a variable follows an actual grammar rule; matching a terminal consumes the identical input symbol. A derivation of w gives a successful sequence of these moves, so every generated string is accepted. Conversely, any accepting run must have used valid productions and matched every terminal, with no unfinished stack symbols or unread input. Reading those production choices gives a derivation of w. Both directions matter.

How to handle a state limit

First build the correct chains. Then look for identical remaining push sequences that can share a suffix of intermediate states. Do not merge merely because two circles look similar; merging must preserve which pushes remain. The 2025 paper explicitly asks for shared chains in its fixed draft. Check that shared exits cannot assemble a right side not in the grammar.

Fresh practice

For S→0S1|ε, list the stack replacement for each production and expand the long replacement into single-symbol moves. Include input matching and the finish check.

Show the construction

Initialize $ then S. In main q, S→0S1 is q —ε,S→1→ u —ε,ε→S→ v —ε,ε→0→ q. The other rule is q —ε,S→ε→ q. Add loops 0,0→ε and 1,1→ε to consume the input. Add q —ε,$→ε→ f, with f the only accept state and no outgoing moves. The resulting stack after the long production is 0S1 followed by the old stack remainder. Match all input and empty the to-do list before acceptance.

lessons.title: Turn balanced runs into grammar rules
lessons.description: Safe normalization and every push–pop pairing.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

PDA to CFG: name a balanced stretch of computation · chap2_PDA4.pdf, pages 1–10

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: balanced variable meaning and normal assumptions
  • PDF pages 3–6: concatenation, wrapping and empty rules
  • PDF pages 7–10: source example, counts and derivation

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

What the sixteen variables are actually for

With four PDA states, the standard conversion introduces one variable Aₚᵩ for each ordered pair of states p,q: 4×4=16 variables. That does not mean the PDA suddenly has sixteen states. We are building a grammar whose variables summarize different kinds of journey through the original machine.

Aₚᵩ means: strings consumed by a run that starts in p with an empty stack and ends in q with an empty stack. The same run pattern can sit above a protected existing stack: it may build and clear extra work but never pop below that baseline. Merely having the same stack at both endpoints is not enough if the run disturbed the protected contents in between.

The PDA first needs a single accepting state, empty-stack completion, and transitions that each push or pop one symbol. The next deck explains that normalization carefully.

Think of a balanced segment as a subroutine that promises: “Whatever stack was underneath me, I'll leave it alone and clean up everything I add.” Aₚᵩ names that contract together with its entry and exit states. The grammar doesn't store a stack snapshot. It describes strings that can be read while honoring that contract.

Those subscripts name the start and finish of a whole trip. Imagine borrowing some workspace, doing a subroutine, then returning with the old workspace untouched. Aₚq names the input consumed by such a trip from p to q. It does not name one arrow. That distinction makes the 16 variables make sense.

Round 1 — Aₚq describes a whole balanced trip · pages 1–3

A variable Aₚq is one grammar variable whose label contains two state names. It describes input strings consumed by a computation that starts in p, ends in q, and leaves the underlying stack untouched. During the trip, temporary symbols may be pushed and popped, but the computation must never pop below its starting stack height. That's the protected baseline condition.

Picture a subroutine borrowing desk space above a sealed folder. It can stack temporary papers and remove them, but must leave the sealed folder intact. Merely ending with a folder that looks the same is not enough if it opened and used the original during the trip. Likewise, equal endpoint stack strings alone do not express the needed condition.

Normalize the PDA to one accepting state, empty stack at acceptance, and transitions that each push or pop one symbol. The next deck explains those modifications. Then A_start,accept describes exactly the complete accepting computations, so it becomes the grammar's start variable.

Round 2 — The three rule families describe three shapes of trip · pages 3–6

Do two balanced trips: Aₚq→AₚrAᵣq. First go p→r while restoring the baseline; then go r→q while restoring it again. The concatenated input spells the whole journey. The intermediate r ranges over every state.

Wrap a balanced trip in a matching push and pop: suppose a move p→r consumes a and pushes t, and a move s→q consumes b and pops that same t. Add Aₚq→aAᵣs b. The inner trip r→s operates above the newly pushed t and returns without consuming it. Then the outer pop removes it. a or b may be ε, contributing no terminal.

The four labels have roles: p is before the push; r after it; s before the matching pop; q after it. r and s need not be adjacent states or equal. Pairing a push with every pop of the same stack symbol generates candidate productions; impossible inner trips simply cannot derive terminal strings.

Do nothing: Aₚp→ε. With zero moves, start and finish at p with unchanged stack and empty consumed input. It does not imply Aₚq→ε for arbitrary different endpoints.

Round 3 — The “16 states” confusion is really 16 variables · pages 7–10

The example PDA has four states. Ordered endpoint pairs give 4×4=16 grammar variables A₁₁,…,A₄₄. These are not 16 states of a new PDA. Concatenation rules use triples p,r,q: 4³=64 generated rules before simplification. The formula is compact because listing every one is repetitive; each still has a concrete endpoint meaning.

The bottom-marker push 1→2 and pop 3→4 yield A₁₄→A₂₃, because both consume ε. Pair the zero-push loop at 2 with either zero-pop move, obtaining A₂₃→0A₂₂1 and A₂₃→0A₂₃1. With A₂₂→ε, a derivation is A₁₄⇒A₂₃⇒0A₂₃1⇒00A₂₂11⇒0011. The outer $ pair wraps the whole computation; each inner 0/1 pair matches one pushed zero.

The language here uses n≥1, unlike the earlier n≥0 example: original q₁ is no longer accepting. Reused circle labels do not mean the acceptance condition stayed the same.

Round 4 — Why those three shapes cover every balanced computation

For soundness, induct on a finite derivation tree. Empty rules do nothing; concatenation joins two valid balanced trips; wrapping performs a matching push, a valid inner trip and its matching pop. Thus each generated string corresponds to a valid computation.

For completeness, induct on the number of transitions in a balanced computation. Zero transitions uses Aₚp→ε. If the stack returns to baseline at an intermediate point, split there and use a concatenation rule on the two shorter trips. If it never returns early, its first push is matched by the last pop; the middle is a shorter balanced trip above that symbol, so use a wrapping rule. Inducting on transitions, rather than input length, matters because ε moves can add transitions without adding characters.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Two ways a balanced journey can be built

A balanced journey can consist of two balanced journeys in sequence. If r is the intermediate state, add

Apq→AprArq.A_{pq}\to A_{pr}A_{rq}.Apq​→Apr​Arq​.

The right side says: do p→r work, then r→q work. For each p,q,r, this is a possible decomposition. It doesn't say every input takes every route.

Or the journey pushes a symbol t, performs some balanced work above it, then pops that same t. If a push transition goes p→r while consuming a, and a matching pop goes s→q while consuming b, add

Apq→aArsb.A_{pq}\to aA_{rs}b.Apq​→aArs​b.

a and b may be ε. The inner variable covers the part between the push and its matching pop. The pushed symbol's identity must match; a push of 0 cannot be paired with a pop of $ just because the state arrows line up.

Finally Aₚₚ→ε permits doing nothing: same start and end state, no stack change, no input consumed.

Work the deck's four-state example

The normalized machine for positive 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n pushes $ from state 1 to 2, pushes zeros in state 2, begins popping zeros on the move to state 3, continues popping there, and pops $ from 3 to accepting 4.

Pair the outside $ push and pop: A14→A23A_{14}\to A_{23}A14​→A23​. Their input labels are both ε, so nothing is printed around the inner variable.

Pair a zero push 2→2 with the zero pop 3→3: A23→0A231A_{23}\to0A_{23}1A23​→0A23​1. Pair that push with the first zero pop 2→3: A23→0A221A_{23}\to0A_{22}1A23​→0A22​1. Use A₂₂→ε to finish the smallest balanced interior.

Now derive 0011:

A14⇒A23⇒0A231⇒00A2211⇒0011.A_{14}\Rightarrow A_{23}\Rightarrow0A_{23}1\Rightarrow00A_{22}11\Rightarrow0011.A14​⇒A23​⇒0A23​1⇒00A22​11⇒0011.

Every rule is tied to an actual push/pop pair. The matching grammar nesting reflects matching stack lifetimes.

Decode the four subscripts by their jobs

Letter Where it sits in the wrapped run
p before the outside push
r immediately after that push
s immediately before its matching pop
q after that pop

So Aₚᵩ names the whole wrapped journey, while Aᵣₛ names just the inside. The source's table lists p,r,s,q in this order to keep those roles visible. The p and q in one rule are allowed to coincide with other listed states; these letters name roles, not necessarily four distinct circles.

With four states, the full construction also lists 4³=64 concatenation rules, one for each choice of p,q,r, and four Aₚₚ→ε rules. An exam may require the complete construction even if most variables later prove useless. Counts come from choices of endpoints and middle states, not from new PDA states appearing out of nowhere.

Why the general construction needs concatenation too

A run may return to its baseline halfway through, then start a new balanced section. That isn't one push wrapped around the entire run. The concatenation rules capture these side-by-side sections. If a nonempty balanced run has no intermediate return to baseline, its first push must be matched by its final pop, which gives the wrapping case. This decomposition supports an induction on run length.

The reverse direction follows the grammar: empty rule does nothing; concatenation joins two valid runs; wrapping adds a matching push and pop around a valid inner run. That establishes exact correspondence, not just a few example strings.

Keep: Aₚᵩ is a name for balanced work between states. Four states give sixteen such names because both endpoints matter.

One connected check: In Aₚᵩ→aAᵣₛb, which two transitions determine p,r,s,q, and why must their stack symbols agree?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Each grammar variable names a balanced trip between two states. Start with that trip meaning, then the intimidating subscripts become labels for its endpoints.

This direction looks scarier because one grammar variable represents an entire balanced piece of a computation, not one machine state. The recipe is mechanical once that meaning is clear. It appears on all six inspected Midterm 2 papers.

First normalize the PDA

The course construction requires: one accepting state; empty stack on acceptance; each transition pushes one symbol or pops one symbol, never both and never neither.

A general final-state PDA doesn't automatically have these properties. Use a fresh bottom marker $ and a new start that pushes it. From each old accepting state, allow an ε move into a new drain state. The drain pops working symbols, then pops $ into the sole new accept state. Old accepting states cease to be accepting.

Why a separate drain? If you add free pops to the old states, the machine may throw away stack data and then continue its ordinary input-reading transitions, accepting extra strings. Once in the drain, it must never return to the computation. Entering the drain early cannot accept a longer input because the drain consumes no more real input.

A replace transition a,X→Y becomes a,X→ε into a private intermediate state, then ε,ε→Y into the destination. A no-stack-change transition a,ε→ε becomes a,ε→D followed by ε,D→ε through a private intermediate state, using a permitted dummy symbol D. Respect restrictions on Γ and on extra states; past questions often require reusing available symbols or states. A fresh marker is the safe unrestricted construction, not permission to violate a constrained problem.

What Aₚq means

For each ordered state pair p,q, make a variable Aₚq. It generates strings that can carry the machine from p to q with no net stack change while leaving any pre-existing stack below that computation untouched. Merely returning to the same stack after messing with its old contents is not the intended balanced segment.

The grammar's start is Aₛf, where s is the normalized start and f the sole accept state. If there are four PDA states, there are 4×4=16 variables. Sixteen variables is not sixteen steps and not a requirement to draw a sixteen-state automaton. Each variable names a different start/end pair.

The three families of rules

  1. Do nothing: Aₚp→ε for every p.
  2. Join two balanced segments: Aₚq→AₚrAᵣq for every p,q,r.
  3. Wrap a balanced middle with a matching push/pop: if p —a,ε→t→ r and s —b,t→ε→ q, add

Apq→aArsb.A_{pq}\to aA_{rs}b.Apq​→aArs​b.

Read it in time order: push t while consuming a; do a balanced middle from r to s above that t; pop the same t while consuming b. The outer variable uses p,q, the whole segment's endpoints. The inner variable uses r,s, the states after the push and before the pop.

a or b may be ε; erase that ε when writing the right side. The stack symbol t is not copied into the generated string. The grammar generates the input labels, not the stack history.

Work the actual slide example

PDA 4 pages 7–10 uses start 1, accept 4, and these moves:

1 — ε,ε→$ → 2
2 — 0,ε→0 → 2
2 — 1,0→ε → 3
3 — 1,0→ε → 3
3 — ε,$→ε → 4

This language is 0ⁿ1ⁿ with n≥1. State 1 is not accepting, and there is no zero-pair shortcut.

For each stack symbol, list every push × every pop of that symbol:

Stack symbol Push p→r / input a Pop s→q / input b Rule
$ 1→2 / ε 3→4 / ε A₁₄→A₂₃
0 2→2 / 0 2→3 / 1 A₂₃→0A₂₂1
0 2→2 / 0 3→3 / 1 A₂₃→0A₂₃1

Then include Aₚq→AₚrAᵣq for all 4³=64 triples and Aₚp→ε for all four p. You may specify these families symbolically unless the question demands listing every rule. If it asks only the wrapped rules, supply only that requested family plus the pairing table; don't waste the exam writing 64 unrelated rows.

Trace a derivation: A₁₄⇒A₂₃⇒0A₂₃1⇒00A₂₂11⇒0011. A₂₂→ε closes the innermost balanced segment.

Why the rule families are sufficient

In a nonempty balanced computation, either the stack returns to its initial level at an intermediate point, splitting the run into two balanced segments, or it first pushes a symbol that stays under the middle until the matching final pop. These are the join and wrap cases. Induction on computation length supplies a derivation. Conversely, each grammar rule combines actual balanced runs, so induction on the derivation yields a valid run. The start/end normalization then makes generated strings exactly accepted inputs.

Fresh practice

There are push moves 1 —a,ε→X→ 2 and 2 —ε,ε→X→ 3, and pop moves 4 —b,X→ε→ 5 and 3 —ε,X→ε→ 4. List every wrapped rule caused by X.

Show the four pairings

A₁₅→aA₂₄b; A₁₄→aA₂₃; A₂₅→A₃₄b; A₂₄→A₃₃. Two pushes times two pops gives four pairings. Do not omit a pairing because you can't immediately imagine a successful middle; a variable with no terminal derivation simply contributes no strings.

lessons.title: Check determinism properly
lessons.description: The course’s four-way test, reject completion, and acceptance.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

DPDA: determinism is about competing enabled moves · chap2_DPDA1.pdf, pages 1–6

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: determinism changes PDA language power
  • PDF pages 3–4: function output and competing enabled moves
  • PDF pages 5–6: acceptance, empty stack and epsilon loops

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

One table cell isn't the whole decision

For a DFA, the current state and next input symbol select exactly one move. For a PDA, a move may read input or ε, and may pop the top or ε. Several differently labeled transitions can therefore be enabled at the same situation. Determinism must rule out those competing actions, not merely forbid two answers in one cell.

Suppose the machine is in q, the next input is 0, and the stack top is X. It could potentially use any of these:

Transition lookup What it would do
δ(q,0,X) read the zero and pop X
δ(q,0,ε) read the zero without popping
δ(q,ε,X) pop X without reading
δ(q,ε,ε) move without reading or popping

If two are available, the machine has a choice right now. Different labels do not make that choice disappear.

Imagine two buttons available at once: read the next symbol, or take a free ε move. Each button may have only one destination, but you still have a choice between buttons. Determinism must eliminate that competition too. Counting destinations inside separate table cells does not settle which actions are simultaneously available.

Round 1 — Determinism means one enabled action, not one arrow per label · pages 1–4

An NFA's nondeterminism can be compiled into a finite checklist because its possible states come from a fixed finite set. A PDA's configurations include arbitrarily long stacks. The analogous collection need not fit into finitely many states with one deterministic stack. The theorem is that deterministic context-free languages form a proper subfamily of context-free languages; this observation motivates it but is not the full separation proof.

The DPDA transition output is one pair (next state, pushed symbol) or ∅ for undefined. It no longer returns an arbitrary set of pairs. But that alone does not prevent conflicting moves, because ε moves can compete with symbol-consuming moves.

For current state q, upcoming actual symbol a and actual top x, four table entries could apply: δ(q,a,x), δ(q,a,ε), δ(q,ε,x), δ(q,ε,ε). They correspond to inspect both; read input without inspecting stack; inspect stack without reading input; inspect neither. If two were available, the machine would still have a choice even though each individual cell contained one output.

The course uses an exactly-one-defined condition for every q,a,x with a∈Σ and x∈Γ. Other presentations use an at-most-one condition with partial transitions. For the exam, use this course's stated convention. Exactly one is stronger: a situation with all four entries empty needs completion, usually through rejection. Do not swap conventions halfway through a construction.

Round 2 — ε in a pop slot does not ask whether the stack is empty

This deserves its own sentence because it causes so much trouble: ε in the pop slot means no stack symbol is required or removed. That move can apply when the stack is nonempty too. Therefore it competes with an x-pop move when x is actually on top. Similarly, an ε-input move may be available while real input remains.

The four-way condition quantifies actual x∈Γ. An empty stack has no actual top x. Only no-pop alternatives can work there; a defined pop transition cannot conjure a symbol out of emptiness. Determinism does not mean every input must successfully finish.

Round 3 — Two ways the unique run can fail · pages 5–6

First source example: the only defined action is an ε-input move that pops 0. With input 0 and empty stack, it cannot execute because the required 0 is absent. No input gets consumed, and the run is stuck. That rejects the input.

Second example: the only available action consumes ε, pops nothing and pushes 1. It can repeat forever, producing 1,11,111,… on the stack while the input 0 never advances. There is a unique infinite run, but no accepting computation consuming the whole input. This also fails to accept.

For acceptance, retain the course's end-of-input accepting-state condition; for a nonempty input, reaching an accepting state before consuming all symbols is insufficient. A failed or looping path is not transformed into success by the label “deterministic.” Later, when discussing Turing machines, we will distinguish explicitly rejecting from looping. Keep that distinction separate from the language-level fact that both are nonacceptance.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Read the course definition precisely

This course's DPDA definition requires exactly one of those four entries to be nonempty, for every state q, input symbol a, and stack symbol x. Each nonempty entry returns one pair (next state, symbol to push) rather than a set of alternative pairs.

Some treatments use “at most one” and permit partial transitions. For these slides and exam questions, use the stated exactly-one convention. The next deck completes missing cases with rejecting behavior.

An entry equal to ∅ means there is no transition. A pair such as (r,ε) is an actual transition to r that pushes nothing. Those are very different: no action versus a legal action with no push.

Work one collision

Suppose δ(q,0,ε)=(r,X): read 0, push X. Also suppose δ(q,ε,X)=(s,ε): pop X without reading. When the next input is 0 and the current top is X, both can run. One consumes input and increases the stack; the other consumes nothing and decreases it. Each individual entry has one output, but the machine is nondeterministic.

To repair the design, the state must distinguish the phases in which those actions are allowed, or one of the conflicting moves must be removed while preserving the intended language. Writing the arrows farther apart on the page doesn't fix the collision.

Deterministic does not mean “will accept or reject quickly”

An ε cycle may keep running without consuming the next input symbol. A configuration may become stuck when the input or stack is empty and its required action is unavailable. The four-way condition is stated over actual alphabet symbols; ε is the no-consumption option, not a real member of the input alphabet.

Acceptance is still about a computation that has consumed the whole input and is in an accepting state. Visiting an accepting state while unread input remains isn't enough. This is unlike a Turing machine's accepting halt state, which will be introduced later.

The broader connection

Nondeterminism adds no language-recognition power to DFAs versus NFAs, but deterministic PDAs are more restricted than general PDAs. A stack does not make every midpoint guess deterministic. The absence of a visible separator can matter because the machine may not know when to stop pushing and start popping.

Keep: check the four entries together for every concrete situation. The source's definition controls the required completeness. Next we apply that test to the counted-block PDA.

One connected check: Why can an ε transition conflict with a 0 transition even though ε and 0 are different labels?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

The question is which actions are actually available at the same moment. An epsilon move can compete with a real-input move, even if their table cells look separate.

“Deterministic” means there is no choice between simultaneously applicable moves. For PDAs, checking only “one destination per table cell” is not enough: an input move and an ε move in different cells can both be applicable.

The four-way conflict

Suppose the current state is q, next input symbol is a, and top stack symbol is X. All four kinds of transitions could apply:

δ(q,a,X),δ(q,a,ε),δ(q,ε,X),δ(q,ε,ε).\delta(q,a,X),\quad\delta(q,a,\varepsilon),\quad\delta(q,\varepsilon,X),\quad\delta(q,\varepsilon,\varepsilon).δ(q,a,X),δ(q,a,ε),δ(q,ε,X),δ(q,ε,ε).

They respectively read/pop, read/no-pop, no-read/pop, no-read/no-pop. Recall that “no-pop” does not mean “stack empty.” Therefore δ(q,0,ε) and δ(q,ε,$) conflict when the next input is 0 and the stack top is $. Different columns don't save you.

The course convention, DPDA 1 page 4, requires exactly one of these four entries to be nonempty for each q,a,X, with a∈Σ and X∈Γ. Entries output a single pair (state,push-symbol), not a set of pairs. Reject-state completion is used for missing combinations. Other texts often use a partial-transition “at most one” formulation; follow this course's table convention on its exams.

A complete small example

Language: B={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}B=\{0^m1^n\mid m\geq n\geq0\}B={0m1n∣m≥n≥0}, from 2020 Problem 2. Let q₀ push a 0 on each input 0. On the first 1, pop a 0 and enter q₁. In q₁, each 1 pops a 0. A later 0 must reject because block order would break. Both q₀ and q₁ are accepting: leftover zeros are allowed, and n may be zero.

With stack alphabet Γ={0}, the nonempty DPDA entries are:

State Input Pop Output
q₀ 0 ε (q₀,0)
q₀ 1 0 (q₁,ε)
q₁ 0 ε (qᵣ,ε)
q₁ 1 0 (q₁,ε)
qᵣ ε ε (qᵣ,ε)

All other entries are ∅. For each real input symbol and possible stack top 0, exactly one relevant entry is nonempty. If the stack is actually empty and the next symbol is 1, the pop-0 instruction can't be executed, so the input is rejected. The sink's ε loop is rejection by failing to read the remaining input; qᵣ is never accepting.

For 001, the run ends in q₁ with one 0 still on the stack. It accepts. Final-state PDA acceptance does not generally require an empty stack. We enforce empty-stack finishing in some constructions because that particular language or conversion needs it.

Why a PDA is not always convertible to an equivalent DPDA

DFA and NFA recognize the same languages. PDA and DPDA do not: deterministic context-free languages form a proper subclass of context-free languages. Subset construction cannot solve this by making each possible stack configuration a finite state; stacks have unbounded length, so there may be infinitely many configurations.

A fixed stack bound is different. If a PDA is guaranteed to use at most m stack cells, there are finitely many stack strings, and an NFA can use states (q,stack). Start (q₀,ε), accept all pairs whose q is accepting, and simulate each legal stack update. This is the idea behind 2022 Problem 4(b). The bound must be uniform over all inputs; saying each individual run uses finitely many cells is not enough.

Fresh practice

At q, transitions include 0,ε→0 looping to q and ε,$→ε going to an accept state. Explain a concrete configuration where the machine has two applicable choices. Does putting each move into a different table column fix it?

Show the reasoning

Use configuration (q,0,$). The 0 move can consume the next symbol and push 0 without popping. The ε move can instead pop $. Both are applicable before the same input symbol. The columns are δ(q,0,ε) and δ(q,ε,$); they belong to the same four-way conflict check. Separate columns do not make the computation deterministic. A repair must preserve the language while removing that simultaneous choice, often by changing where empty or zero-only strings are accepted.

lessons.title: Design under exam constraints
lessons.description: Weighted counts, limited states, and a complete existence proof.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

PDA: finite control plus a stack of unfinished obligations · chap2_PDA1.pdf, pages 1–11

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: stack memory and LIFO
  • PDF pages 4–7: equal-block PDA and full configuration traces
  • PDF pages 8–9: six-tuple and transition types
  • PDF pages 10–11: accept states, epsilon and nine-column table

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Why give a machine a stack?

For 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, after reading n zeros the machine owes n matching ones. A DFA has only finitely many states, so it cannot keep a different state for every possible debt. A PDA adds a stack: a potentially unbounded pile where we can touch only the top. Push one marker per zero; pop one per one. Now the size of the debt is stored outside the finite control.

The state remembers the phase—still reading zeros, or already matching ones. The stack remembers the amount owed. Mixing those jobs makes diagrams feel random. Separating them makes the arrows follow from the requirement.

Think of each pushed zero as an IOU: “a future 1 must pay for this.” The $ marker says there are no more IOUs underneath. The control state says whether issuing new IOUs is still allowed. Once payment starts, a new zero isn't “more of the same”; it violates the required block order. That's why we need both the stack and the phase state.

Each zero hands the machine an IOU: “you owe me one matching one later.” The stack keeps the unpaid IOUs. The state remembers whether we are still collecting zeros or already paying with ones. Both jobs matter. A balanced total cannot rescue input whose zeros and ones arrived in the wrong order.

Round 1 — State remembers the phase; stack remembers the debt · pages 1–3

For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, every zero creates an obligation: a matching one must arrive later. Push one marker for each zero; pop one for each one. The finite state records whether we are still reading zeros or have switched to ones. Both pieces matter. Counts alone would wrongly allow 0101, and phase alone cannot remember an arbitrarily large count.

A stack allows access only at its top: last in, first out. A cafeteria plate pile captures this access rule. It does not mean the stack is physically finite in the mathematical model; its alphabet is finite, but the number of stored symbols has no fixed bound. Push adds a top symbol; pop removes the top symbol; replacing means pop then push. The model cannot reach into the middle and remove whichever marker is convenient.

Round 2 — Read every field of an arrow · pages 4–9

An arrow a,b→c means consume input a, pop stack symbol b, push c, and move to the arrow's destination state. ε in the input field means consume no input. ε in the pop field means do not inspect or remove the top. ε in the push field means add nothing. These are three independent fields. In particular, ε in the pop field is not an empty-stack test.

0,ε→0 reads a zero and pushes a zero. 1,0→ε reads a one and removes a matching zero. ε,ε→$ installs a bottom marker without input. ε,$→ε removes that marker when it is exposed. $ is a stack symbol, not an input character. It makes “all unmatched zeros are gone” visible through the top-only interface.

Use a configuration record (state, unread input, stack) with top written leftmost. For 0011:

(q₁, 0011, ε)
(q₂, 0011, $)        install bottom marker
(q₂, 011, 0$)        read first zero
(q₂, 11, 00$)        read second zero
(q₃, 1, 0$)          read first one, switch phase
(q₃, ε, $)           read second one
(q₄, ε, ε)           remove marker, accept

For 00011, one zero marker remains after input ends, so the marker-removal move is unavailable and q₄ cannot be reached. For 00111, matching the two zeros leaves one unread one; reaching q₄ early does not accept the whole input. For ε, q₁ itself accepts. That explains F={q₁,q₄}, including why there can be two accepting states.

Round 3 — The huge type is only a three-field lookup · pages 8–11

The PDA tuple adds Γ, the stack alphabet, to the finite-state fields. Its transition type is

δ:Q×Σε×Γε→P(Q×Γε).\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\Gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q\times\Gamma_\varepsilon).δ:Q×Σε​×Γε​→P(Q×Γε​).

Input: current state, next-input choice, pop requirement. Output: a set of (next state, symbol to push) options. The power set permits multiple options or none. Destination entries are pairs because the transition must specify both movement and stack output.

Here Σₑ={0,1,ε} and Γₑ={0,$,ε}. Three input choices times three pop choices gives nine columns per row. That's why the formal table looks wider than an NFA table. Empty cells mean no option. A table of all nonempty transitions plus “all others ∅” can be a complete specification, provided every displayed entry has the correct pair/set format.

The slide sometimes writes stack contents with braces. Read those as ordered stack displays, not mathematical sets: [0,0,$] has two zero markers, and their multiplicity matters. Using a string such as 00$ avoids that notation trap.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the deck's counted-block machine

Use $ as a fresh bottom marker. It is a stack symbol, not an input symbol. Push it before processing a nonempty candidate. During the zero phase, each input 0 pushes a 0. The first 1 changes to the matching phase and pops a 0. Further ones keep popping. When the top becomes $, an ε move can remove it and enter accept.

There are no input-consuming transitions for 0 after the matching phase begins: that enforces block order. There is no matching 1 transition when only $ remains: that prevents too many ones. The original start is accepting to include ε when n=0.

Trace 0011, writing the stack top first:

Work completed Stack Meaning
initialize $ no zeros owed yet
read first 0 0$ owe one 1
read second 0 00$ owe two
read first 1 0$ owe one
read second 1 $ debt paid
finish by ε move empty enter accept with input consumed

001 leaves an unpaid marker. 00111 has an extra input symbol after the markers run out. 0101 tries to return to the zero phase. All reject, for different clauses of the language.

Read an arrow without guessing

A label a, b → c says: consume input symbol a, pop stack-top b, push c. ε in the input position consumes nothing. ε in the pop position means do not pop, not “test that the stack is empty.” ε in the push position means push nothing.

So 0, ε → 0 reads a zero and adds a marker without removing the old top. 1, 0 → ε reads a one and removes a zero marker. ε, $ → ε tests for and removes the actual bottom marker without reading input.

The formal symbols describe those three jobs

A PDA is (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,F)(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,F)(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0​,F). Q, Σ, q₀, F still mean states, input alphabet, start, accepting states. Γ is the stack alphabet. The transition type

δ:Q×Σε×Γε→P(Q×Γε)\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\Gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q\times\Gamma_\varepsilon)δ:Q×Σε​×Γε​→P(Q×Γε​)

takes a state, an input choice, and a pop choice; returns a set of (next state, push choice) pairs. The power set P\mathcal PP allows zero, one, or several alternatives. It is not an unordered representation of the stack—the stack itself remains ordered.

Acceptance requires some run to consume all input and finish in an accepting state. General final-state acceptance does not also require an empty stack; this construction uses $ to enforce the intended balance before accepting.

Keep: state = phase; stack = ordered pending obligations. Next we use nondeterminism when the input does not tell us which obligation to check or where the midpoint lies.

One connected check: For 001, which obligation is still on the stack, and why does entering an accepting state early not magically consume it or the remaining input?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

Now stress the design where it can break: empty input, wrong order, leftover obligations, and a branch that guesses at the wrong time. A diagram needs a reason for every accepted case.

The recurring exam move is: give you an unfamiliar count condition, restrict the states or alphabet, and ask you to turn it into a machine. Memorizing “push zeros, pop ones” won't cover all those variations. The useful habit is to translate the condition into units of stack work.

Weighted counts: a complete derivation

2022 Problem 2 uses 0ᵐ1ⁿ with 0.5n≤m≤1.5n, for nonnegative integer m,n. Multiply the condition by 2: n≤2m≤3n. This suggests pushing two markers per zero, then popping 1,2,or3 markers for each one. Successful emptying means the total number popped is exactly 2m.

But why can every total in that interval be achieved? Write t=2m. If n≤t≤2n, choose t−n twos and 2n−t ones. These counts are nonnegative, sum to n, and sum in value to t. If 2n≤t≤3n, choose t−2n threes and 3n−t twos; again n choices with total t. This proves the “if the inequality holds, a successful set of choices exists” direction. The other direction follows since n numbers each between 1 and 3 sum to a value between n and 3n. For n=0, the inequality forces m=0 and the empty sum works.

A seven-state PDA plan

Use states s,p,h,r,u,v,f, input {0,1}, stack {X,$}, accept f. Here X corresponds to the exam's working stack symbol 0; if copying the exact problem, use its required symbol 0.

s — ε,ε→$ → p
p — 0,ε→X → h
h — ε,ε→X → p
p — ε,ε→ε → r
r — 1,X→ε → r       pop one
r — 1,X→ε → u       begin pop two or three
u — ε,X→ε → r       finish pop two
u — ε,X→ε → v       begin pop three
v — ε,X→ε → r       finish pop three
r — ε,$→ε → f

The p→h→p cycle pushes twice per zero. The r choices consume exactly one 1 while popping one, two or three X's. The phase switch forbids zeros after the first one. The final marker check forces exact total balance. ε is accepted. This is the promised construction plus its reason, not merely a diagram that happens to accept one example.

For 001, four markers were pushed but one 1 can pop at most three, so all branches fail to finish. For 011, two markers were pushed; choosing one pop for each 1 empties them and accepts. A requested simulation tree must still show the losing branches.

State limits: store the right thing in the right place

The 2021 paper asks for a PDA with at most two states recognizing binary strings whose number of ones is divisible by six. A six-state DFA would remember the remainder in its state. A PDA can instead store a remainder symbol 1,…,5 on the stack, keeping remainder 0 as empty stack in an accepting control state. It doesn't need an unbounded counter for this problem; its stack alphabet is an alternate finite storage location.

This illustrates a design choice, not a universal shortcut. If the exam restricts Γ, you cannot invent extra symbols to beat the state limit. Write a small table of configuration meanings (control state plus stack top) before drawing arrows.

A minimality proof for a one-state PDA

In the 2020 language B={0ᵐ1ⁿ | m≥n≥0}, ε must accept. A one-state final-state PDA therefore has its only state accepting. It also must accept 01 by some run starting with an empty stack. That same run can be replayed on another 01, leaving any old stack content underneath: it never needs to pop below the level where its own first run began, and ε in a pop field does not test emptiness. The control state is still the same. Thus it accepts 0101, which violates block order. Contradiction.

The model assumptions matter: this is final-state acceptance and the course's no-pop ε convention. Do not transplant the proof unexamined to a model with empty-stack tests or a different acceptance rule.

Fresh practice

Design the stack accounting for 0ᵐ1ⁿ satisfying n≤3m≤2n. Give a phase plan and prove why every permitted count pair can be handled.

Show the design and existence proof

Push three X's per zero, using a three-step chain that consumes one 0. In the one phase, choose to pop one or two X's per consumed 1. Accept by bottom-marker removal. Every successful run has n≤3m≤2n. Conversely, take 3m−n twos and 2n−3m ones. Both counts are nonnegative, they total n, and their weighted sum is 3m. Choose those pop paths to accept. The empty case m=n=0 is covered. Use intermediate states for extra ε pushes/pops and enforce the zero-then-one phase order.

lessons.title: Program a Turing machine on paper
lessons.description: Tape, head, phases, configurations, correctness and halting.
lessons.html:
First, build the mental model

Turing machines: a finite program with a rewritable workspace · chap3_TM1.pdf, pages 1–8

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: memory access and immediate halting
  • PDF pages 3–4: same-order copy comparison
  • PDF pages 5–6: seven-tuple, alphabets and transition action
  • PDF pages 7–8: initial tape and left boundary

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

What changes when the stack isn't enough?

A PDA can only inspect the top of its stack. A Turing machine, or TM, has a tape and a head that moves left or right. It can read a cell, overwrite it, move, and come back later. The finite state still stores the current phase of the program; the tape stores the growing work.

The tape has no fixed upper bound on usable cells. That does not mean infinitely many cells are processed in one move. At every finite point in a computation, only finitely much work has happened. “Unbounded workspace” and “infinite work for free” are completely different claims.

Now the machine gets a writable notebook. It can mark something, walk away, and come back to read the mark. That is a huge change from a stack that only exposes its top. But there is no teleporting: the head still moves cell by cell, and every mark needs a stated meaning.

Round 1 — The tape is a workspace you can revisit · pages 1–2

Finite automata retain a bounded state summary. A PDA adds an unbounded stack but only exposes its top. A Turing machine adds a tape whose cells can be read, overwritten and revisited by moving left or right. That's the new power: the machine can leave marks and come back to them later.

“Unrestricted memory” on the slide concerns access compared with a stack. A TM still has strict local mechanics: one head reads one cell, one transition writes one symbol and moves one cell. It cannot teleport to an arbitrary address or inspect infinitely many cells at once. The tape is unbounded in the model; each finite computation visits only finitely many cells.

Unlike DFA/PDA acceptance after the full input has been processed, entering q_accept or q_reject halts a TM immediately. A correctly designed TM must inspect what the language requires before choosing either state. The model does not force it to scan every original input cell first.

Round 2 — Same order is why this job needs revisiting · pages 3–4

The language {w#w:w∈{0,1}*} asks for two identical strings in the same order. For w=01, the accepted input is 01#01, not 01#10. A simple push-first-half/pop-second-half strategy naturally compares reverse order, which is the wrong job here.

The TM marks the next unmatched symbol on the left, remembers whether it was 0 or 1 in its finite state, crosses #, finds the next unmatched symbol on the right, compares and marks it, then returns left. Each round matches the corresponding position. Marks x mean “already handled,” not an extra input symbol supplied by the user.

Before accepting, check exactly one separator, legal input symbols, no unmatched left symbols and no extra unmatched right symbols. # accepts because w=ε is permitted. 0# and #0 reject because lengths differ. 01#00 rejects at the second comparison. These cases explain why merely finding one matching pair is insufficient.

Round 3 — Every field of the formal machine · pages 5–8

The seven-tuple is (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,q_accept,q_reject). Γ is the tape alphabet, containing the input alphabet Σ plus blank and any work markers. Blank ⊔ is not an input symbol; it fills cells beyond the input. There is one designated accepting state and a distinct rejecting state.

δ(q,a)=(r,b,L)\delta(q,a)=(r,b,L)δ(q,a)=(r,b,L)

means: while in state q scanning tape symbol a, overwrite that cell with b, enter state r, and move the head left. The output is a triple. L and R are directions, not symbols written on the tape. The state is held by the control; it is not itself a tape character.

Initially w₁…wₙ occupies cells 1 through n; all later cells are blank; the head scans cell 1. For ε, cell 1 is already blank. This course uses a left-bounded tape: attempting to move left from cell 1 leaves the head there. That boundary convention matters when replacing stay-put moves later.

The displayed transition type includes Q broadly, but accepting/rejecting states have no further executed transitions because halting takes immediate effect. Many formal definitions write the domain with those halting states removed. Both descriptions encode the same intended mechanics when the halting convention is stated.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

One transition does three specific things

δ(q,a)=(r,b,R)\delta(q,a)=(r,b,R)δ(q,a)=(r,b,R) means: in state q reading tape symbol a, write b in this cell, move the head one cell right, and enter r. With L, move left instead. At the tape's left boundary, the course model keeps the head there when it attempts to move farther left.

A blank is an actual tape symbol. ε is a zero-length string or no-consumption notation in other models. A blank cell is not “no cell,” and writing a blank is a real write operation. Tape symbols may include marks such as x that never appear in the original input alphabet.

Build the slide's matching idea: w#w

The separator # tells us where the first copy ends. On input 01#01, mark the first unprocessed left symbol, remember whether it was 0 or 1 in the finite control, cross the separator, and compare it with the first unprocessed right symbol. Mark that symbol too. Return to the left portion and repeat.

After the first round, marks stand where the two zeros were. After the second, both ones are marked too. Finally verify that no extra unmatched symbol remains on the right. Accept only then.

For 01#00, the second comparison fails. For 01#010, the first two comparisons succeed but the final leftover check fails. For malformed input with a missing or extra separator, the machine must reject through its format checks. Matching the examples isn't enough; each clause of the language needs a reason in the program.

What belongs in the seven-part definition?

(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,qaccept,qreject)(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,q_{accept},q_{reject})(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0​,qaccept​,qreject​): states; input alphabet; tape alphabet; transition rule; start; accepting halt state; rejecting halt state. Γ includes the blank and all input symbols. Σ excludes the blank. The accepting and rejecting states are distinct and halt immediately when entered.

This differs from a finite automaton or PDA: visiting their accepting state does not necessarily end the run, and acceptance is evaluated after the input is consumed. A TM's program must arrange its checks before entering accept.

The proof has two separate jobs

Correctness says successful comparisons and the final leftover check establish exactly two equal blocks. Halting says the procedure finishes: each round marks another left input symbol; each sweep crosses a finite occupied region; there are only finitely many unmarked left symbols. A convincing trace of 01#01 proves neither claim for every input, but it makes the invariant visible.

Keep: state = program phase; tape = editable memory; head = current location. Next we use repeated marking to test a numerical pattern in the input length.

One connected check: Why must the w#w machine check for extra right-side symbols after all left-side symbols have been matched?

Now use that model in the worked lesson below. For a missing link, open the whole-course map.

The tape is a workspace we can mark and revisit. Describe the tape encoding and phase first; otherwise a long arrow trace is just a list of unexplained movements.

A Turing machine has a tape it can read and write, plus a head that moves. Unlike a stack, you can revisit earlier positions. This lets the machine use marks, repeated scans, and work areas. The exam often gives a plan and asks you to compile it into a precise diagram.

Decode one transition

δ(q,a)=(r,b,R)\delta(q,a)=(r,b,R)δ(q,a)=(r,b,R) means: in state q, reading tape symbol a, write b in that cell, move right, and enter r. a→b,R is the diagram label. a→R is shorthand for a→a,R: keep the symbol, move right.

There is no input-consuming versus ε move distinction like in an NFA. Every step reads the cell under the head, even when that cell is blank. The blank symbol ⊔ is a real tape symbol. It is not ε.

The seven-part definition is (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q₀,q_accept,q_reject). Σ is the input alphabet; Γ is the tape alphabet and contains the blank and any marks. Standard course definitions exclude blank from Σ. Historical problems can use their own explicit notation; identify any special convention in the question rather than silently changing it.

Entering q_accept or q_reject halts immediately. This differs from a DFA's final-state-at-end rule. The TM must itself perform all needed checks before accepting. A state reached too early does not wait around to read the rest.

Read a configuration

A configuration records current state, tape, and head position. In u q v, the state symbol q is inserted immediately before the cell being scanned, which is the first symbol of v. q is not written on the tape.

Suppose δ(q₀,0)=(q₁,x,R). Then

q₀ 01#01  ⇒  x q₁ 1#01

The old 0 became x; the head now scans 1. If δ(q₁,1)=(q₂,1,L), then

x q₁ 1#01  ⇒  q₂ x1#01

The tape is x1#01 and q₂ scans x. Keep a blank explicitly when the head scans beyond the written input. At the tape's left boundary, the course model keeps the head there if instructed to move left.

A complete toy machine

Task: replace every 0 in a binary input by 1 and halt at the first blank. One working state q does it:

State/read Write Move Next
q / 0 1 R q
q / 1 1 R q
q / ⊔ ⊔ R accept

On 01: q01⊔⇒1q1⊔⇒11q⊔⇒11⊔q_accept⊔. Every step is accounted for, including the halting step. On ε the first cell is blank, so it halts immediately. This isn't a difficult language; it teaches the mechanics needed for a long exam construction.

Build a serious TM from phases

For the slide language {w#w∣w∈{0,1}∗}\{w\#w\mid w\in\{0,1\}^*\}{w#w∣w∈{0,1}∗}:

  1. Select the next unmarked left symbol; mark it x. The state remembers whether it was 0 or 1.
  2. Scan past # to the first unmarked right symbol; compare it and mark it x.
  3. Return across the right block to #, then through the left block until the correct left marker boundary.
  4. Repeat. When no left symbols remain, check that the right side contains only marks, then accept.

Do not merge two return phases if the same read symbol needs different actions. The course's TM 3 page 10 explains why x means “keep moving left” in one phase but “turn around” in another. A state means what job am I currently doing?, including what information must survive the scan.

Proof obligations for a decider

Invariant: after k completed rounds, the first k symbols on each side were equal and are marked; unmarked suffixes are untouched. Correctness: a mismatch rejects; finishing both sides establishes equality; any equal pair can complete all rounds. Halting: each successful round marks another left symbol; finite scans reach a marker or blank; hence only finitely many rounds occur. Do not forget malformed inputs when the problem requires checking them.

A recognizer accepts members but may reject or loop on nonmembers. A decider halts on every input. A correct-looking acceptance trace alone proves neither total correctness nor termination.

Fresh practice

For δ(q,a)=(r,b,L), compute the next configuration from 01 q a10. Identify the old scanned cell, the rewritten cell, and the new scanned cell.

Show the answer

The old scanned cell is a. Write b there, then move left onto the preceding 1. The next configuration is 0 r 1b10. The tape is 01b10; r appears before the new scanned 1. The state symbol is not part of the tape.
