models.title: NFA 2 — A transition returns a collection of options

sections.concepts: power set, full transition types and empty entries
formal accepting path with epsilon factors

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: unary alphabet, cycles and divisibility
  • PDF pages 4–5: epsilon example and branching
  • PDF pages 6–9: power set, full transition types and empty entries
  • PDF page 10: formal accepting path with epsilon factors

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The whole idea

We need a precise way to write “zero, one, or several possible next states.” The output of an NFA transition is a set. The function still gives one answer for each request; that answer is the entire option set. This repairs the informal “δ isn't a function anymore” wording in NFA1.

A move can hand back no destination, one destination, or several. So we need a container that handles all three cases: a set. The braces are doing a real job. The empty set means the container has no destinations; ε means a move consumes no input. Those two are not interchangeable.

Round 1 — Counting by walking around a cycle · pages 1–3

A unary alphabet has exactly one symbol. With Σ={0}, the only way strings differ is their length. A two-state cycle returns to its accepting starting point after 0,2,4,… zeros. A three-state cycle does so after 0,3,6,… zeros. An ε branch chooses either cycle without consuming a zero, so their union accepts lengths divisible by 2 or 3.

Here 0ᵏ means k copies of symbol 0, not the arithmetic number zero raised to a power. k=0 gives ε. Zero is divisible by 2 and 3, so the initial ε-accessible cycle starts must account for empty input. A branch accepting does not require the other branch to accept too.

Round 2 — The braces are the type of the answer · pages 4–9

Take the three-state a/b example. Its direct moves are: q₁ on b→q₂ and on ε→q₃; q₂ on a→q₂ or q₃ and on b→q₃; q₃ on a→q₁. All other direct moves are absent. q₁ is both start and accepting. Therefore ε accepts immediately, and a accepts by q₁→εq₃→aq₁. baba has an accepting route; babba does not.

Now the formal function:

δ:Q×Σε→P(Q),Σε=Σ∪{ε}.\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q),\qquad\Sigma_\varepsilon=\Sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}.δ:Q×Σε​→P(Q),Σε​=Σ∪{ε}.

The colon announces a function's type. × groups input fields. The arrow points from input type to output type. Σₑ adds ε as an allowed transition label, not as an ordinary character of Σ. P(Q), the power set, is the collection of every subset of Q.

If Q={q₁,q₂}, then P(Q)={∅,{q₁},{q₂},{q₁,q₂}}. There are four possible destination sets because each of two states is either included or excluded: 2×2=2². With n states, the count is 2ⁿ. Each transition returns exactly one of these sets. That set can contain zero, one or several states.

Why is q₂ instead of {q₂} wrong in an NFA table? Because the required output is a collection. q₂ is one state; {q₂} is the singleton collection containing it. A single address and a one-item mailing list have different formats. This distinction concerns transition outputs, not the number of accepting states. Both DFA and NFA may have many accepting states.

An empty table entry should mean ∅, not an unnamed new state. When no path survives, the possible-state set is ∅. Unioning ∅ with {q₂} returns {q₂}: the empty collection contributes no destination. Do not insert ∅ as if it were a member alongside q₂.

Round 3 — Why the formal run may have more steps than input symbols · page 10

An input can be written w=y₁…yₘ with each yᵢ either an input symbol or ε. For input a, a valid factorization is ε·a. It still spells a; ε contributes length zero. That lets the state sequence record ε moves too.

The rule rᵢ₊₁∈δ(rᵢ,yᵢ₊₁) says the next state must be one member of the offered destination set. It replaces the DFA's equality with membership. Start at q₀, make legal moves spelling the entire input, and finish in F. Existence of one such finite path establishes acceptance. A branch stuck early establishes failure of that branch, not necessarily rejection of the entire NFA.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the types before reading the formula

For a DFA, asking “from q on 1?” returns one state, say r. For an NFA it may return {r,s}, {r}, or ∅. Braces say “a set containing these states.” ∅ says “there are no options.” The accepting set F is a separate object listing states where a fully consumed run may finish.

The power set 𝒫(Q) is the collection of all subsets of Q. If Q={a,b}, its possible output sets are ∅, {a}, {b}, {a,b}. Each state has an in/out choice, hence 2×2=4 subsets. With three states there are 2³=8. The power set is where the function's answers live; it is not a new kind of accepting state.

Σ names actual input symbols. Σε means Σ∪{ε}, allowing the table to ask about a no-input move as well. Thus δ:Q×Σε→𝒫(Q) reads: state plus a symbol-or-ε request goes in; a set of possible destinations comes out.

Work the slide's actual table

Pages 8–9 have four states. From q₁ on 1 the answer is {q₁,q₂}. From q₂ on ε it is {q₃}. From q₃ on 1 it is {q₄}, and q₄ accepts.

Trace 11. Start {q₁}. The first 1 reaches q₁ and q₂; the free q₂→q₃ move adds q₃. Current possibilities are {q₁,q₂,q₃}. On the second 1, q₁ contributes {q₁,q₂}; q₂ contributes ∅; q₃ contributes {q₄}. Combine those destinations, then close under ε: {q₁,q₂,q₃,q₄}. Accept because q₄ is possible after the whole string.

Notice the empty contribution from q₂. Union with ∅ adds nothing. We do not insert an object called ∅ into the set of NFA states. “No candidate from this branch” is different from “a candidate at a state named empty set.” The latter becomes a useful name only in the converted DFA.

Why the formal run can be longer than the string

Page 10 allows w=y₁…yₘ with each yᵢ either a real symbol or ε. For input 11, one accepting path can be labeled 1,ε,1. Concatenating those labels still gives 11: the ε contributes zero characters. The state sequence has a step for every move, so m need not equal the number of input characters.

The condition rᵢ₊₁∈δ(rᵢ,yᵢ₊₁) says the chosen next state must be one of the legal options. A run chooses one option each time; the acceptance definition asks whether any suitable run exists.

Next connection: NFA3 makes the whole current option set into one DFA state. Connected check: distinguish δ(q₁,1)={q₁,q₂} from F={q₄}: what question does each set answer?

nfa 2 — a transition returns a collection of options chap1_nfa2.pdf # nfa 2 — a transition returns a collection of options

## the whole idea

we need a precise way to write “zero, one, or several possible next states.” **the output of an nfa transition is a set.** the function still gives one answer for each request; that answer is the entire option set. this repairs the informal “δ isn't a function anymore” wording in nfa1.

a move can hand back no destination, one destination, or several. so we need a container that handles all three cases: a set. the braces are doing a real job. the empty set means the container has no destinations; ε means a move consumes no input. those two are not interchangeable.

## round 1 — counting by walking around a cycle · pages 1–3

a **unary alphabet** has exactly one symbol. with σ={0}, the only way strings differ is their length. a two-state cycle returns to its accepting starting point after 0,2,4,… zeros. a three-state cycle does so after 0,3,6,… zeros. an ε branch chooses either cycle without consuming a zero, so their union accepts lengths divisible by 2 or 3.

here 0ᵏ means k copies of symbol 0, not the arithmetic number zero raised to a power. k=0 gives ε. zero is divisible by 2 and 3, so the initial ε-accessible cycle starts must account for empty input. a branch accepting does not require the other branch to accept too.

## round 2 — the braces are the type of the answer · pages 4–9

take the three-state a/b example. its direct moves are: q₁ on b→q₂ and on ε→q₃; q₂ on a→q₂ or q₃ and on b→q₃; q₃ on a→q₁. all other direct moves are absent. q₁ is both start and accepting. therefore ε accepts immediately, and `a` accepts by q₁→εq₃→aq₁. `baba` has an accepting route; `babba` does not.

now the formal function:

\[\delta:q\times\sigma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal p(q),\qquad\sigma_\varepsilon=\sigma\cup\{\varepsilon\}.\]

the colon announces a function's type. × groups input fields. the arrow points from input type to output type. σₑ adds ε as an allowed transition label, not as an ordinary character of σ. p(q), the **power set**, is the collection of every subset of q.

if q={q₁,q₂}, then p(q)={∅,{q₁},{q₂},{q₁,q₂}}. there are four possible destination sets because each of two states is either included or excluded: 2×2=2². with n states, the count is 2ⁿ. each transition returns exactly one of these sets. that set can contain zero, one or several states.

why is q₂ instead of {q₂} wrong in an nfa table? because the required output is a collection. q₂ is one state; {q₂} is the singleton collection containing it. a single address and a one-item mailing list have different formats. this distinction concerns transition outputs, not the number of accepting states. both dfa and nfa may have many accepting states.

an empty table entry should mean ∅, not an unnamed new state. when no path survives, the possible-state set is ∅. unioning ∅ with {q₂} returns {q₂}: the empty collection contributes no destination. do not insert ∅ as if it were a member alongside q₂.

## round 3 — why the formal run may have more steps than input symbols · page 10

an input can be written w=y₁…yₘ with each yᵢ either an input symbol or ε. for input `a`, a valid factorization is ε·a. it still spells `a`; ε contributes length zero. that lets the state sequence record ε moves too.

the rule rᵢ₊₁∈δ(rᵢ,yᵢ₊₁) says the next state must be **one member** of the offered destination set. it replaces the dfa's equality with membership. start at q₀, make legal moves spelling the entire input, and finish in f. existence of one such finite path establishes acceptance. a branch stuck early establishes failure of that branch, not necessarily rejection of the entire nfa.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## build the types before reading the formula

for a dfa, asking “from q on 1?” returns one state, say r. for an nfa it may return {r,s}, {r}, or ∅. braces say “a set containing these states.” ∅ says “there are no options.” the accepting set f is a separate object listing states where a fully consumed run may finish.

the **power set** 𝒫(q) is the collection of all subsets of q. if q={a,b}, its possible output sets are ∅, {a}, {b}, {a,b}. each state has an in/out choice, hence 2×2=4 subsets. with three states there are 2³=8. the power set is where the function's answers live; it is not a new kind of accepting state.

σ names actual input symbols. σε means σ∪{ε}, allowing the table to ask about a no-input move as well. thus δ:q×σε→𝒫(q) reads: **state plus a symbol-or-ε request goes in; a set of possible destinations comes out**.

## work the slide's actual table

pages 8–9 have four states. from q₁ on 1 the answer is {q₁,q₂}. from q₂ on ε it is {q₃}. from q₃ on 1 it is {q₄}, and q₄ accepts.

trace `11`. start {q₁}. the first 1 reaches q₁ and q₂; the free q₂→q₃ move adds q₃. current possibilities are {q₁,q₂,q₃}. on the second 1, q₁ contributes {q₁,q₂}; q₂ contributes ∅; q₃ contributes {q₄}. combine those destinations, then close under ε: {q₁,q₂,q₃,q₄}. accept because q₄ is possible after the whole string.

notice the empty contribution from q₂. union with ∅ adds nothing. we do **not** insert an object called ∅ into the set of nfa states. “no candidate from this branch” is different from “a candidate at a state named empty set.” the latter becomes a useful name only in the converted dfa.

## why the formal run can be longer than the string

page 10 allows w=y₁…yₘ with each yᵢ either a real symbol or ε. for input `11`, one accepting path can be labeled 1,ε,1. concatenating those labels still gives `11`: the ε contributes zero characters. the state sequence has a step for every move, so m need not equal the number of input characters.

the condition rᵢ₊₁∈δ(rᵢ,yᵢ₊₁) says the chosen next state must be one of the legal options. a run chooses one option each time; the acceptance definition asks whether any suitable run exists.

**next connection:** nfa3 makes the whole current option set into one dfa state. **connected check:** distinguish δ(q₁,1)={q₁,q₂} from f={q₄}: what question does each set answer?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: equivalent languages and DFA embedding
  • PDF pages 3–10: all eight subsets, reachable sets and example trace
  • PDF pages 11–13: formal subset construction, closure and invariant

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The whole idea

The NFA branches, but its set of states is finite. So we can ask a deterministic machine to keep a checklist: which NFA states are still possible after the input read so far? Every possible checklist gets one DFA state. That is subset construction. The braces label the contents of one memory record; they do not turn the new DFA into a branching machine.

Here's the mental switch: the DFA is the clerk holding the whole checklist, not one of the candidates on it. {q₁,q₂} is one clerk's current record. Reading a symbol deterministically produces the next record. That's why a circle with braces can still be one ordinary DFA state.

The NFA has several possible bookmarks; the DFA is one clerk holding the entire bookmark list. Hold up: one list can contain several names while still being one list. That is why {q₁,q₃} names one DFA state. The clerk updates the whole list after each symbol. No guessing remains in that update.

Round 1 — One clerk holds the entire bookmark list · pages 1–4

The NFA may have many possible current states. The DFA simulation stores their complete set as one summary. Think of one clerk holding a checklist of surviving bookmarks. The clerk itself has one current checklist, not several simultaneous DFA states. That is why a DFA circle may be labeled {q₁,q₃} without becoming an NFA.

For three original states there are eight possible lists: ∅, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}. The slide abbreviates q₁ as 1 inside set labels; no numeric computation is intended. Some lists never occur. The full power-set construction includes them before optional reachability cleanup.

The easy conversion DFA→NFA keeps the states and wraps each destination in braces: δₙ(q,a)={δᴅ(q,a)}. Set every ε entry to ∅. The difficult direction is NFA→DFA, because the DFA must summarize all alternatives. “Equivalent” means same accepted language; it does not mean same number of states or same diagram.

Round 2 — Do the three-state example without skipping ε · pages 5–10

Use the previous deck's direct moves. Its start ε-closure is {1,3}, since q₁ can reach q₃ without input. From {1,3} on b, only q₁ has a b move, reaching q₂. q₂ has no ε move, so the next set is {2}. On a, q₂ reaches q₂ and q₃, giving {2,3}. On the next a, q₂ contributes {2,3} and q₃ contributes {1}; ε from q₁ additionally reaches q₃, already included. Final set {1,2,3} accepts because it contains the original accepting q₁. This traces the slide's baa.

The complete update table, including initially unreachable subsets, is:

DFA summary a b
∅ ∅ ∅
{1} ∅ {2}
{2} {2,3} {3}
{3} {1,3} ∅
{1,2} {2,3} {2,3}
{1,3} {1,3} {2}
{2,3} {1,2,3} {3}
{1,2,3} {1,2,3} {2,3}

From start {1,3}, the reachable lists are {1,3}, {2}, {3}, {2,3}, {1,2,3}, and ∅. For example, bb reaches {3} and bbb reaches ∅. Removing unreachable states preserves the accepted language because no input run ever visits them. If an exam requests the full prescribed construction first, show it before simplifying.

Round 3 — Unpack the monster-looking union · pages 11–13

δ′(R,a)=⋃r∈RE(δ(r,a)).\delta'(R,a)=\bigcup_{r\in R}E(\delta(r,a)).δ′(R,a)=r∈R⋃​E(δ(r,a)).

R is the current checklist; r is one original NFA state on it; a is the next input symbol. δ(r,a) collects that state's direct a-destinations. E adds all ε-reachable states, including the destinations themselves. The big union combines those collections for every r in R. The prime on δ′ distinguishes the new DFA's function from the original NFA's δ.

The start is E({q₀}). Accepting summaries satisfy R∩F≠∅: the intersection with the old accepting-state set is nonempty. Intersection means members present in both sets. This is exactly “at least one surviving accepting possibility.”

Why it works: initially the checklist contains precisely the NFA's no-input possibilities. If it is correct before a symbol, following every matching move and then all ε moves produces precisely the possibilities afterward. Induction carries that claim through the whole input. The final intersection test then agrees with NFA acceptance. The invariant is the proof; the table is one instance of the construction.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the update rule

Suppose the current checklist is R and the next input symbol is a. Look at every state r in R, follow its a-arrows, collect the destinations, then include every state reachable from those destinations by ε moves. That creates one uniquely determined next checklist.

The start checklist is E({q₀}), where E means ε-closure: include q₀ and all states reachable by zero or more ε-arrows. A checklist accepts when it contains at least one NFA accepting state. Nothing more complicated is hidden in the formula R∩F≠∅: intersection keeps members shared by R and F; “not empty” says at least one accepting possibility survives.

Trace the exact slide example

The three-state NFA on page 3 starts at q₁, which has an ε move to q₃; q₁ is accepting. Therefore the converted start is {q₁,q₃}, already accepting because ε has an accepting run at q₁.

Pages 10–11 give baa:

before input       {q₁,q₃}
after b            {q₂}
after ba           {q₂,q₃}
after baa          {q₁,q₂,q₃}

The final set contains q₁, so accept. To see one union explicitly, page 6 starts with {q₁,q₂} and reads a: q₁ contributes no destination; q₂ contributes q₂ and q₃. The result is {q₂,q₃}. ∅∪{q₂,q₃}={q₂,q₃}. An empty contribution doesn't create an extra candidate.

What the empty DFA state means

If the checklist becomes ∅, every NFA candidate has died. Another symbol cannot restart a nonexistent run. Thus ∅→∅ on every symbol in the DFA. This is a real state whose remembered fact is “no candidates remain.” In the old NFA, a missing arrow meant a branch died. Same behavior, different representation.

With three original states there are eight possible subsets. The textbook construction includes all of them; some are unreachable from the start. Here any subset containing q₁ but omitting q₃ is unreachable because closure would immediately include q₃. Remove unreachable states only after satisfying any exam requirement to display the complete prescribed construction.

Why the proof works for every input

At zero symbols, closure records exactly the possible starts. Assume the checklist is exact after a prefix. Every legal next run must consume the next symbol from one of those states, followed by any ε moves; the update lists exactly those possibilities. No legal run is omitted and no impossible run is invented. Induction gives the exact checklist after every prefix. The final “contains an accepting state” test then agrees with NFA acceptance.

In the formula δ′(R,a)=⋃ᵣ∈ᴿ E(δ(r,a)), the prime marks the new transition function and ⋃ means collect the members from all the listed sets. It is the table procedure written compactly.

Connected check: explain why starting at {q₁} would already be wrong in this example before processing the first symbol. Then say which start-state property the proof would lose.

models.title: NFA 4 — Use free handoffs to assemble whole-language machines
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–7: union construction and piecewise cases
  • PDF pages 8–11: concatenation handoff and retained moves
  • PDF pages 12–16: star, fresh start and correctness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The whole idea

Union, concatenation and star are instructions about whole accepted pieces. We want machine wiring that respects those instructions. ε-arrows let us hand control from one component to another without secretly adding an extra character. That is their job here. They are not decorative buffers.

You have two working checkers. Now we need plumbing that joins their jobs without secretly eating a symbol or restarting the input. ε is the free handoff: change where the checking continues, keep the unread input where it is. The tricky shit is deciding which handoffs are legal and when.

Round 1 — ε hands off control without stealing a character · pages 1–7

For union, imagine a reception desk with two doors to two departments. The desk chooses which checker to enter; it does not consume part of the customer's document. That is why the fresh start has ε arrows to both original starts and no 0/1 arrows of its own. If the alphabet is a/b, the same reasoning applies. The dispatch mechanism is independent of the input symbols.

Before joining machines, rename states so their state sets are disjoint. Otherwise both could contain a q₁ and you might accidentally merge unrelated rooms. Keep all old transitions. Accept in either machine's original accepting states. A successful new path chooses one department and then follows its old checker on the entire input. Conversely, any successful old path remains available through its ε entrance. That's both directions of the union proof.

The piecewise δ definition is a dispatch table: if q belongs to Q₁ use δ₁; if q belongs to Q₂ use δ₂; at the new start on ε return {q₁,q₂}; at the new start on a real symbol return ∅. A missing last case would leave the formal function incompletely specified.

Round 2 — Concatenation must choose where the first job ends · pages 8–11

For A₁◦A₂, start in machine 1. From each of its accepting states, add an ε handoff to machine 2's start. Keep its old arrows too: a valid first piece may be short or long, so different runs may hand off at different times. Only machine 2's accepting states are final for the combined machine.

The expression Q₁\F₁ means “states in Q₁ except its accepting states.” The special F₁ case adds the new ε destination to the old ones using union; it does not overwrite the old ε moves. For real-symbol moves, retain δ₁ unchanged.

Any accepting combined path consumes some prefix x before handoff and a suffix y afterward. The first checkpoint guarantees x∈A₁; the final checkpoint guarantees y∈A₂; therefore xy∈A₁◦A₂. Conversely, if such an x/y split exists, follow its two accepting runs and the connecting ε. Empty x or y is allowed exactly when the corresponding original language contains ε.

Round 3 — Star means complete another chunk, not restart whenever · pages 12–16

Star needs zero or more complete A-chunks. Add a fresh accepting start with an ε arrow to the original start. Keep old accepting states accepting, and add ε arrows from them back to the old start. Each loop around completes one more valid chunk. Zero chunks accepts at the fresh start.

Why not simply make the old start accepting? Suppose the old machine has a 0 loop at its nonaccepting start and a 1 arrow to its accepting state, with no other arrows. Its language is 01. Relabeling the old start accepting would accept 0, although 0 cannot be assembled from complete 01 chunks. A fresh start accepts ε without blessing every nonempty path that returns to the old start. This is a teaching counterexample, separate from the unlabeled slide diagram.

The fresh start has no incoming arrows in this construction. It does not “loop to itself” merely because it accepts. Accepting is a final-state property, not an arrow. The alphabet still consists of the original real input symbols; ε is a free control move. Those three facts prevent the exact confusion that makes star diagrams look like arbitrary bullshit.

To prove correctness, divide an accepting run at each added restart arrow. Each consumed chunk belongs to A. Conversely, concatenate accepting old runs for any finite list of A-members and connect them with the ε restarts. The fresh accepting start handles the list with no chunks.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Derive the three constructions

For union, the complete input may belong to either language. Add a fresh start with ε-arrows to both old starts. Preserve both components' accepting states. One successful component is enough.

For concatenation, the input must be a valid first piece followed by a valid second piece. Add ε-arrows from each first-component accept to the second start. Keep only second-component accepts as final accepts. A candidate may guess a boundary at any successful first-piece endpoint; another candidate may keep reading in the first component. A successful run must eventually finish both obligations.

For star, the input is zero or more complete pieces from one language. Add a fresh accepting start to handle zero pieces, with an ε-arrow into the old start. From old accepting states, add ε-arrows back to the old start so another piece may begin. Keep the old accepting states accepting too: you may finish after a complete positive number of pieces.

Follow one stable example

Use A={01} throughout this example. Its NFA has S→T on 0 and T→U on 1, with S starting and U accepting. Other symbol moves are absent. For A*, add accepting start Z, Z→S on ε, and U→S on ε.

The input 0101 has a successful run:

Z --ε--> S --0--> T --1--> U --ε--> S --0--> T --1--> U

All four symbols are consumed and U accepts. The empty string accepts at Z. Input 001 fails: after its first zero the candidate is at T, which has no zero move. “Repeat pieces” does not mean you may repeat arbitrary fragments of a piece. 001 cannot be cut into complete 01 blocks.

Why the extra start matters

The slides' pages 13–14 warn against simply making the old start accepting. A different original machine might return to its start after a nonempty string that it previously rejected. Changing that state's status would newly accept the string, even if it is not a concatenation of valid old pieces.

Here is a separate counterexample, with its changed target stated explicitly: an NFA for 01 has old start S looping on 0, then S→T on 1, with T accepting. Making S accepting would accept 0. But (01)* contains no nonempty all-zero string, since every nonempty piece ends in 1. A fresh accepting start avoids that bug. It provides exactly the zero-piece option without changing the meaning of visits to old S.

Read the case definition as “whose state is this?”

The piecewise δ table preserves an old state's old moves except at the handoff points. Set union adds the new ε destination without deleting existing ε destinations. The fresh start has no ordinary input moves; its ε moves enter components. Q is the combined state set; F separately specifies where a completed input may accept. Rename overlapping component state labels first so they really are distinct states.

A correctness argument cuts an accepting run at the handoffs to recover valid pieces. In reverse, join accepting runs for valid pieces using those handoffs. That's why the construction recognizes exactly the combined language.

Next connection: regular expressions describe these same three operations as formulas. Connected check: for concatenation, explain what would go wrong if first-component accepting states remained accepting even when the second language does not contain ε.

before joining machines, rename states so their state sets are disjoint. otherwise both could contain a q₁ and you might accidentally merge unrelated rooms. keep all old transitions. accept in either machine's original accepting states. a successful new path chooses one department and then follows its old checker on the entire input. conversely, any successful old path remains available through its ε entrance. that's both directions of the union proof.

the piecewise δ definition is a dispatch table: if q belongs to q₁ use δ₁; if q belongs to q₂ use δ₂; at the new start on ε return {q₁,q₂}; at the new start on a real symbol return ∅. a missing last case would leave the formal function incompletely specified.

## round 2 — concatenation must choose where the first job ends · pages 8–11

for a₁◦a₂, start in machine 1. from each of its accepting states, add an ε handoff to machine 2's start. keep its old arrows too: a valid first piece may be short or long, so different runs may hand off at different times. only machine 2's accepting states are final for the combined machine.

the expression q₁\f₁ means “states in q₁ except its accepting states.” the special f₁ case adds the new ε destination to the old ones using union; it does not overwrite the old ε moves. for real-symbol moves, retain δ₁ unchanged.

any accepting combined path consumes some prefix x before handoff and a suffix y afterward. the first checkpoint guarantees x∈a₁; the final checkpoint guarantees y∈a₂; therefore xy∈a₁◦a₂. conversely, if such an x/y split exists, follow its two accepting runs and the connecting ε. empty x or y is allowed exactly when the corresponding original language contains ε.

## round 3 — star means complete another chunk, not restart whenever · pages 12–16

star needs zero or more complete a-chunks. add a **fresh accepting start** with an ε arrow to the original start. keep old accepting states accepting, and add ε arrows from them back to the old start. each loop around completes one more valid chunk. zero chunks accepts at the fresh start.

why not simply make the old start accepting? suppose the old machine has a 0 loop at its nonaccepting start and a 1 arrow to its accepting state, with no other arrows. its language is 0*1. relabeling the old start accepting would accept `0`, although `0` cannot be assembled from complete 0*1 chunks. a fresh start accepts ε without blessing every nonempty path that returns to the old start. this is a teaching counterexample, separate from the unlabeled slide diagram.

the fresh start has no incoming arrows in this construction. it does not “loop to itself” merely because it accepts. accepting is a final-state property, not an arrow. the alphabet still consists of the original real input symbols; ε is a free control move. those three facts prevent the exact confusion that makes star diagrams look like arbitrary bullshit.

to prove correctness, divide an accepting run at each added restart arrow. each consumed chunk belongs to a. conversely, concatenate accepting old runs for any finite list of a-members and connect them with the ε restarts. the fresh accepting start handles the list with no chunks.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## derive the three constructions

for union, the complete input may belong to either language. add a fresh start with ε-arrows to both old starts. preserve both components' accepting states. one successful component is enough.

for concatenation, the input must be a valid first piece followed by a valid second piece. add ε-arrows from each first-component accept to the second start. keep only second-component accepts as final accepts. a candidate may guess a boundary at any successful first-piece endpoint; another candidate may keep reading in the first component. a successful run must eventually finish both obligations.

for star, the input is zero or more complete pieces from one language. add a **fresh accepting start** to handle zero pieces, with an ε-arrow into the old start. from old accepting states, add ε-arrows back to the old start so another piece may begin. keep the old accepting states accepting too: you may finish after a complete positive number of pieces.

## follow one stable example

use a={01} throughout this example. its nfa has s→t on 0 and t→u on 1, with s starting and u accepting. other symbol moves are absent. for a*, add accepting start z, z→s on ε, and u→s on ε.

the input `0101` has a successful run:

```text
z --ε--> s --0--> t --1--> u --ε--> s --0--> t --1--> u
```

all four symbols are consumed and u accepts. the empty string accepts at z. input `001` fails: after its first zero the candidate is at t, which has no zero move. “repeat pieces” does not mean you may repeat arbitrary fragments of a piece. `001` cannot be cut into complete `01` blocks.

## why the extra start matters

the slides' pages 13–14 warn against simply making the old start accepting. a different original machine might return to its start after a nonempty string that it previously rejected. changing that state's status would newly accept the string, even if it is not a concatenation of valid old pieces.

here is a separate counterexample, with its changed target stated explicitly: an nfa for 0*1 has old start s looping on 0, then s→t on 1, with t accepting. making s accepting would accept `0`. but (0*1)* contains no nonempty all-zero string, since every nonempty piece ends in 1. a fresh accepting start avoids that bug. it provides exactly the zero-piece option without changing the meaning of visits to old s.

## read the case definition as “whose state is this?”

the piecewise δ table preserves an old state's old moves except at the handoff points. set union adds the new ε destination without deleting existing ε destinations. the fresh start has no ordinary input moves; its ε moves enter components. q is the combined state set; f separately specifies where a completed input may accept. rename overlapping component state labels first so they really are distinct states.

a correctness argument cuts an accepting run at the handoffs to recover valid pieces. in reverse, join accepting runs for valid pieces using those handoffs. that's why the construction recognizes **exactly** the combined language.

**next connection:** regular expressions describe these same three operations as formulas. **connected check:** for concatenation, explain what would go wrong if first-component accepting states remained accepting even when the second language does not contain ε.

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: expression versus language and search semantics
  • PDF pages 3–5: six inductive cases, empty language and empty string
  • PDF pages 6–7: decimal expression and required digits
  • PDF pages 8–13: structural induction and base NFAs

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The job: describe patterns without drawing every state

A machine reads a string and gives a verdict. A regular expression describes which strings belong. Same target, different tool: a checker versus a compact recipe. Don't read a regular expression as one giant literal word. Its operations build sets of possible words.

Start with the slide expression (0∪1)0∗(0\cup1)0^*(0∪1)0∗. The first parentheses say “choose 0 or 1.” The final part says “append zero or more copies of 0.” That generates 0, 1, 00, 10, 000, 100, and so on. It cannot generate 101: after the first position, only zeros are permitted. It cannot generate the empty string: the first choice still owes us one symbol.

Treat an expression as a recipe for possible strings. A choice picks a recipe, concatenation cooks one part then the next, and star repeats a whole recipe some finite number of times. Zero repetitions makes nothing: ε. First identify the chunk under the star, or you will repeat the wrong damn thing.

Round 1 — An expression is a recipe; its language is the food it can make · pages 1–5

0 is an expression describing the one-string language {0}. 0* describes ε,0,00,… . 01 uses concatenation: a zero followed by a one. The expression itself is a finite piece of notation; its described language may contain infinitely many strings. Keep the recipe and its outputs separate.

The six definition cases are three building blocks and three ways to combine them. The blocks are a symbol a∈Σ, ε, and ∅. The combinations are union, concatenation and star of already-valid expressions. Inductive definition means you start from the blocks and repeatedly apply these formation rules. An expression must have a finite construction history; you cannot introduce a new operation and declare it regular because it looks convenient.

The usual precedence is star first, concatenation second, union last. Thus 0∪10* means either a single 0 or a 1 followed by zeros. Parentheses override grouping. In (0∪1)0*, first choose exactly one bit, then append any number of zeros. In (0∪1)*, repeat the bit-choice operation any number of times. Moving the star changes the whole damn language.

ε is the empty string, so concatenating it changes nothing: Rε=R. ∅ is the empty language, so there is no string available for concatenation: R∅=∅. Union with ∅ changes nothing; union with ε adds the option of empty input if it was absent. Star always permits zero repetitions, hence ∅* describes {ε}. The mathematical notation sometimes writes an expression and its language interchangeably; mentally keep their types separate.

The grep example searches for a matching substring inside a line. That explains the surrounding Σ* in the formal line language. A mathematical RE describes whole strings unless substring matching is explicitly part of the task. Practical programming regex engines can have extra features; use the course's six operations for theoretical claims.

Round 2 — Decode the decimal example one requirement at a time · pages 6–7

D means a choice of digit from 0 through 9; DD* means at least one digit. The initial (+∪−∪ε) chooses a plus sign, minus sign, or no sign. Then the expression offers three alternatives:

  • DD*: integer-looking strings such as 72.
  • DD*.D*: at least one digit before the literal decimal point; possibly none after it, such as 2.1 or 7..
  • D*.DD*: possibly no digits before the point, but at least one after it, such as .01.

The period is a literal terminal here, not a wildcard. -.01 combines the minus option with the third alternative. Why not simply D*.D*? Both digit groups could be empty, accepting .. The two asymmetric alternatives enforce “at least one digit somewhere.” This is the core design skill: each piece pays for a specific clause of the target format.

Round 3 — Why checking six cases proves the whole theorem · pages 8–13

We want: every language described by an RE has a finite automaton. For symbol a, use a two-state NFA with one a-arrow from start to accept; every other transition is empty. For ε, use one accepting start with no moves. For ∅, use one nonaccepting start with no moves.

Now assume the smaller expressions already have equivalent NFAs. Their union, concatenation and star have NFAs by the constructions just proved. Those are all the ways an RE can be formed, so every finite expression is covered. This is structural induction: the induction follows the recipe tree rather than counting integers. The reverse theorem, automaton→RE, still needs its own argument. One direction of “if and only if” never buys you the other for free.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Three building blocks, three operations

A literal a describes the one-element language {a}. The expression ε describes {ε}, a set containing one string of length zero. The expression ∅ describes the empty language: no choices at all. Those last two are different as hell: an order containing a zero-length item versus no available item.

Operation What you actually do Example
Union R∪SR\cup SR∪S Choose a string from either recipe 0 ∪ 1 gives 0 or 1
Concatenation RSRSRS Choose from R, then from S; join in that order (0 ∪ 1)1 gives 01 or 11
Star R∗R^*R∗ Choose zero, one, or more R-strings and join them (01)* gives ε, 01, 0101, …

Star repeats its whole operand. 01* means a mandatory 0 followed by any number of ones. (01)* repeats pairs. Parentheses are doing actual work here.

The language of an expression R is written L(R)L(R)L(R). So L(1)={1}L(1)=\{1\}L(1)={1}, while L(1∗)={ε,1,11,111,…}L(1^*)=\{\varepsilon,1,11,111,\ldots\}L(1∗)={ε,1,11,111,…}. A language name such as A or E does not secretly add a star.

Build one from the requirement

“Exactly one 1” gives us three jobs: any zeros before it, the one mandatory 1, any zeros after it. Therefore 0∗10∗0^*10^*0∗10∗. For 00100, choose two zeros, then 1, then two zeros. For 00110, no choice can account for the second 1. That explains both inclusion and exclusion.

“Even length” becomes ((0∪1)(0∪1))∗((0\cup1)(0\cup1))^*((0∪1)(0∪1))∗: each repetition contributes two symbols. Zero repetitions contributes length zero, which is even. If the question requires positive even length, one pair must be mandatory. Check the boundary before celebrating.

Why machines and expressions match

For each basic expression, draw a tiny NFA. For union, concatenate, or star, use the corresponding ε-handoff construction. A complicated expression is assembled from smaller expressions; its NFA is assembled in the same shape. This is structural induction: prove the base pieces, then prove each assembly operation preserves the claim. You aren't checking infinitely many expressions one by one.

The decimal-number example, assembled from its requirements

Let D stand for a decimal digit choice, 0 through 9. The slide expression is

(+∪−∪ε)(DD∗∪DD∗.D∗∪D∗.DD∗).(+\cup-\cup\varepsilon)(DD^*\cup DD^*.D^*\cup D^*.DD^*).(+∪−∪ε)(DD∗∪DD∗.D∗∪D∗.DD∗).

The first parentheses choose a plus sign, a minus sign, or no sign. The three body alternatives cover an integer such as 72; digits followed by a dot and optional more digits such as 2.1 or 7.; or optional digits, a dot, then at least one digit such as .01. Here the dot is a literal decimal point, not a wildcard. DD* means at least one digit because its first D is mandatory.

Why not simply D*.D*? Both starred parts could choose zero digits, accepting . by itself. The mandatory D in each decimal alternative prevents that. For -.01, choose minus, then the third body alternative with zero digits before the dot and two afterward. Every chunk now has a reason.

Keep: expression operators manipulate languages; concatenation preserves order; star includes zero repetitions. Next we actually assemble an NFA from a recipe.

One connected check: In (0 ∪ 1)0*, which exact part prevents ε, and which exact part prevents 11?

reverse reading and limits of visual guessing

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: bottom-up expression construction
  • PDF page 3: small NFA, segmentation and formal table
  • PDF pages 4–5: reverse reading and limits of visual guessing

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The whole idea: an expression has a structure; the machine follows it

The deck builds an NFA for (ab∪a)∗(ab\cup a)^*(ab∪a)∗. Read that from the outside inward: repeat a block zero or more times; each block is either ab or a. So the machine needs a place where one block ends and another may begin. That place must also accept, because zero blocks is allowed.

Use q₁ as the start and accepting state, and q₂ as “we consumed the a of an ab block and still owe a b.” Now the arrows have reasons:

State Read a Read b
q₁ {q₁, q₂} ∅
q₂ ∅ {q₁}

From q₁ on a, one branch finishes the single-letter block a and returns to q₁. Another branch treats that same a as the first half of ab and goes to q₂. It is one input symbol consumed along two alternative interpretations. We didn't duplicate the input or require both branches to work.

Now make the recipe run. Each little expression gets a little checker; the construction connects their entrances and exits. The big question is whether those connections consume exactly the chunks the recipe permits. We will trace the slide’s actual chunks, because “just connect the machines” hides the part you need to understand.

Round 1 — Build the expression from the inside out · pages 1–2

The target (ab∪a)* means a sequence of chunks, each either ab or a. It does not mean any string over a and b. Every b needs an immediately preceding a belonging to the same chunk; a b cannot stand alone. Examples: ε, a, ab, aa, aba, abab. Reject b, ba and abb.

Start with one-arrow machines for a and b. Join the a machine to the b machine with ε to build ab. For the union, add a fresh start whose ε branches choose the ab machine or the separate a machine. For star, add another fresh accepting start and ε restart arrows from the old accepting states. Each level has a different job: concatenate inside a chunk, choose a chunk type, then repeat chunks.

This construction follows the expression's structure mechanically. It can create redundant states because correctness, not minimum size, is its goal. Simplifying afterward is a separate task. On an exam requesting a particular procedure, show the procedure before offering a smaller equivalent machine.

Round 2 — Why the two-state shortcut works · page 3

The smaller machine starts and accepts at q₁. On a, q₁ offers {q₁,q₂}. Staying at q₁ treats that a as a complete one-symbol chunk. Moving to q₂ treats it as the first half of ab; q₂ then demands b and returns to q₁. No other moves exist.

Trace aba: start {q₁}; after a, {q₁,q₂}; after b, {q₁}; after a, {q₁,q₂}. Accept because q₁ survives. For abb: after ab the set is {q₁}; the extra b has no matching move, giving ∅ and rejection. For ε, the initial q₁ already accepts.

The table's ε column is entirely ∅. An NFA does not have to use ε transitions. Its nondeterminism can come entirely from multiple same-symbol destinations, as it does here. Conversely, drawing a single start and accept does not make it deterministic; q₁ has two possible a moves.

Proof from the chunks: every return to q₁ consumes either a or ab. Therefore an accepting run spells a concatenation of allowed chunks. Given any allowed chunk list, choose q₁→q₁ for a and q₁→q₂→q₁ for ab. This yields an accepting path. That's the language equivalence, not just a handful of traces.

Round 3 — Reading a graph backward into a recipe · pages 4–5

The second example starts at state 1, loops there on a, crosses to accepting state 2 on b, and loops there on a or b. Before the crossing: a*. The crossing: b. After it: (a∪b). In order, ab(a∪b)*.

This expression accepts exactly strings with at least one b. The first b provides the crossing, with any earlier symbols necessarily a. For aa, no crossing occurs; reject. For ba, cross immediately and then loop; accept. For ε, there is no b; reject.

Here the graph has a single clean one-way crossing, so the recipe is visible. With several mutually connected states, guessing the expression gets unreliable. The next deck gives a procedure for replacing each possible journey with an expression, one removed state at a time.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Follow a whole string, including the dead branches

Trace aba. Start with {q₁}. After the first a, candidates are {q₁,q₂}. On b, q₁ contributes nothing and q₂ contributes q₁, leaving {q₁}. On the final a, candidates are {q₁,q₂} again. q₁ is present, so accept. Its successful interpretation is ab followed by a.

Trace abb. After ab, only q₁ remains. It has no b arrow, so the set becomes ∅ and the input rejects. An NFA doesn't get to resurrect a dead branch because the remaining letter is inconvenient.

ε accepts immediately at q₁. b rejects. aa accepts as a + a. These checks cover different reasons the construction might fail; they are not a proof for every string.

Where the bigger slide construction comes from

The mechanical conversion can use more states and ε arrows: build ab, build a, join them by union, then wrap the result in star. Those ε arrows route control without consuming a letter. The compact table above packages the same language more efficiently. Different state counts do not mean different answers; compare accepted strings.

To justify correctness, follow completed blocks. Every successful return to q₁ consumes either a or ab, so an accepting run spells a concatenation of permitted blocks. Conversely, any chosen sequence of those blocks has a path: take the self-return interpretation for a, or the q₂ detour for ab. That is the two-direction argument: no extras, none missing.

The reverse problem is coming

An NFA with an a-loop before a mandatory b, then arbitrary a or b afterward, has expression a∗b(a∪b)∗a^*b(a\cup b)^*a∗b(a∪b)∗. You can see it by reading the stages. Messier diagrams need a general method: remove a state while preserving the paths that used to go through it. That is the next deck's job.

Keep: give every state an unfinished obligation. The arrows become consequences of that meaning instead of random doodles.

One connected check: Does aab have a successful block decomposition? Identify it before tracing the table.

the smaller machine starts and accepts at q₁. on a, q₁ offers {q₁,q₂}. staying at q₁ treats that a as a complete one-symbol chunk. moving to q₂ treats it as the first half of ab; q₂ then demands b and returns to q₁. no other moves exist.

trace `aba`: start {q₁}; after a, {q₁,q₂}; after b, {q₁}; after a, {q₁,q₂}. accept because q₁ survives. for `abb`: after ab the set is {q₁}; the extra b has no matching move, giving ∅ and rejection. for ε, the initial q₁ already accepts.

the table's ε column is entirely ∅. an nfa does not have to use ε transitions. its nondeterminism can come entirely from multiple same-symbol destinations, as it does here. conversely, drawing a single start and accept does not make it deterministic; q₁ has two possible a moves.

proof from the chunks: every return to q₁ consumes either a or ab. therefore an accepting run spells a concatenation of allowed chunks. given any allowed chunk list, choose q₁→q₁ for a and q₁→q₂→q₁ for ab. this yields an accepting path. that's the language equivalence, not just a handful of traces.

## round 3 — reading a graph backward into a recipe · pages 4–5

the second example starts at state 1, loops there on a, crosses to accepting state 2 on b, and loops there on a or b. before the crossing: a*. the crossing: b. after it: (a∪b)*. in order, a*b(a∪b)*.

this expression accepts exactly strings with at least one b. the first b provides the crossing, with any earlier symbols necessarily a. for `aa`, no crossing occurs; reject. for `ba`, cross immediately and then loop; accept. for ε, there is no b; reject.

here the graph has a single clean one-way crossing, so the recipe is visible. with several mutually connected states, guessing the expression gets unreliable. the next deck gives a procedure for replacing each possible journey with an expression, one removed state at a time.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## follow a whole string, including the dead branches

trace `aba`. start with `{q₁}`. after the first `a`, candidates are `{q₁,q₂}`. on `b`, q₁ contributes nothing and q₂ contributes q₁, leaving `{q₁}`. on the final `a`, candidates are `{q₁,q₂}` again. q₁ is present, so accept. its successful interpretation is `ab` followed by `a`.

trace `abb`. after `ab`, only q₁ remains. it has no `b` arrow, so the set becomes ∅ and the input rejects. an nfa doesn't get to resurrect a dead branch because the remaining letter is inconvenient.

ε accepts immediately at q₁. `b` rejects. `aa` accepts as `a` + `a`. these checks cover different reasons the construction might fail; they are not a proof for every string.

## where the bigger slide construction comes from

the mechanical conversion can use more states and ε arrows: build `ab`, build `a`, join them by union, then wrap the result in star. those ε arrows route control without consuming a letter. the compact table above packages the same language more efficiently. different state counts do not mean different answers; compare **accepted strings**.

to justify correctness, follow completed blocks. every successful return to q₁ consumes either `a` or `ab`, so an accepting run spells a concatenation of permitted blocks. conversely, any chosen sequence of those blocks has a path: take the self-return interpretation for `a`, or the q₂ detour for `ab`. that is the two-direction argument: no extras, none missing.

## the reverse problem is coming

an nfa with an `a`-loop before a mandatory `b`, then arbitrary `a` or `b` afterward, has expression \(a^*b(a\cup b)^*\). you can see it by reading the stages. messier diagrams need a general method: remove a state while preserving the paths that used to go through it. that is the next deck's job.

**keep:** give every state an unfinished obligation. the arrows become consequences of that meaning instead of random doodles.

**one connected check:** does `aab` have a successful block decomposition? identify it before tracing the table.

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: original graph and GNFA setup
  • PDF pages 4–5: state-one elimination
  • PDF pages 6–9: state-two elimination and empty-loop meaning
  • PDF page 10: final expression and preservation argument

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The job: remove a circle, preserve every possible journey

A GNFA is a finite graph whose arrows carry regular expressions. One arrow may stand for a whole chunk of input. The point is to summarize longer and longer paths until only a start and an accept state remain. Their connecting expression then describes the language.

Picture a station k that we want to erase. A trip from i to j can either avoid k or enter k, loop there some number of times, and leave. Those are the only two kinds of trip we need to account for at this elimination step.

Call the entry label R₁, loop label R₂, exit label R₃, and existing direct label R₄. The replacement is

R1R2∗R3∪R4.R_1R_2^*R_3\cup R_4.R1​R2∗​R3​∪R4​.

Read it as a sentence: enter, do any number of loops, exit; OR use the old route. This is not a spell to memorize without knowing what each chunk pays for.

Imagine closing a station on a rail map while preserving every possible journey label. You must replace routes through that station with direct connections, including any number of laps around its loop. Deleting the station first would delete valid trips. The scary formula is bookkeeping for those missing journeys.

Round 1 — We are compressing paths, not erasing their behavior · pages 1–3

The original three-state DFA starts at 1; states 2 and 3 accept. Its transitions are: 1 on a→2, on b→3; 2 on a→1, on b→2; 3 on a→2, on b→1. State 1 has no loop. Before manipulating the giant expression, keep that little road network clear.

Add a new start s with an ε arrow to 1. Add a new final state f, with ε arrows from old accepting 2 and 3 to f. The old states stop serving as final endpoints; the ε exits preserve their old acceptance choices. Empty input remains rejected because there is no ε-only path from s to f.

A GNFA, generalized nondeterministic finite automaton, allows a whole regular expression on an arrow. Traversing it consumes a string described by that label. A label ab∪c means consume ab or consume c. It does not mean arbitrarily reading a, b or c one symbol at a time along that arrow.

Round 2 — Remove state 1 and pay for every route through it · pages 4–5

For the new 3→2 edge, there was already an a route. Going through 1 contributes b then a, or ba. So the replacement is ba∪a. The order matters: ab would describe a different route.

For 2→2, the old b loop remains, and the detour 2→1→2 contributes aa, giving aa∪b. For 2→3, the detour contributes ab. For 3→3, the detour contributes bb. From s, the ε entrance followed by 1→2 contributes a; followed by 1→3 contributes b. Old ε exits to f remain.

No loop at 1 means we may traverse it once without circling. Formally its loop label is ∅ and ∅*=ε. Multiplying an entrance by ε and an exit concatenates just entrance and exit. Confusing absent edge ∅ with free edge ε is exactly how a plausible-looking answer starts accepting extra strings.

Round 3 — Remove state 2; the star is doing real work now · pages 6–9

Now 2 has loop aa∪b. An arbitrary stay at 2 consumes any finite sequence of aa-blocks and b-blocks, including none. That is (aa∪b)*. Thus s→3 becomes a(aa∪b)*ab ∪ b: enter 2 on a, stay there as long as desired, exit on ab, or use the direct b route.

Keep four temporary names instead of trying to remember the whole mess: P is the new s→3 label; T is 3's new loop; U is 3→f; V is s→f. The worked table and calculations below spell out all four labels. Removing 3 then gives PT*U∪V. Temporary names shorten the bookkeeping without changing the actual expressions.

Round 4 — What the final formula is claiming · page 10

The final answer is

(a(aa∪b)∗ab∪b)((ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb)∗((ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε)∪a(aa∪b)∗. \bigl(a(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup b\bigr) \bigl((ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup bb\bigr)^* \bigl((ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*\cup\varepsilon\bigr) \cup a(aa\cup b)^*. (a(aa∪b)∗ab∪b)((ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb)∗((ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε)∪a(aa∪b)∗.

Read the three large factors as enter 3, loop there, exit; read the last union alternative as bypass 3. No new operation appeared just because the line became ugly as hell. Every factor is still concatenation, union or star.

The preservation claim at each removal is: paths whose internal states have been eliminated are represented by the current edge labels. A path either avoids the newly removed state or enters it, loops finitely often and exits. Conversely, every chosen piece of the replacement expression expands into such an old path. Applying that argument repeatedly preserves the language through the final two-state graph. Tests can catch an incorrect label, but this route argument explains arbitrary input lengths.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Work the slide example one edge at a time

After state 1 is removed in Example 1.68, the relevant labels include:

Journey Label
start s → 2 a
2 → 2 aa ∪ b
2 → 3 ab
s → 3 b
3 → 2 ba ∪ a
3 → 3 bb
2 → accept ε
3 → accept ε

Now remove state 2. For s → 3, enter on a, loop on (aa ∪ b)*, exit on ab. Keep the direct b route too. New label: a(aa∪b)∗ab∪ba(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup ba(aa∪b)∗ab∪b.

For 3 → 3, entering 2 costs (ba ∪ a), its loop is unchanged, and returning to 3 costs ab. Keep old bb. New loop: (ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb(ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*ab\cup bb(ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗ab∪bb.

For s → accept, use a(aa ∪ b)*ε, which simplifies to a(aa ∪ b)*. For 3 → accept, keep the old ε option as well: (ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε(ba\cup a)(aa\cup b)^*\cup\varepsilon(ba∪a)(aa∪b)∗∪ε.

Notice the discipline: each new label is explained by an actual route. We don't rearrange the letters because concatenation is ordered.

Recombine the remaining routes

To finish, give the four remaining labels short temporary names: P for s→3, T for 3's loop, U for 3→accept, and V for s→accept. Removing state 3 gives PT*U ∪ V. Substitute the expressions just calculated if the question requests the full final RE. The giant final formula is only “enter, loop, exit, or go directly” again; its size hides no new operation.

Two easy places to break the construction

No edge means ∅, not ε. ∅ says “this journey is impossible.” ε says “the journey is possible while consuming nothing.” Replacing a missing edge by ε creates free travel and can change the language.

But a missing loop contributes ∅∗={ε}\emptyset^*=\{\varepsilon\}∅∗={ε} as a language: take zero loops. Thus an entry and exit can still form a route even if k has no self-loop. Zero visits around the loop is different from a free entrance into k.

Update every remaining ordered pair, including self-loops, using the labels before deleting k. Then remove k and its incident edges. Mixing half-updated labels can accidentally account for paths multiple times or produce the wrong expression structure.

Keep: eliminate a state by replacing its possible journeys, not by deleting its behavior. The next deck makes this route argument a formal conversion algorithm.

One connected check: If i→k is a, k has no loop, k→j is b, and i→j is c, what two kinds of journey must the new label preserve?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: GNFA type and normalization
  • PDF pages 3–5: elimination formula and every ordered pair
  • PDF page 6: recursion, termination and NFA entry

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The mental model: each arrow is a summary of hidden paths

At the beginning, most labels are single symbols. After states are removed, an arrow summarizes all the ways to travel between its endpoints through the already-removed states. That sentence is the invariant: the fact we maintain after every step. It is what makes the final expression trustworthy.

A regular expression on an arrow describes a set of strings, not one action like a DFA's single-symbol move. Traversing an ε-labeled arrow consumes nothing; an ∅ label permits no traversal. A run can split its input into chunks matching its arrow labels.

Hold up: the same δ symbol is doing a different job now. In a GNFA, give it two stations and it tells you the expression labeling travel between them. It is not being asked for “the next state after this letter.” Once the input and output types are clear, the formula has somewhere to live.

Round 1 — δ has changed jobs again · pages 1–2

For a DFA, δ takes a state and input symbol and returns the next state. For an NFA, it returns a set of possible next states. For a GNFA, δ takes two endpoint states and returns the regular expression labeling their connection. Do not read every delta in this course as the same damn function.

δ:(Q−{qaccept})×(Q−{qstart})→R.\delta:(Q-\{q_{accept}\})\times(Q-\{q_{start}\})\to\mathcal R.δ:(Q−{qaccept​})×(Q−{qstart​})→R.

Q minus a singleton means all states except that one. The first coordinate cannot be the accept state because no arrows leave it. The second cannot be the start because no arrows enter it. R, written here as calligraphic ℛ, is the set of regular expressions over Σ. The output can be ∅, so the formal table can have an entry for every allowed pair even when no physical arrow is drawn.

There is exactly one designated start and one designated accept. That is why the tuple contains q_start and q_accept rather than F. Add them fresh, connect start to the old start by ε, and old accept states to the new accept by ε. Merge parallel arrows by union. Keep existing loops. Missing arrows get ∅. This normalization makes the elimination procedure uniform.

Round 2 — Read the four-label rule in the right order · pages 3–5

Choose an internal state k to remove. For remaining endpoints i and j, name i→k as R₁, k→k as R₂, k→j as R₃, and i→j as R₄. The new edge is R₁R₂*R₃∪R₄. Entry, any number of loops, exit, OR the old bypass.

“All pairs” includes i=j. If you skip self-pairs, you can lose loops created by a detour through k. Use the old labels for the whole removal round. Compute a new table separately, then replace the old table; otherwise a halfway-updated edge can sneak newly summarized journeys into the wrong calculation.

For a small teaching instance, suppose entry=a, loop=b, exit=c and bypass=d. The result ab*c∪d accepts ac, abc, abbc,… and d. It does not accept a alone, because entering without leaving does not reach j. If entry is ∅, the detour is impossible regardless of the loop. If only the loop is ∅, the detour still allows ac. These are different cases.

Round 3 — Recursion is a smaller copy of the same job · page 6

convert(G) asks for an expression describing normalized graph G. If G has two states, return the label from start to accept. Otherwise remove one internal state, forming G′, and call convert(G′). Base case is the two-state graph. Recursive step reduces the number of states by one. A finite graph cannot keep losing states forever, so the algorithm terminates.

The correctness proof follows that reduction: removal preserves the language, and the two-state graph's single usable start-to-accept label describes exactly its accepted strings. Different removal orders may produce different-looking expressions with the same language; syntactic equality is not required.

The final slide asks whether starting from an NFA is okay. Yes: its ordinary labels and ε labels are already regular expressions. Normalize its start/final states, union parallel labels, and eliminate states directly. Subset construction is needed when the required output is a DFA. NFA→RE via GNFA does not require first creating the potentially much larger DFA.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

First put the graph in the required shape

Add a fresh start s with an ε arrow to the old start. Add a fresh sole accept f; put ε arrows from each old accepting state to f. Old accepting states become ordinary states. Now no arrow needs to enter s, and no arrow needs to leave f. The fresh endpoints prevent us from accidentally deleting the boundary of an accepting computation.

If two arrows share endpoints, combine labels by union. Fill missing permitted connections with ∅. This gives a label for every ordered pair whose source is not f and whose destination is not s.

The formal line

δ:(Q−{f})×(Q−{s})→R\delta:(Q-\{f\})\times(Q-\{s\})\to\mathcal Rδ:(Q−{f})×(Q−{s})→R

says: choose a source state other than f and a destination other than s; receive a regular expression. Here Q is the state set; − removes the named element; × forms ordered pairs; R\mathcal RR means the collection of regular expressions. Unlike a DFA transition table, the second input to this δ is a destination state, not an alphabet symbol.

DFA and NFA use the same preparation

A DFA already has single-symbol labels. An NFA may have parallel arrows and ε arrows. Both can be put into the GNFA shape directly. NFA→GNFA does not require subset construction first: the GNFA still allows alternative paths. Subset construction solves a different job—making a deterministic one-symbol-at-a-time machine.

For example, if an NFA has both 0 and ε arrows from p to q, the GNFA label is 0 ∪ ε. It means either consume one zero or consume nothing on that connection. It does not mean consume both.

Why one elimination is valid

Remove k. Any old path between surviving states can be split at its encounters with surviving states. A segment through k consists of entry, zero or more k-loops, and exit. The replacement expression records exactly those segments. Conversely, any string chosen from a replacement label can be expanded back into an old path. Both directions matter: preserving old paths alone would still permit accidentally adding new ones.

Each step removes one state. Since the graph began finite, eventually just s and f remain. Their edge describes exactly the original accepting paths. That proves termination and correctness for different reasons: fewer states gives termination; preserved path language gives correctness.

Keep: DFA/NFA→GNFA→RE compresses paths. NFA→DFA tracks candidate states. Different destination objects, different construction.

One connected check: Why would adding a fresh accepting state with a 1 arrow, instead of ε, change the language?

if two arrows share endpoints, combine labels by union. fill missing permitted connections with ∅. this gives a label for every ordered pair whose source is not f and whose destination is not s.

the formal line

\[\delta:(q-\{f\})\times(q-\{s\})\to\mathcal r\]

says: choose a source state other than f and a destination other than s; receive a regular expression. here q is the state set; `−` removes the named element; `×` forms ordered pairs; \(\mathcal r\) means the collection of regular expressions. unlike a dfa transition table, the second input to this δ is a **destination state**, not an alphabet symbol.

## dfa and nfa use the same preparation

a dfa already has single-symbol labels. an nfa may have parallel arrows and ε arrows. both can be put into the gnfa shape directly. nfa→gnfa does **not** require subset construction first: the gnfa still allows alternative paths. subset construction solves a different job—making a deterministic one-symbol-at-a-time machine.

for example, if an nfa has both `0` and ε arrows from p to q, the gnfa label is `0 ∪ ε`. it means either consume one zero or consume nothing on that connection. it does not mean consume both.

## why one elimination is valid

remove k. any old path between surviving states can be split at its encounters with surviving states. a segment through k consists of entry, zero or more k-loops, and exit. the replacement expression records exactly those segments. conversely, any string chosen from a replacement label can be expanded back into an old path. both directions matter: preserving old paths alone would still permit accidentally adding new ones.

each step removes one state. since the graph began finite, eventually just s and f remain. their edge describes exactly the original accepting paths. that proves termination and correctness for different reasons: **fewer states** gives termination; **preserved path language** gives correctness.

**keep:** dfa/nfa→gnfa→re compresses paths. nfa→dfa tracks candidate states. different destination objects, different construction.

**one connected check:** why would adding a fresh accepting state with a `1` arrow, instead of ε, change the language?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: nonregularity, counts versus adjacent changes
  • PDF pages 3–4: necessary condition and quantified statement
  • PDF pages 5–6: pigeonhole and run positions
  • PDF pages 7–9: loop decomposition and bounds

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The question: when is a finite number of states not enough?

A DFA can remember parity with two states. Could it remember the exact number of leading zeros so it can demand that many ones afterward? For {0n1n:n≥0}\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}{0n1n:n≥0}, the number may be arbitrarily large. “It needs to count” is a useful suspicion, but not yet a proof: plenty of counting tasks only need a remainder. We need a consequence that every DFA must obey.

Suppose a DFA has p states. Read p symbols. The computation has visited p+1 state positions: the initial state plus one after each symbol. With only p different states, some state was visited twice. That's the pigeonhole principle: more visits than available distinct places forces a repeat.

A finite-state checker eventually has to reuse a memory situation on a long enough accepted input. Reusing a state creates a loop. Now we can replay that loop and ask whether the language’s rule survives. That is the whole engine; the theorem’s alphabet soup tells us exactly when we are allowed to use it.

Round 1 — “It needs to count” is a suspicion, not a proof · pages 1–2

For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, the machine must match an arbitrarily large number of leading zeros with trailing ones. Finite memory sounds inadequate, but the exam needs an argument ruling out every possible DFA design. Saying “I can't draw one” only reports your own failed design attempt.

The adjacent-pattern example shows why intuition can screw you over. C requires equally many individual 0s and 1s. D requires equally many adjacent 01 and 10 occurrences. An occurrence is an adjacent pair; overlaps count. In 01010, there are two 01s and two 10s, but three zeros and two ones.

Every 01 is a switch into the 1-region, and every 10 switches back. For a nonempty binary string, the two counts balance exactly when first and last symbols agree. If it starts 0 and ends 1, there is one extra 01; reverse endpoints give one extra 10. ε has both counts zero too. So D is regular: remember the first and current last symbol, with ε accepted. Individual counts C do not collapse into that bounded endpoint summary.

Round 2 — Who chooses what in the theorem? · pages 3–4

The statement is: if A is regular, there is an integer p≥1 such that every accepted string s with length at least p has some split s=xyz satisfying three requirements. y is nonempty; x and y together fit within the first p symbols; repeating y any number i≥0 keeps the string in A.

p is a threshold, not a chosen example string. x is the prefix before the loop, y the loop's consumed substring, z the suffix after it. Concatenation xyz means those exact three pieces in that order. y⁰=ε deletes y; y¹=y leaves it once; y²=yy doubles it. x and z stay fixed.

The quantifier order matters: ∃p, then ∀s, then ∃x,y,z, then ∀i. “For every” means all allowed choices; “there exists” means at least one suitable choice. The split can depend on s. Once selected, it must work for every i. A different successful split for every i is not what the theorem says.

This is a necessary condition for regularity. Regularity guarantees it. Showing a few strings pump does not establish regularity. To use the lemma against regularity, we must show the promised condition cannot hold.

Round 3 — The loop is forced by too many visits and too few rooms · pages 5–9

Assume a DFA for A has p states. Reading the first p symbols records p+1 visits, including the starting state before any input. Pigeonhole principle: placing more visits than available states forces two visits to the same state. Choose their positions j<l in the slide's q₁,…,qₙ₊₁ numbering.

The characters before the first visit form x=s₁…sⱼ₋₁. Those between the visits form y=sⱼ…sₗ₋₁. The rest form z=sₗ…sₙ. The two visits are distinct positions, so l−j>0 and y is nonempty. Both are among the first p+1 visits, so l−1≤p and |xy|≤p.

At the end of x the machine is at the loop state. Reading y returns to that same state. Reading it twice returns there twice; skipping it leaves the machine there already. In every case the unchanged z starts from the same state and reaches the old accepting endpoint. That's the mechanism behind “for all i.”

If A has no strings as long as p, the conditional promise about long members has no counterexample. This is called vacuous truth. The lemma does not insist every regular language contain long strings. A finite language is regular and may satisfy the threshold condition simply because there are no eligible strings.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

A repeat turns a path into a reusable loop

Split the input into three consecutive pieces. x gets us to the repeated state the first time. y takes us around the loop back to that same state. z finishes the original accepting journey.

Because the state after y is exactly the state before y, the rest of the machine cannot tell whether we took that loop zero times, once, twice, or a hundred times. Following z afterward still reaches accept. The DFA has no secret memory outside its current state. That's the whole damn mechanism.

The notation xyizxy^izxyiz means x, then i copies of y, then z. With i=0, y disappears; with i=1, it is the original string; with i=2, y is duplicated. We are editing a substring, not moving letters around.

Decode the theorem in its actual order

If L is regular, there exists a pumping length p such that every s in L with length at least p can be split as s=xyz satisfying:

  1. ∣y∣>0|y|>0∣y∣>0: the loop consumes at least one symbol.
  2. ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p: the loop fits within the first p symbols.
  3. xyiz∈Lxy^iz\in Lxyiz∈L for every integer i≥0: every repetition count still works.

∣y∣|y|∣y∣ is the number of symbols in y. ∈\in∈ means “is a member of.” The theorem promises at least one suitable split, not every split. p belongs to the assumed machine; we don't get to declare p=3 because that makes an example convenient.

Why this helps prove impossibility

To show a language is not regular, assume a DFA exists and receive its unknown p. Choose a legal long string. Then show that no allowed split can keep all repetitions in the language. That contradicts the required loop property.

Be careful with the deck's counting examples. Equal numbers of 0 and 1 is not the same requirement as equal numbers of adjacent 01 and 10. The latter can be tracked using boundary information: in a binary string, changes from 0 to 1 and back alternate. Similar-looking counts can need radically different memory.

Keep: pumping is a necessary consequence of finite state memory. It is a tool for ruling regularity out, not a general way to establish regularity. Next we turn the mechanism into a complete quantified proof.

One connected check: Why does returning to the same state matter more than merely reading the same symbol twice?
