equal counts, prefix bound and choosing one witness

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–5: equal ordered blocks and three split cases
  • PDF pages 6–9: equal counts, prefix bound and choosing one witness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The job: make the machine's promised loop impossible

We will prove L={0n1n:n≥0}L=\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}L={0n1n:n≥0} is not regular. Membership requires two things: all zeros precede all ones, and their counts match. 0011 belongs; 0101 has equal counts but the wrong order; 001 has the right order but wrong counts.

A proof must handle an unknown machine, unknown pumping length, and whichever legal split the theorem might supply. Checking one favorite split won't cut it. The trick is to choose a string that pins all legal loops into a useful region.

This proof is a game with strict ownership rules. The alleged machine supplies its memory bound; we choose a long input; the loop can be any legal one; then we choose how many times to repeat it. If we cherry-pick a convenient loop, the proof is bullshit. We have to defeat every legal loop.

Round 1 — Build a proof from the promise you are attacking · pages 1–2

Assume B={0ⁿ1ⁿ:n≥0} is regular. The lemma then supplies a pumping length p. We do not choose p=5 and pretend we handled all possibilities. We choose the witness in response to an arbitrary p: s=0ᵖ1ᵖ. It belongs to B and has length 2p≥p.

Now take any split s=xyz satisfying |y|>0 and |xy|≤p. The first p symbols are all zero, so y=0ᵏ for some integer k with 1≤k≤p. Pump i=2. The result has p+k zeros and p ones, so it is outside B. This defeats every legal split, contradicting the promised existence of a successful one. Therefore B is not regular.

Read the logic as a challenge: “Give me whatever p your alleged DFA provides. I'll hand you a long accepted string for which none of the legal loop choices can keep the promise.” The opponent analogy only represents quantifier order; no machine is actually playing a game.

Round 2 — Why the slides also discuss splits beyond the first block · pages 3–5

The deck gives a stronger case analysis that does not need the |xy|≤p restriction for this particular B. A nonempty contiguous y in 0ᵖ1ᵖ can contain only zeros, only ones, or cross the boundary from zeros to ones.

Only zeros: doubling increases zeros only. Only ones: doubling increases ones only. Crossing: y=0ᵃ1ᵇ with a,b>0, so yy contains a 1 followed later by a 0. The pumped string no longer has all zeros before all ones. Every case violates B. Notice that the third case attacks order, while the first two attack counts.

You may use the shorter prefix-bound proof on an exam unless the question demands the slide's particular argument. Both are rigorous. But you must know what the extra case analysis buys and which condition each contradiction uses.

Round 3 — Change the language, and that old reason may stop working · pages 6–9

Now C={w:#0(w)=#1(w)} permits any order. Reuse the witness 0ᵖ1ᵖ, but do not reuse “a zero appears after a one, therefore reject.” In C, 0101 is perfectly valid. The membership rule changed.

Without the prefix bound, the split x=ε, y=0ᵖ1ᵖ, z=ε can be repeated forever while keeping equal counts. This is why we use |xy|≤p to confine y to zeros. Then pumping changes one count and not the other, which genuinely violates C. The bound is doing essential logical work, not filling a checklist for decoration.

Why is one chosen witness enough when the theorem says every long member? Because a universal promise fails when even one eligible member fails. But you still must defeat every allowed split of that witness. “One bad string” and “one bad split” sit under different quantifiers. Mixing them is the classic proof-killer.

The clean exam paragraph should include: assumption of regularity, arbitrary pumping length, witness membership and length, arbitrary legal split, forced form of y, chosen i, exact violated language condition, contradiction. Each sentence pays for one obligation. None needs fancy prose.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

One complete proof, with the reasons exposed

Assume L is regular. Then it has a pumping length p≥1. Choose s=0p1ps=0^p1^ps=0p1p. This choice depends on p: whatever finite memory the supposed machine has, we give it that many zeros followed by that many ones. s is in L, and its length 2p is at least p, so the lemma applies.

Take any split s=xyz satisfying ∣xy∣≤p|xy|\le p∣xy∣≤p and ∣y∣>0|y|>0∣y∣>0. The first p symbols of s are all zeros. Since x together with y ends within those first p positions, y contains only zeros. Since it is nonempty, y=0ky=0^ky=0k for some k with 1≤k≤p.

Choose i=0. The pumped string is xz=0p−k1pxz=0^{p-k}1^pxz=0p−k1p. It has fewer zeros than ones because k≥1. Therefore xz is not in L. But the pumping lemma promised that every repetition count, including zero, remains in L. Contradiction. Thus L is not regular.

Where the proof actually earns its conclusion

The phrase “take any split” is backed by the argument about the first p positions. We never selected x or y ourselves. If someone gives us a different legal x and y, its y still consists of k≥1 zeros, and the same failure still happens.

For a concrete illustration, let p=4 and s=00001111. Maybe y is the first zero; maybe it is the middle two zeros; maybe it is all four. Deleting it always leaves fewer than four zeros and still four ones. The illustration helps you see the mechanism; the variable-k argument proves all p and all legal splits.

Why the exact language matters

The slide discussion also considers strings with equal numbers of zeros and ones in any order. If a proof says “pumping creates a 0 after a 1, so reject,” that only works for the ordered-block language. It fails for the unordered equal-count language: order is allowed there.

The prefix-bound proof above still works for that second language. Choose the same witness, force y to contain only zeros, and break the counts. Notice the repair: we used a condition that actually defines the target language.

What to write under exam conditions

State the assumption; introduce the unknown p; choose and validate s; describe every legal y; choose i; show a precise failed membership condition; conclude contradiction. Those are logical obligations, not decorative sentences.

Keep: the witness is your choice; the decomposition is not. Use the prefix bound to control every decomposition. Next we adapt this strategy when the failed condition is duplication or a square length.

One connected check: If the target language were all strings containing at least one 1, which line of this proof would stop giving a contradiction?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–7: negation, quantifier dependencies and implication
  • PDF pages 8–9: double-copy witness and midpoint reasoning
  • PDF pages 10–12: square lengths, inequalities and p=1 edge

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The mental model: control the damage, don't memorize one string

Pumping proofs have a fixed negotiation. You assume regularity; the lemma supplies p; you choose a sufficiently long member s; the hypothetical machine gets a legal split; you choose a repetition count that makes membership fail. The order matters. You must beat every legal split of your chosen s, not just a convenient one.

Write the plan in ordinary words first: “The loop is trapped in this region. Changing that region destroys this relationship.” Then translate the relationship into counts, positions, or arithmetic.

“Every option fails” and “one option fails” are wildly different promises. Think of testing keys: one bad key does not prove the door cannot be opened. Pumping proofs live or die on that distinction. We will put each choice in the right person’s hands before touching the witness string.

Round 1 — Negation reverses who has to supply the evidence · pages 1–7

“For every n, a formula holds” is disproved by finding one n where it fails. “There exists a successful choice” is disproved by showing every allowed choice fails. That is why ∀ and ∃ swap when negated. The condition itself must be negated too.

For pumping, failure of the promise reads: for every p≥1, choose an s∈A of length at least p; for every legal split s=xyz with y nonempty and |xy|≤p, find an i≥0 making xyⁱz∉A. The order permits s to depend on p, and i to depend on the split. It does not permit choosing p conveniently after seeing the string or choosing only the easiest split.

The slide writes legal-split conditions as the premise of an implication. Why? Splits that are illegal need no counterattack. If y is empty or x/y extend beyond the permitted prefix, the lemma never offered that split as a valid witness. models.title: CFGs: a variable is unfinished work, a terminal is finished output
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–5: grammar objects, derivation and tree
  • PDF pages 6–7: phrase analogy and context independence
  • PDF pages 8–11: four-tuple, yields and generated language
  • PDF page 12: balanced parentheses and completeness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Start with what a grammar is trying to do

A DFA checks a completed string. A grammar builds strings. We still care about a language—a set of completed strings—but now ask which ones the construction rules can produce. There is no input head and no accepting circle in a grammar.

The deck's grammar is:

A→0A1∣B,B→#.A\to0A1\mid B,\qquad B\to\#.A→0A1∣B,B→#.

A and B are variables: placeholders for unfinished work. 0, 1, and # are terminals: finished output symbols that stay put. A is the starting variable. The vertical bar means “or,” so A has two alternative rules. The arrow means “you may replace this variable with that right-hand side.”

Aight, we are changing jobs: checking a finished string versus building possible strings. A variable is an unfinished job ticket. A rule replaces that ticket with new work or finished output. Terminals are the printed symbols that stay. Follow one ticket until the entire line contains finished output; that is a derivation.

Round 1 — A grammar builds; a recognizer checks · pages 1–5

Aight, switch jobs deliberately. A machine starts with an input and checks it. A grammar starts with a pending instruction and builds possible outputs. Its language is the collection of completed outputs. These are two ways to describe which strings belong, not two names for the same physical process.

In the slide grammar A→0A1, A→B, B→#, A and B are variables: unfinished jobs. The symbols 0,1,# are terminals: finished output that no grammar rule rewrites. Here # is a literal printed symbol, not “number of.” A is the start variable.

Take A→0A1 three times: A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111. Each use adds one zero to the left and one one to the right while leaving one pending A inside. Then A→B and B→# finish the middle, giving 000#111. The derivation is the sequence of whole intermediate strings. A parse tree records which rule expanded each variable; its terminal leaves, read left to right, give the output. Branch order matters.

Why exactly 0ⁿ#1ⁿ? Every recursive use adds one matched pair; the only exit prints #. Conversely, for any n≥0, use the wrapping rule n times, then the exit. For n=0, A⇒B⇒#; no zeros or ones are needed. Those two directions establish the whole language.

Round 2 — “Context-free” does not mean “meaningless” · pages 6–9

The noun-phrase example expands labeled phrase slots until only words remain. A variable named ⟨Noun-Phrase⟩ can be a single symbol in the grammar even though its label is long. Angle brackets help distinguish the label from printed English words.

A rule A→w may replace an A wherever it appears; it does not inspect its neighbors before becoming legal. That is the relevant meaning of context-free. It says something about the rule's left side, not about whether the generated sentence has real-world meaning.

The four-tuple (V,Σ,R,S) has finite variable set V, finite terminal set Σ, finite production-rule set R, and start S∈V. V and Σ are disjoint: a symbol cannot simultaneously be a rewriteable job and finished output. Each rule has one variable on the left and any finite string of variables/terminals on the right, possibly ε. The role called S may be filled by A, as in the slide. Again, a role name is not a required literal label.

Round 3 — Read “yields” one replacement at a time · pages 10–11

If A→w is a rule, uAv⇒uwv. Here u and v are the untouched surrounding strings; w is the replacement. They may contain variables too. The arrow ⇒ means one derivation step. The starred arrow ⇒* means zero or more steps. Zero steps permits u⇒*u; it does not mean every variable can disappear.

The language definition {w∈Σ*:S⇒*w} requires two things: w contains only terminals, and a finite derivation from S reaches it. An intermediate string containing A is not yet a language member. An infinite rewrite that never finishes generates no completed string.

Round 4 — Balanced parentheses require order as well as counts · page 12

For S→aSb|SS|ε, read a as an opening parenthesis and b as closing. aSb wraps one balanced expression; SS concatenates two; ε supplies the empty expression. For aabbab, derive S⇒SS⇒aSbS⇒aaSbbS⇒aabbS⇒aabbaSb⇒aabbab. Every replacement changes one selected S; ε removes that selected occurrence only.

Every generated string has equal a/b counts and no prefix with more b than a. ba has equal totals but violates the prefix condition, so it is not balanced. For the reverse direction, every nonempty balanced string can be split after the closing b matched to its first a: it has form a u b v with u,v balanced. Use wrapping for u and concatenation for v, recursively. Length decreases in the inner pieces, eventually reaching ε. That's why the rules cover every balanced string, not merely some nice-looking examples.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Run the rules all the way to completion

Begin with A. Choose its wrapping rule three times, then finish:

A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.A\Rightarrow0A1\Rightarrow00A11\Rightarrow000A111\Rightarrow000B111\Rightarrow000\#111.A⇒0A1⇒00A11⇒000A111⇒000B111⇒000#111.

At 00A11, the zeros and ones are already output. A is the one unfinished job between them. Applying A→0A1 replaces that A, leaving its surrounding output untouched. We didn't replace the entire line with 0A1.

Each wrapping adds one zero on the left and one one on the right. Switching to B stops the wrapping; B→# puts a separator in the middle. Therefore the generated language is {0n#1n:n≥0}\{0^n\#1^n:n\ge0\}{0n#1n:n≥0}. n is the number of wraps. With zero wraps, A→B→# gives #. ε is not generated: no rule finishes with no terminal at all.

Why this can do what a DFA cannot

The growing expression stores unfinished structure. Every additional wrap leaves one more 1 waiting on the right. A finite grammar can describe arbitrarily deep nesting because its rules can reuse a variable. The finite rulebook does not impose a fixed bound on the size of a derivation.

A parse tree records the same construction as a tree. A node labeled A has children 0, A, 1 when that rule is used. Read the terminal leaves left to right to recover the completed string. The tree preserves who created whom, which a final string alone does not show.

Decode the formal package

G=(V,Σ,R,S)G=(V,\Sigma,R,S)G=(V,Σ,R,S) names a grammar. V is its finite set of variables; Σ is its finite terminal alphabet; R is its finite rule set; S is the starting variable. In this example S—the formal slot name—is filled by the variable A. The actual start does not have to be called S.

uAv⇒uwvuAv\Rightarrow uwvuAv⇒uwv says a rule A→w can replace A wherever it appears, with the same surrounding strings u and v retained. “Context-free” means the rule does not inspect those surroundings before permitting replacement. ⇒∗\Rightarrow^*⇒∗ means zero or more derivation steps.

The last slide adds two different ways to grow structure

For S→aSb|SS|ε, interpret a as an opening parenthesis and b as a closing one. S→aSb wraps one balanced structure inside a matched pair. S→SS places two balanced structures side by side. S→ε finishes with nothing. For aabbab, one derivation is S⇒SS⇒aSbS⇒aaSbbS⇒aabbS⇒aabbaSb⇒aabbab. Each arrow replaces one S.

Equal counts alone are insufficient: ba has one of each but closes before anything opens. A balanced-parentheses string must have equal final counts and every prefix must contain at least as many openings as closings. Wrapping and concatenation preserve both conditions. Conversely, split a nonempty balanced string after the close matching its first opening: inside that pair and after it are smaller balanced strings, exactly the wrapping and side-by-side jobs. This connects grammar rules to nested structure, the reason stacks will be useful.

What a correctness proof has to establish

Every derivation here produces matching outer blocks because each wrap adds exactly one of each symbol and the only finishing option inserts #. Conversely, any desired n can be produced by choosing n wraps then finishing. This proves both “no wrong strings” and “every required string.” Merely deriving 000#111 proves only one example.

Keep: variables are pending jobs; rules replace one pending job; terminals are finished output. Next we use grammar structure to control arithmetic grouping and identify ambiguity.

One connected check: At 00A11, why can the next step produce 000A111 but not 000A11?

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck

  • PDF pages 4–6: grammar union and DFA conversion

  • PDF pages 10–12: leftmost derivations and inherent ambiguity

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The question: who belongs together?

sections.concepts: helpers, exact final grammar and preservation

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: normal-form shapes and start exception
  • PDF pages 3–4: source grammar and fresh start
  • PDF pages 5–6: nullable consequences by occurrence
  • PDF pages 7–9: unit elimination and retained rules
  • PDF page 10: helpers, exact final grammar and preservation

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Why the hell are we rewriting the grammar?

A rule can currently do several things at once: print terminals, create three pending jobs, hand off to one other variable, or produce nothing. That flexibility is convenient for writing a grammar, but awkward for algorithms that must reason about every derivation.

Chomsky normal form, CNF, limits a rule to one of two ordinary shapes:

A→BCorA→a.A\to BC\qquad\text{or}\qquad A\to a.A→BCorA→a.

The first splits one pending job into two pending jobs. The second finishes one job by printing one terminal. Capital letters here stand for variables, lowercase a for a terminal. They are shape examples, not the only letters allowed.

If ε belongs to the language, the new start may also have a rule to ε; that start must not appear on a right-hand side. CNF is a format for a grammar. It does not mean the language becomes regular, deterministic, or unambiguous.

Picture a job ticket. “Print a” completes it. “Do B, then C” tears it into two ordered subtickets. A variable is the ticket's label, not output printed on the page. This analogy maps only the pending-work structure: it does not introduce a real worker, time cost, or a rule that jobs must take equal time. CNF makes every ticket use one of those two shapes.

Aight, imagine a messy kitchen where a recipe step can do six jobs, delegate to another recipe, or produce nothing. CNF makes every ordinary instruction do one of two things: split into two jobs, or print one finished symbol. Same possible finished strings. Cleaner instructions. The hard part is preserving every choice while we clean this shit up.

Round 1 — Standardize the jobs without changing the outputs · pages 1–4

Think of converting a messy instruction manual into two permitted instruction types: “do these two subtasks, in order” or “print this one symbol.” That is the whole CNF project. We preserve the completed terminal strings. We do not promise to preserve every old intermediate string, tree shape or number of derivation steps.

A→BC has two variables on the right. A→a has one terminal. A→B is a pure handoff and forbidden; A→ab prints two terminals and is forbidden; A→aB mixes types and is forbidden. Only the start may have an ε rule, if empty input belongs to the language. The start must not appear on any right side. These are shape conditions, not claims about which letters you must use.

Read the grammar punctuation before using it. In S→ASA|aB, the arrow means “S may be replaced by”; the vertical bar means or, separating two alternatives. It does not print a bar into the output. ASA means three consecutive jobs, in that order. ε is the empty string: no printed symbol. A production is one such replacement rule. In a derivation, ⇒ records one actual replacement, while ⇒* means zero or more replacements.

The slide begins with S→ASA|aB, A→B|S, B→b|ε. Add a fresh S₀→S because the old S appears inside ASA and therefore cannot remain the designated CNF start. S₀ is a new label with a special role; it does not automatically gain ε. Since the old S always eventually prints at least one a, this particular grammar does not generate ε.

Round 2 — Follow the disappearing work through its parents · pages 5–6

A variable is nullable when it can derive ε, directly or through other rules. B→ε means a B job may contribute nothing. In S→aB, preserving that choice requires S→a. In A→B, preserving it gives A→ε, so A becomes nullable too. B→b stays: the choice to print b is still valid.

Now each A occurrence in ASA can contribute nothing independently. Keep ASA and add AS, SA and S. The middle S stays because it cannot derive ε. The generated rule S→S makes no progress and will be removed in the unit phase. An ε-production's effect is preserved at places that use its variable; it is not a license to delete arbitrary surrounding symbols.

See a complete old derivation: S⇒ASA⇒BSA⇒SA⇒aBA⇒aA⇒aB⇒ab. Here is the same run with the missing reasons filled in:

Current work Rule used Result What changed
S S→ASA ASA Split the initial job into three ordered jobs.
ASA A→B BSA Replace only the left A occurrence.
BSA B→ε SA That B prints nothing; S and A stay.
SA S→aB aBA S prints an a and leaves a B job.
aBA B→ε aA This B also contributes nothing.
aA A→B aB The remaining A delegates to B.
aB B→b ab Finish the last job by printing b.

Both disappearing choices were legitimate B→ε uses; the final B used B→b instead. A nullable variable can disappear on one occurrence and print something on another. Treating “nullable” as “always empty” would lose valid outputs.

Round 3 — A unit rule delegates; copy the actual work · pages 7–9

S→S changes nothing, so remove it. S₀→S says the new start may do whatever S can do; copy S's nonunit alternatives to S₀. A→B supplies A→b. A→S supplies A with S's nonunit alternatives. Keep the original S and B alternatives too, because other productions still refer to those variables.

For each unit chain X⇒*Y consisting only of variable-to-variable steps, let X inherit Y's nonunit alternatives. This includes chains longer than one link and cycles. A finite reachable-variable set is safer than repeatedly rewriting the same unit cycle forever.

Round 4 — Helpers are packaging, not a new language · page 10

For aB, introduce U→a and use UB. For ASA, introduce A₁→SA and use AA₁. Expanding AA₁ restores ASA exactly; expanding UB restores aB. No letters are reordered or discarded. A₁ is a fresh variable label, not A multiplied by 1.

The complete final grammar is displayed in the worked model below; it follows the slide. Check each alternative individually: AA₁, UB, AS and SA are two variables; a and b are one terminal. The designated start S₀ occurs only on left sides. There are no unit or unwanted ε rules. That is the shape check.

The language check has two directions. Every omitted nullable occurrence can be restored by its old ε derivation; every copied unit alternative can be preceded by its old unit chain; every helper can be expanded back. Conversely, compress those old ε subtrees, unit chains and long right sides into the new productions. Each local change preserves terminal outputs, so the whole conversion does too. A pretty final grammar with no such reasoning is only half the job.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

First understand what “can disappear” means

Use the slide grammar:

S→ASA∣aB,A→B∣S,B→b∣ε.S\to ASA\mid aB,\quad A\to B\mid S,\quad B\to b\mid\varepsilon.S→ASA∣aB,A→B∣S,B→b∣ε.

B can finish with nothing via B→ε, so B is nullable. A can disappear too: A→B→ε. S cannot: every completed S derivation eventually uses an aB, so at least one a remains.

Nullable does not mean “delete this variable everywhere.” B can also produce b. Removing that possibility would mutilate the language. Nullable means we must preserve both choices: it may contribute something, or contribute nothing.

The crucial example: two A occurrences are two independent jobs

In S→ASA, the left A and right A are separate occurrences. Each may disappear. So retain these four right-hand sides:

Left A Right A Result
keep keep ASA
keep omit AS
omit keep SA
omit omit S

The middle S stays: it is not nullable. Do not omit it just because its letter looks like another variable. The choices are based on derivability of ε, not typography.

S→aB additionally supplies S→a when B disappears. We are replacing the effect of an ε-producing subtree with a shorter parent rule. That is why deleting ε rules after adding alternatives preserves nonempty strings.

Remove handoffs, then package large right-hand sides

A unit rule A→B only delegates to another variable without printing anything. Replace it by B's possible nonunit work. For chains, follow all reachable unit links. For cycles, collect reachable variables once; looping around forever contributes no completed terminal output.

Then aB must become two variables: introduce U→a and replace it by UB. ASA has three variables; introduce A₁→SA and replace it by AA₁. The helper is a package for the last two jobs. It does not reorder them.

With a fresh start S₀ and the slide's simplifications, a final CNF grammar is:

S0→AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAS→AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAA→b∣AA1∣UB∣a∣AS∣SAA1→SAU→aB→b. \begin{aligned} S_0&\to AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ S&\to AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ A&\to b\mid AA_1\mid UB\mid a\mid AS\mid SA\\ A_1&\to SA\qquad U\to a\qquad B\to b. \end{aligned} S0​SAA1​​→AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→b∣AA1​∣UB∣a∣AS∣SA→SAU→aB→b.​

Each ordinary right-hand side is two variables or one terminal. There is no S₀→ε because the original language did not contain ε.

What the normal form buys us

For a nonempty string of length n, a CNF parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves and n−1 binary splits: 2n−1 rule applications. The grammar may still have many possible trees, but each tree's size is now tied to the input length. Later, this gives finite algorithms for membership.

Keep: nullable removal preserves disappearing jobs; unit removal bypasses pure handoffs; helpers preserve ordered work while standardizing its size. Next we make these operations systematic enough to survive cycles and repeated variables.

One connected check: Why does replacing ASA only by AS lose a possibility, even though AS is one correct alternative?

for each unit chain x⇒*y consisting only of variable-to-variable steps, let x inherit y's nonunit alternatives. this includes chains longer than one link and cycles. a finite reachable-variable set is safer than repeatedly rewriting the same unit cycle forever.

## round 4 — helpers are packaging, not a new language · page 10

for ab, introduce u→a and use ub. for asa, introduce a₁→sa and use aa₁. expanding aa₁ restores asa exactly; expanding ub restores ab. no letters are reordered or discarded. a₁ is a fresh variable label, not a multiplied by 1.

the complete final grammar is displayed in the worked model below; it follows the slide. check each alternative individually: aa₁, ub, as and sa are two variables; a and b are one terminal. the designated start s₀ occurs only on left sides. there are no unit or unwanted ε rules. that is the shape check.

the language check has two directions. every omitted nullable occurrence can be restored by its old ε derivation; every copied unit alternative can be preceded by its old unit chain; every helper can be expanded back. conversely, compress those old ε subtrees, unit chains and long right sides into the new productions. each local change preserves terminal outputs, so the whole conversion does too. a pretty final grammar with no such reasoning is only half the job.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## first understand what “can disappear” means

use the slide grammar:

\[s\to asa\mid ab,\quad a\to b\mid s,\quad b\to b\mid\varepsilon.\]

b can finish with nothing via b→ε, so b is **nullable**. a can disappear too: a→b→ε. s cannot: every completed s derivation eventually uses an `ab`, so at least one `a` remains.

nullable does not mean “delete this variable everywhere.” b can also produce `b`. removing that possibility would mutilate the language. nullable means we must preserve **both** choices: it may contribute something, or contribute nothing.

## the crucial example: two a occurrences are two independent jobs

in s→asa, the left a and right a are separate occurrences. each may disappear. so retain these four right-hand sides:

| left a | right a | result |
|---|---|---|
| keep | keep | asa |
| keep | omit | as |
| omit | keep | sa |
| omit | omit | s |

the middle s stays: it is not nullable. do not omit it just because its letter looks like another variable. the choices are based on derivability of ε, not typography.

s→ab additionally supplies s→a when b disappears. we are replacing the effect of an ε-producing subtree with a shorter parent rule. that is why deleting ε rules **after adding alternatives** preserves nonempty strings.

## remove handoffs, then package large right-hand sides

a unit rule a→b only delegates to another variable without printing anything. replace it by b's possible nonunit work. for chains, follow all reachable unit links. for cycles, collect reachable variables once; looping around forever contributes no completed terminal output.

then `ab` must become two variables: introduce u→a and replace it by ub. `asa` has three variables; introduce a₁→sa and replace it by aa₁. the helper is a package for the last two jobs. it does not reorder them.

with a fresh start s₀ and the slide's simplifications, a final cnf grammar is:

\[
\begin{aligned}
s_0&\to aa_1\mid ub\mid a\mid as\mid sa\\
s&\to aa_1\mid ub\mid a\mid as\mid sa\\
a&\to b\mid aa_1\mid ub\mid a\mid as\mid sa\\
a_1&\to sa\qquad u\to a\qquad b\to b.
\end{aligned}
\]

each ordinary right-hand side is two variables or one terminal. there is no s₀→ε because the original language did not contain ε.

## what the normal form buys us

for a nonempty string of length n, a cnf parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves and n−1 binary splits: 2n−1 rule applications. the grammar may still have many possible trees, but each tree's size is now tied to the input length. later, this gives finite algorithms for membership.

**keep:** nullable removal preserves disappearing jobs; unit removal bypasses pure handoffs; helpers preserve ordered work while standardizing its size. next we make these operations systematic enough to survive cycles and repeated variables.

**one connected check:** why does replacing asa only by as lose a possibility, even though as is one correct alternative?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: nullable algorithm and fresh start
  • PDF pages 3–4: unit closure and source wording correction
  • PDF page 5: terminal isolation and binary chain
  • PDF pages 6–8: cycle termination and empty-only grammar

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The mental model: change the wiring, keep the possible outputs

Every conversion stage should answer the same question: “How can I reconstruct an old derivation from this new one, and a new derivation from an old one?” If you only check that the final grammar looks like CNF, you can still have the wrong language. Format and equivalence are separate obligations.

We need an order because one repair can create the next kind of unwanted rule. Removing ε rules can create unit rules, so doing unit removal first would leave new handoffs behind.

A recipe can delegate to another recipe that delegates straight back. If your cleanup keeps chasing that loop, you never finish. So we collect what is reachable, remember what we already found, and stop when nothing new appears. That stopping point is a fixed point; it is bookkeeping with a termination reason.

Round 1 — Stop playing whack-a-mole with ε rules · pages 1–2, 6–8

The source cycle S→B|ε, B→S|ε shows why naive editing can loop forever. Remove S→ε and B can recreate it; remove B→ε and S can recreate it. The grammar is finite, but an undisciplined procedure can keep repeating the same work.

Compute the nullable set first. Initially mark variables with an explicit ε rule. Repeatedly mark X when it has a rule whose entire right side consists of already-marked variables. A terminal blocks that reasoning because it cannot disappear. Stop when a complete pass adds no new variable. This stable result is a fixed point. Each productive pass marks something new and there are finitely many variables, so termination is guaranteed.

For the cycle, S and B are both nullable immediately. Add fresh S₀→S and preserve S₀→ε. Generate omission alternatives once, retaining originals, then remove ε rules of nonstart variables. Record handled combinations instead of reintroducing them indefinitely. The original language is only {ε}, so after eliminating unit-only dead ends the final useful CNF grammar can simply be S₀→ε.

Round 2 — A set of reachable delegates kills unit cycles · pages 3–4

A unit rule has exactly one variable on the right, such as A→B. For each X, compute Unit(X), the variables reachable from X using zero or more unit rules. Include X itself: its existing nonunit productions must survive. If X→Y and Y→Z, then Z belongs to Unit(X). If Z→X, you have a cycle, not an instruction to repeat forever.

For every Y in Unit(X), copy each nonunit Y→u as X→u. Then discard unit rules. Page 3's wording says to remove both A→B and B→u; deleting B→u globally would be unsafe when other rules still need B. The intended language-preserving move copies B's work to A and retains B's work. This is a source wording correction, not permission to silently alter the target grammar.

Round 3 — Make one complicated rule obey the two permitted shapes · page 5

Teaching example: X→aBCd. Introduce U→a and V→d. Replace the rule by X→UBCV, then split it into X→UY₁, Y₁→BY₂, Y₂→CV, using fresh helpers. Expand the helpers and you recover the exact ordered string aBCd.

Do not replace a rule X→a by X→U unnecessarily; that creates a forbidden unit rule. Terminal wrappers are needed when a terminal appears in a right side of length at least two. A right side of three or more variables needs a binary chain. A two-variable right side already has the correct shape.

Round 4 — Turn the recipe into checks you can actually use

After fresh start, nullable handling, unit handling, terminal isolation and binary splitting, inspect the result against the definition. Every ordinary alternative must be one terminal or two variables. The designated start must not occur on a right side. Its ε rule must be present exactly when the old language included ε.

Also inspect freshness: helper labels cannot accidentally collide with old variables. Inspect order: BC differs from CB. Inspect occurrences: three nullable appearances create up to 2³ choices before duplicates are merged. Duplicate productions do not change a grammar's language, but losing a distinct omission alternative can.

The conversion is systematic because each stage solves one precise violation. If a rule is still illegal at the end, identify which violation remains instead of restarting the whole procedure. The normal form is a tool for later algorithms; there is no claim that it makes the grammar smallest or easiest for a human to read.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Step 1: protect the start and find all nullable variables

Create S₀→S, with fresh S₀ appearing on no right-hand side. If the original grammar can generate ε, only this protected start will keep that ability in the final CNF.

Find nullable variables by repeated marking. First mark variables with a direct ε rule. Then mark A whenever it has a rule whose entire right-hand side consists of already-nullable variables. A terminal blocks this: a printed a cannot disappear. Repeat until a full pass adds nothing. This is a fixed point: further application changes nothing.

Why repeat? In A→B, B→C, C→ε, A is nullable indirectly. One left-to-right scan could miss it depending on rule order. With finitely many variables, each productive pass adds a mark and the process eventually stops.

Step 2: replace disappearing subtrees with explicit choices

For each rule, choose independently which nullable occurrences to omit. Keep the original rule too. For X→ABA with A nullable and B not nullable, the possibilities are ABA, AB, BA, B. The two As share a variable name but represent separate positions in a derivation.

Do not retain an ordinary empty right-hand side after this stage. Preserve S₀→ε exactly when the original start was nullable. Then remove the original ε rules from other variables.

Cycles need no special magic. With S→B|ε and B→S|ε, both variables are nullable; the language is just {ε}. The protected start may generate ε, but there is no terminal-producing work to invent. A conversion that manufactures a from this grammar is obviously wrong.

Here's the bit that makes the omission rule click. In an old derivation, a nullable variable might spend five steps becoming ε. In the new grammar, its parent can choose an alternative that leaves that position out immediately. Same finished word; fewer internal moves. We preserve the possible output, not the exact history of how it got printed.

Step 3: follow unit reachability, then copy real work

A unit rule has exactly one variable on its right, such as A→B. For each A, find every B reachable by zero or more unit rules. Copy every nonunit B-production onto A. Then remove unit rules.

Example: A→B, B→C, C→a|DE. A needs A→a|DE, and B needs B→a|DE. C keeps its original alternatives. The slides' CNF2 page 3 wording about removing B→u should not be read as deleting the nonunit production being copied; doing that can destroy valid outputs. Retain the useful nonunit rules.

Step 4: make terminal leaves and binary splits explicit

For X→aBCd, use U→a and V→d, then X→UBCV. Break the four-variable sequence into a chain, for example X→UH₁, H₁→BH₂, H₂→CV. Reading the leaves still gives a, then B's output, then C's, then d. Fresh helpers prevent collisions with existing variable meanings.

A rule X→a is already valid. Do not replace it by X→U unless you also remove the new unit rule afterward. The goal is standard shape, not maximum helper count.

A final audit you can actually perform

Check every right-hand side's shape; ensure only the protected start may produce ε; ensure that start never occurs on a right-hand side; inspect repeated nullable positions; inspect unit chains and cycles; compare a few boundary strings to catch errors. Finite examples can expose a mistake, but the stage-by-stage derivation argument establishes equivalence for all strings.

Keep: compute closures first, then rewrite from the complete information. Next, a PDA will execute pending grammatical work using a stack.

One connected check: Why can removing ε rules create unit rules, and why does that determine the order of the conversion stages?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: stack memory and LIFO
  • PDF pages 4–7: equal-block PDA and full configuration traces
  • PDF pages 8–9: six-tuple and transition types
  • PDF pages 10–11: accept states, epsilon and nine-column table

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Why give a machine a stack?

For 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, after reading n zeros the machine owes n matching ones. A DFA has only finitely many states, so it cannot keep a different state for every possible debt. A PDA adds a stack: a potentially unbounded pile where we can touch only the top. Push one marker per zero; pop one per one. Now the size of the debt is stored outside the finite control.

The state remembers the phase—still reading zeros, or already matching ones. The stack remembers the amount owed. Mixing those jobs makes diagrams feel random. Separating them makes the arrows follow from the requirement.

Think of each pushed zero as an IOU: “a future 1 must pay for this.” The $ marker says there are no more IOUs underneath. The control state says whether issuing new IOUs is still allowed. Once payment starts, a new zero isn't “more of the same”; it violates the required block order. That's why we need both the stack and the phase state.

Each zero hands the machine an IOU: “you owe me one matching one later.” The stack keeps the unpaid IOUs. The state remembers whether we are still collecting zeros or already paying with ones. Both jobs matter. A balanced total cannot rescue input whose zeros and ones arrived in the wrong order.

Round 1 — State remembers the phase; stack remembers the debt · pages 1–3

For 0ⁿ1ⁿ, every zero creates an obligation: a matching one must arrive later. Push one marker for each zero; pop one for each one. The finite state records whether we are still reading zeros or have switched to ones. Both pieces matter. Counts alone would wrongly allow 0101, and phase alone cannot remember an arbitrarily large count.

A stack allows access only at its top: last in, first out. A cafeteria plate pile captures this access rule. It does not mean the stack is physically finite in the mathematical model; its alphabet is finite, but the number of stored symbols has no fixed bound. Push adds a top symbol; pop removes the top symbol; replacing means pop then push. The model cannot reach into the middle and remove whichever marker is convenient.

Round 2 — Read every field of an arrow · pages 4–9

An arrow a,b→c means consume input a, pop stack symbol b, push c, and move to the arrow's destination state. ε in the input field means consume no input. ε in the pop field means do not inspect or remove the top. ε in the push field means add nothing. These are three independent fields. In particular, ε in the pop field is not an empty-stack test.

0,ε→0 reads a zero and pushes a zero. 1,0→ε reads a one and removes a matching zero. ε,ε→$ installs a bottom marker without input. ε,$→ε removes that marker when it is exposed. $ is a stack symbol, not an input character. It makes “all unmatched zeros are gone” visible through the top-only interface.

Use a configuration record (state, unread input, stack) with top written leftmost. For 0011:

(q₁, 0011, ε)
(q₂, 0011, $)        install bottom marker
(q₂, 011, 0$)        read first zero
(q₂, 11, 00$)        read second zero
(q₃, 1, 0$)          read first one, switch phase
(q₃, ε, $)           read second one
(q₄, ε, ε)           remove marker, accept

For 00011, one zero marker remains after input ends, so the marker-removal move is unavailable and q₄ cannot be reached. For 00111, matching the two zeros leaves one unread one; reaching q₄ early does not accept the whole input. For ε, q₁ itself accepts. That explains F={q₁,q₄}, including why there can be two accepting states.

Round 3 — The huge type is only a three-field lookup · pages 8–11

The PDA tuple adds Γ, the stack alphabet, to the finite-state fields. Its transition type is

δ:Q×Σε×Γε→P(Q×Γε).\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\Gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q\times\Gamma_\varepsilon).δ:Q×Σε​×Γε​→P(Q×Γε​).

Input: current state, next-input choice, pop requirement. Output: a set of (next state, symbol to push) options. The power set permits multiple options or none. Destination entries are pairs because the transition must specify both movement and stack output.

Here Σₑ={0,1,ε} and Γₑ={0,$,ε}. Three input choices times three pop choices gives nine columns per row. That's why the formal table looks wider than an NFA table. Empty cells mean no option. A table of all nonempty transitions plus “all others ∅” can be a complete specification, provided every displayed entry has the correct pair/set format.

The slide sometimes writes stack contents with braces. Read those as ordered stack displays, not mathematical sets: [0,0,$] has two zero markers, and their multiplicity matters. Using a string such as 00$ avoids that notation trap.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the deck's counted-block machine

Use $ as a fresh bottom marker. It is a stack symbol, not an input symbol. Push it before processing a nonempty candidate. During the zero phase, each input 0 pushes a 0. The first 1 changes to the matching phase and pops a 0. Further ones keep popping. When the top becomes $, an ε move can remove it and enter accept.

There are no input-consuming transitions for 0 after the matching phase begins: that enforces block order. There is no matching 1 transition when only $ remains: that prevents too many ones. The original start is accepting to include ε when n=0.

Trace 0011, writing the stack top first:

Work completed Stack Meaning
initialize $ no zeros owed yet
read first 0 0$ owe one 1
read second 0 00$ owe two
read first 1 0$ owe one
read second 1 $ debt paid
finish by ε move empty enter accept with input consumed

001 leaves an unpaid marker. 00111 has an extra input symbol after the markers run out. 0101 tries to return to the zero phase. All reject, for different clauses of the language.

Read an arrow without guessing

A label a, b → c says: consume input symbol a, pop stack-top b, push c. ε in the input position consumes nothing. ε in the pop position means do not pop, not “test that the stack is empty.” ε in the push position means push nothing.

So 0, ε → 0 reads a zero and adds a marker without removing the old top. 1, 0 → ε reads a one and removes a zero marker. ε, $ → ε tests for and removes the actual bottom marker without reading input.

The formal symbols describe those three jobs

A PDA is (Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0,F)(Q,\Sigma,\Gamma,\delta,q_0,F)(Q,Σ,Γ,δ,q0​,F). Q, Σ, q₀, F still mean states, input alphabet, start, accepting states. Γ is the stack alphabet. The transition type

δ:Q×Σε×Γε→P(Q×Γε)\delta:Q\times\Sigma_\varepsilon\times\Gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal P(Q\times\Gamma_\varepsilon)δ:Q×Σε​×Γε​→P(Q×Γε​)

takes a state, an input choice, and a pop choice; returns a set of (next state, push choice) pairs. The power set P\mathcal PP allows zero, one, or several alternatives. It is not an unordered representation of the stack—the stack itself remains ordered.

Acceptance requires some run to consume all input and finish in an accepting state. General final-state acceptance does not also require an empty stack; this construction uses $ to enforce the intended balance before accepting.

Keep: state = phase; stack = ordered pending obligations. Next we use nondeterminism when the input does not tell us which obligation to check or where the midpoint lies.

One connected check: For 001, which obligation is still on the stack, and why does entering an accepting state early not magically consume it or the remaining input?

```text
(q₂, 0011, $)        install bottom marker
(q₂, 011, 0$)        read first zero
(q₂, 11, 00$)        read second zero
(q₃, 1, 0$)          read first one, switch phase
(q₃, ε, $)           read second one
(q₄, ε, ε)           remove marker, accept
```

for `00011`, one zero marker remains after input ends, so the marker-removal move is unavailable and q₄ cannot be reached. for `00111`, matching the two zeros leaves one unread one; reaching q₄ early does not accept the whole input. for ε, q₁ itself accepts. that explains f={q₁,q₄}, including why there can be two accepting states.

## round 3 — the huge type is only a three-field lookup · pages 8–11

the pda tuple adds γ, the stack alphabet, to the finite-state fields. its transition type is

\[\delta:q\times\sigma_\varepsilon\times\gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal p(q\times\gamma_\varepsilon).\]

input: current state, next-input choice, pop requirement. output: a set of `(next state, symbol to push)` options. the power set permits multiple options or none. destination entries are pairs because the transition must specify both movement and stack output.

here σₑ={0,1,ε} and γₑ={0,$,ε}. three input choices times three pop choices gives nine columns per row. that's why the formal table looks wider than an nfa table. empty cells mean no option. a table of all nonempty transitions plus “all others ∅” can be a complete specification, provided every displayed entry has the correct pair/set format.

the slide sometimes writes stack contents with braces. read those as ordered stack displays, not mathematical sets: `[0,0,$]` has two zero markers, and their multiplicity matters. using a string such as `00$` avoids that notation trap.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## build the deck's counted-block machine

use `$` as a fresh bottom marker. it is a stack symbol, not an input symbol. push it before processing a nonempty candidate. during the zero phase, each input `0` pushes a `0`. the first `1` changes to the matching phase and pops a `0`. further ones keep popping. when the top becomes `$`, an ε move can remove it and enter accept.

there are no input-consuming transitions for `0` after the matching phase begins: that enforces block order. there is no matching `1` transition when only `$` remains: that prevents too many ones. the original start is accepting to include ε when n=0.

trace `0011`, writing the stack **top first**:

| work completed | stack | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| initialize | `$` | no zeros owed yet |
| read first `0` | `0$` | owe one `1` |
| read second `0` | `00$` | owe two |
| read first `1` | `0$` | owe one |
| read second `1` | `$` | debt paid |
| finish by ε move | empty | enter accept with input consumed |

`001` leaves an unpaid marker. `00111` has an extra input symbol after the markers run out. `0101` tries to return to the zero phase. all reject, for different clauses of the language.

## read an arrow without guessing

a label `a, b → c` says: consume input symbol a, pop stack-top b, push c. ε in the input position consumes nothing. ε in the pop position means **do not pop**, not “test that the stack is empty.” ε in the push position means push nothing.

so `0, ε → 0` reads a zero and adds a marker without removing the old top. `1, 0 → ε` reads a one and removes a zero marker. `ε, $ → ε` tests for and removes the actual bottom marker without reading input.

## the formal symbols describe those three jobs

a pda is \((q,\sigma,\gamma,\delta,q_0,f)\). q, σ, q₀, f still mean states, input alphabet, start, accepting states. γ is the stack alphabet. the transition type

\[\delta:q\times\sigma_\varepsilon\times\gamma_\varepsilon\to\mathcal p(q\times\gamma_\varepsilon)\]

takes a state, an input choice, and a pop choice; returns a **set of (next state, push choice) pairs**. the power set \(\mathcal p\) allows zero, one, or several alternatives. it is not an unordered representation of the stack—the stack itself remains ordered.

acceptance requires some run to consume **all input** and finish in an accepting state. general final-state acceptance does not also require an empty stack; this construction uses `$` to enforce the intended balance before accepting.

**keep:** state = phase; stack = ordered pending obligations. next we use nondeterminism when the input does not tell us which obligation to check or where the midpoint lies.

**one connected check:** for `001`, which obligation is still on the stack, and why does entering an accepting state early not magically consume it or the remaining input?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–5: union of count checks and configuration branching
  • PDF pages 6–7: even palindromes, reverse and midpoint guess

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The problem: the input may not announce the right plan

Consider {aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}\{a^ib^jc^k:i,j,k\ge0,\ i=j\text{ or }i=k\}{aibjck:i,j,k≥0, i=j or i=k}. Read it carefully: there are three blocks in order, and either the a-count matches the b-count or it matches the c-count. Both equalities may hold, but both are not required.

A nondeterministic PDA can branch into two plans. Both store the a-count on the stack. One matches it against b's, then scans c's. The other scans b's without spending the stored markers, then matches against c's. Each branch has its own stack history. There is no shared pile that the first branch can damage for the second.

Two branches can stand in the same state with different stacks. Same room, different backpacks. If you merge them by room number, you lose the exact obligations they carry, and your trace starts accepting nonsense. Keep the state, unread input and ordered stack together as one whole situation.

Round 1 — OR means one full check can succeed · pages 1–5

The language {aⁱbʲcᵏ:i=j or i=k} requires block order a's, then b's, then c's. The equality is an OR, so either equality suffices; both may hold. The PDA stores one a marker per leading a and nondeterministically chooses which equality to verify.

In the upper branch it pops an a for each b, demands all a markers be exhausted, then reads any c suffix. In the lower branch it reads b's without changing the stored a count, then pops an a per c. States enforce block order in both branches. Arbitrarily matching any later symbols would solve a different language.

The slide's a²bc² is aabcc: i=2,j=1,k=2. The upper branch matches its one b against one a and still owes one a match; it cannot complete the i=j check. The lower branch keeps two a markers while reading b, then pops one for each c and reaches acceptance. One failed branch and one successful branch means accept.

A PDA's branch identity must include the entire stack as well as the state and input position. Two branches at q with stacks a$ and aa$ are not equivalent. Merging them into just {q} loses the count that future input needs. This is why the finite-state subset trick does not directly turn every PDA into a DPDA: the number of possible stacks is unbounded.

The ε moves choose phases without consuming symbols. A branch may guess too early or too late and die. Wrong guesses are permitted; a successful path still has to consume the whole input and meet the actual stack requirements.

Round 2 — Reverse comes from stack order · pages 6–7

wᴿ means the symbols of w in reverse order. For w=01, wᴿ=10, so wwᴿ=0110. For w=001, wwᴿ=001100. This language contains even-length palindromes, including ε; it does not include odd-length 010 in this particular construction.

Push each first-half symbol, then guess the midpoint using an ε move. After the switch, read each input symbol only if it matches the top and pop it. If the first half was 01, the stack top-to-bottom is 10$: the reversal is already supplied by last-in-first-out storage. You do not separately reverse the input.

Trace the successful branch of 0110: install $, push 0 giving 0$, push 1 giving 10$, switch without input, read 1 and pop 1, read 0 and pop 0, remove $, finish in accept with no unread input. A branch switching after the first 0 tries to match the next 1 against top 0 and dies. A branch never switching cannot finish the required matching phase.

Round 3 — Why a delimiter changes the design problem

With a promised midpoint marker, such as language {w#wᴿ}, the input itself tells the machine when to switch from pushing to popping. Without it, this NFA-style PDA guesses. This comparison explains what nondeterminism contributes; it is not by itself a proof that no deterministic PDA can recognize the unmarked language. Claims about all possible machines need a separate impossibility argument.

Both examples combine finite phase memory with unbounded structured memory. The stack handles the obligation; the state says what kind of work is currently legal. Keeping those roles separate makes the arrows far less arbitrary.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Follow a concrete case

For aabcc, the counts are i=2, j=1, k=2. The a=b branch spends one of its two markers on the sole b and still owes a b when c begins, so that branch fails. The a=c branch ignores the b, spends two markers on the two c's, and succeeds at the end of input. Therefore the NFA-style acceptance rule—at least one complete successful run—accepts the string.

A single rejecting branch does not reject the whole input. A branch that reaches an accepting state with unread input also does not accept the whole input. Keep the complete condition intact.

Another missing boundary: the midpoint of a palindrome

For {wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}\{ww^R:w\in\{0,1\}^*\}{wwR:w∈{0,1}∗}, wRw^RwR means w reversed. The first half must be matched against its reverse, so a stack's last-in-first-out behavior fits perfectly. Push the first half. At a guessed midpoint, switch by ε to popping and comparing.

Trace 0110. Push 0, then 1, giving stack 10$ top-first. Guess the midpoint. Read the next 1 and pop 1; read the last 0 and pop 0; finish at $ with no input left. The successful guess consumed exactly two symbols before switching.

Why not switch after just the first 0? The next symbol would be 1, but the stack expects 0, so that branch dies. Why not push all four symbols? Then no input remains to discharge the four markers. A bad guess failing is fine; a correct complete path is enough.

What a node in your trace must contain

A PDA configuration needs three pieces: current state, unread input, and entire stack. Two branches at the same state with different stacks are not the same configuration. Merging them as if this were NFA subset construction loses information.

A tree is useful: each node is a full configuration; each edge is one allowed transition. A table is useful too, provided each row retains all three fields. The representation is a tool, not the algorithm's definition. For an exam, label enough that a reader can check the pop condition and input consumption at every step.

Why this connects to grammars

A grammar also chooses among alternatives, some of which cannot generate the desired terminal string. A PDA can store the grammar's pending work and guess which production to use. That's the next deck: not an unrelated trick, but these same branching obligations applied to derivations.

Keep: a PDA branch carries its own state, remaining input, and stack. Nondeterminism guesses a plan; acceptance still demands that the whole plan works.

One connected check: If two branches have the same state and unread input but stacks 01$ and 10$, why can't you combine them into one stack set {0,1,$}?

complete source trace and both-direction invariant

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: equivalence direction and grammar language
  • PDF pages 3–7: reverse push, helper states and matching
  • PDF pages 8–10: complete source trace and both-direction invariant

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The bridge: generating a string and checking a string can cooperate

A grammar chooses how to build output. A PDA can guess those grammar choices while checking them against the supplied input. Its stack means: this is the sequence still owed by the current derivation. The next owed symbol belongs on top, so we can deal with it first.

The deck's grammar is S→aTb∣bS\to aTb\mid bS→aTb∣b, T→Ta∣εT\to Ta\mid\varepsilonT→Ta∣ε. S either produces a single b, or an a, then T's output, then b. T can produce any number of a's. So the language consists of b and all strings of one or more a's followed by one b.

The stack is the machine's to-do list, with the next job on top. Expanding a variable breaks a job into smaller jobs. Matching a terminal checks off finished output against the actual input. Don't let the notation blur those actions together: planning an a and reading an a are two different damn steps.

The stack changes jobs here. Instead of unpaid IOUs from earlier input, it stores the grammar’s future to-do list. The next job has to sit on top. That is why push order matters: shove the list on backward and the machine tries to print the sentence backward. Let’s make that ordering explicit.

Round 1 — The stack becomes a to-do list for a derivation · pages 1–2

The theorem says a language is context-free exactly when some PDA recognizes it. This deck proves CFG→PDA. Start with a grammar and build a machine that guesses a derivation while checking its terminal output against the supplied input.

The source grammar is S→aTb|b and T→Ta|ε. T can make any number of a's: each use of T→Ta adds a pending a, and T→ε stops. Therefore S makes b, or one initial a followed by any number of additional a's and a final b. In compact notation its language is a*b. Recognizing that language directly is easier than the general conversion, but the slide deliberately demonstrates the conversion procedure.

Round 2 — Why the right side gets pushed backward · pages 3–7

For S→aTb, the next input to check is a, then whatever T generates, then b. The stack must therefore have a on top, T underneath, and b underneath T. Push b first, then T, then a. If you push a first, b ends up on top and the machine tries to read the output backward. That ain't a harmless implementation detail.

Initialize with $ and then S. At the main loop, if the top is a variable, nondeterministically choose one of its productions and replace it by the right side. If the top is a terminal t, consume exactly input t and pop it. If only $ remains, remove it and go to the accepting state.

A course PDA transition pushes at most one symbol, so pushing a whole right side is shorthand for a chain through fresh helper states. Those helper states must have only the intended continuation; otherwise another rule could interrupt halfway through the push. Rule expansion consumes ε input. Terminal matching consumes real input. If you include only expansion arrows, you can generate a stack forever while never checking a single input symbol.

Round 3 — Read the slide's aaaab trace as unfinished output · pages 8–9

After initializing S$, choose S→aTb and obtain top-left aTb$. Match the first a: unread input becomes aaab, stack Tb$. Expand T→Ta three times: Tab$, Taab$, Taaab$. Then choose T→ε, leaving aaab$. Match the remaining three a's and b one by one; only $ remains. Remove it, with no input left, and accept.

Notice the subtlety: while T keeps expanding, those extra a's wait below it. They are not consumed until T is removed. The stack represents future required output, not a bag of characters already seen. The old “stack counts previous zeros” example used the same data structure for a different purpose.

Round 4 — Why guessing can't fabricate a wrong string · page 10

At main-loop checkpoints, the already-consumed input prefix followed by the pending stack string above $ is a sentential form derivable from S. A variable expansion applies a genuine production, preserving that statement. A terminal match shifts the first pending terminal into the consumed prefix without changing their concatenation.

If the machine accepts after consuming all input and exhausting pending work, the complete input was generated by the grammar. Conversely, choose a leftmost derivation of any grammar-generated string; the machine can choose the same productions and match its terminals, reaching acceptance. These are the two correctness directions.

A branch that reaches the accepting state with unread input does not accept that input. A branch that expands forever produces no finite accepting run. Neither invalidates the construction; the existence of a correct finite branch is what matters. Nonaccepting branches are not allowed to vote down the successful one.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

There are only two kinds of work

If the stack top is a variable, replace it using a grammar production. This consumes no input, because choosing how to produce a symbol is not the same as matching an actual symbol.

If the top is a terminal, it must equal the next input symbol. Consume that input symbol and pop the matching terminal. If they disagree, that branch has no matching move. A terminal cannot be expanded into something more convenient.

Initialize with S above a fresh bottom marker $. Finish when the pending work is exhausted, by removing $ and entering accept. Input must also be fully consumed.

A complete trace of aaab

Write the stack top first; omit $ in this table only to make the pending work visible.

Move Unread input Pending stack
initialize aaab S
choose S→aTb aaab aTb
match a aab Tb
choose T→Ta aab Tab
choose T→Ta aab Taab
choose T→ε aab aab
match a ab ab
match a b b
match b ε empty

Now $ can be removed and the run can accept. Notice how T→Ta adds a pending a after T. Expanding the variable repeatedly builds more work without consuming input; terminal matching pays it off afterward.

Why pushes appear reversed on the diagram

To leave aTb top-first, physically push b first, then T, then a. The last pushed symbol is on top. That is a consequence of stack order, not a rule that reverses the generated language. If a diagram abbreviates a multi-symbol push, expand it into single pushes in that order using fresh intermediate states.

With a wrong production choice, the machine may get stuck. It can also keep choosing T→Ta forever. Such a branch does not accept. A finite successful derivation supplies a finite successful branch; existence of other bad branches doesn't invalidate it.

Why the conversion is correct

After matching a prefix of the input, the stack records the ungenerated/unmatched remainder of a chosen leftmost derivation. Variable expansion changes that remainder exactly as a grammar step would. Terminal matching removes the next symbol only when it agrees with the input.

Thus a successful run describes a grammar derivation of the entire input. Conversely, a derivation of the input tells the PDA which productions to choose, giving a successful run. This is the two-way language-equality proof; tracing aaab alone is only an illustration.

Keep: expand variables without input; match terminals with input. Next we reverse the bridge: describe a PDA's balanced stack behavior with grammar variables.

One connected check: Why would consuming an a while applying S→aTb, and then consuming another when popping that terminal a, be wrong?

| choose s→atb | `aaab` | atb |
| match `a` | `aab` | tb |
| choose t→ta | `aab` | tab |
| choose t→ta | `aab` | taab |
| choose t→ε | `aab` | aab |
| match `a` | `ab` | ab |
| match `a` | `b` | b |
| match `b` | ε | empty |

now `$` can be removed and the run can accept. notice how t→ta adds a pending a **after** t. expanding the variable repeatedly builds more work without consuming input; terminal matching pays it off afterward.

## why pushes appear reversed on the diagram

to leave `atb` top-first, physically push b first, then t, then a. the last pushed symbol is on top. that is a consequence of stack order, not a rule that reverses the generated language. if a diagram abbreviates a multi-symbol push, expand it into single pushes in that order using fresh intermediate states.

with a wrong production choice, the machine may get stuck. it can also keep choosing t→ta forever. such a branch does not accept. a finite successful derivation supplies a finite successful branch; existence of other bad branches doesn't invalidate it.

## why the conversion is correct

after matching a prefix of the input, the stack records the ungenerated/unmatched remainder of a chosen leftmost derivation. variable expansion changes that remainder exactly as a grammar step would. terminal matching removes the next symbol only when it agrees with the input.

thus a successful run describes a grammar derivation of the entire input. conversely, a derivation of the input tells the pda which productions to choose, giving a successful run. this is the two-way language-equality proof; tracing `aaab` alone is only an illustration.

**keep:** expand variables without input; match terminals with input. next we reverse the bridge: describe a pda's balanced stack behavior with grammar variables.

**one connected check:** why would consuming an `a` while applying s→atb, and then consuming another when popping that terminal `a`, be wrong?
