Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: balanced variable meaning and normal assumptions
  • PDF pages 3–6: concatenation, wrapping and empty rules
  • PDF pages 7–10: source example, counts and derivation

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

What the sixteen variables are actually for

With four PDA states, the standard conversion introduces one variable Aₚᵩ for each ordered pair of states p,q: 4×4=16 variables. That does not mean the PDA suddenly has sixteen states. We are building a grammar whose variables summarize different kinds of journey through the original machine.

Aₚᵩ means: strings consumed by a run that starts in p with an empty stack and ends in q with an empty stack. The same run pattern can sit above a protected existing stack: it may build and clear extra work but never pop below that baseline. Merely having the same stack at both endpoints is not enough if the run disturbed the protected contents in between.

The PDA first needs a single accepting state, empty-stack completion, and transitions that each push or pop one symbol. The next deck explains that normalization carefully.

Think of a balanced segment as a subroutine that promises: “Whatever stack was underneath me, I'll leave it alone and clean up everything I add.” Aₚᵩ names that contract together with its entry and exit states. The grammar doesn't store a stack snapshot. It describes strings that can be read while honoring that contract.

Those subscripts name the start and finish of a whole trip. Imagine borrowing some workspace, doing a subroutine, then returning with the old workspace untouched. Aₚq names the input consumed by such a trip from p to q. It does not name one arrow. That distinction makes the 16 variables make sense.

Round 1 — Aₚq describes a whole balanced trip · pages 1–3

A variable Aₚq is one grammar variable whose label contains two state names. It describes input strings consumed by a computation that starts in p, ends in q, and leaves the underlying stack untouched. During the trip, temporary symbols may be pushed and popped, but the computation must never pop below its starting stack height. That's the protected baseline condition.

Picture a subroutine borrowing desk space above a sealed folder. It can stack temporary papers and remove them, but must leave the sealed folder intact. Merely ending with a folder that looks the same is not enough if it opened and used the original during the trip. Likewise, equal endpoint stack strings alone do not express the needed condition.

Normalize the PDA to one accepting state, empty stack at acceptance, and transitions that each push or pop one symbol. The next deck explains those modifications. Then A_start,accept describes exactly the complete accepting computations, so it becomes the grammar's start variable.

Round 2 — The three rule families describe three shapes of trip · pages 3–6

Do two balanced trips: Aₚq→AₚrAᵣq. First go p→r while restoring the baseline; then go r→q while restoring it again. The concatenated input spells the whole journey. The intermediate r ranges over every state.

Wrap a balanced trip in a matching push and pop: suppose a move p→r consumes a and pushes t, and a move s→q consumes b and pops that same t. Add Aₚq→aAᵣs b. The inner trip r→s operates above the newly pushed t and returns without consuming it. Then the outer pop removes it. a or b may be ε, contributing no terminal.

The four labels have roles: p is before the push; r after it; s before the matching pop; q after it. r and s need not be adjacent states or equal. Pairing a push with every pop of the same stack symbol generates candidate productions; impossible inner trips simply cannot derive terminal strings.

Do nothing: Aₚp→ε. With zero moves, start and finish at p with unchanged stack and empty consumed input. It does not imply Aₚq→ε for arbitrary different endpoints.

Round 3 — The “16 states” confusion is really 16 variables · pages 7–10

The example PDA has four states. Ordered endpoint pairs give 4×4=16 grammar variables A₁₁,…,A₄₄. These are not 16 states of a new PDA. Concatenation rules use triples p,r,q: 4³=64 generated rules before simplification. The formula is compact because listing every one is repetitive; each still has a concrete endpoint meaning.

The bottom-marker push 1→2 and pop 3→4 yield A₁₄→A₂₃, because both consume ε. Pair the zero-push loop at 2 with either zero-pop move, obtaining A₂₃→0A₂₂1 and A₂₃→0A₂₃1. With A₂₂→ε, a derivation is A₁₄⇒A₂₃⇒0A₂₃1⇒00A₂₂11⇒0011. The outer $ pair wraps the whole computation; each inner 0/1 pair matches one pushed zero.

The language here uses n≥1, unlike the earlier n≥0 example: original q₁ is no longer accepting. Reused circle labels do not mean the acceptance condition stayed the same.

Round 4 — Why those three shapes cover every balanced computation

For soundness, induct on a finite derivation tree. Empty rules do nothing; concatenation joins two valid balanced trips; wrapping performs a matching push, a valid inner trip and its matching pop. Thus each generated string corresponds to a valid computation.

For completeness, induct on the number of transitions in a balanced computation. Zero transitions uses Aₚp→ε. If the stack returns to baseline at an intermediate point, split there and use a concatenation rule on the two shorter trips. If it never returns early, its first push is matched by the last pop; the middle is a shorter balanced trip above that symbol, so use a wrapping rule. Inducting on transitions, rather than input length, matters because ε moves can add transitions without adding characters.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Two ways a balanced journey can be built

A balanced journey can consist of two balanced journeys in sequence. If r is the intermediate state, add

Apq→AprArq.A_{pq}\to A_{pr}A_{rq}.Apq​→Apr​Arq​.

The right side says: do p→r work, then r→q work. For each p,q,r, this is a possible decomposition. It doesn't say every input takes every route.

Or the journey pushes a symbol t, performs some balanced work above it, then pops that same t. If a push transition goes p→r while consuming a, and a matching pop goes s→q while consuming b, add

Apq→aArsb.A_{pq}\to aA_{rs}b.Apq​→aArs​b.

a and b may be ε. The inner variable covers the part between the push and its matching pop. The pushed symbol's identity must match; a push of 0 cannot be paired with a pop of $ just because the state arrows line up.

Finally Aₚₚ→ε permits doing nothing: same start and end state, no stack change, no input consumed.

Work the deck's four-state example

The normalized machine for positive 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n pushes $ from state 1 to 2, pushes zeros in state 2, begins popping zeros on the move to state 3, continues popping there, and pops $ from 3 to accepting 4.

Pair the outside $ push and pop: A14→A23A_{14}\to A_{23}A14​→A23​. Their input labels are both ε, so nothing is printed around the inner variable.

Pair a zero push 2→2 with the zero pop 3→3: A23→0A231A_{23}\to0A_{23}1A23​→0A23​1. Pair that push with the first zero pop 2→3: A23→0A221A_{23}\to0A_{22}1A23​→0A22​1. Use A₂₂→ε to finish the smallest balanced interior.

Now derive 0011:

A14⇒A23⇒0A231⇒00A2211⇒0011.A_{14}\Rightarrow A_{23}\Rightarrow0A_{23}1\Rightarrow00A_{22}11\Rightarrow0011.A14​⇒A23​⇒0A23​1⇒00A22​11⇒0011.

Every rule is tied to an actual push/pop pair. The matching grammar nesting reflects matching stack lifetimes.

Decode the four subscripts by their jobs

Letter Where it sits in the wrapped run
p before the outside push
r immediately after that push
s immediately before its matching pop
q after that pop

So Aₚᵩ names the whole wrapped journey, while Aᵣₛ names just the inside. The source's table lists p,r,s,q in this order to keep those roles visible. The p and q in one rule are allowed to coincide with other listed states; these letters name roles, not necessarily four distinct circles.

With four states, the full construction also lists 4³=64 concatenation rules, one for each choice of p,q,r, and four Aₚₚ→ε rules. An exam may require the complete construction even if most variables later prove useless. Counts come from choices of endpoints and middle states, not from new PDA states appearing out of nowhere.

Why the general construction needs concatenation too

A run may return to its baseline halfway through, then start a new balanced section. That isn't one push wrapped around the entire run. The concatenation rules capture these side-by-side sections. If a nonempty balanced run has no intermediate return to baseline, its first push must be matched by its final pop, which gives the wrapping case. This decomposition supports an induction on run length.

The reverse direction follows the grammar: empty rule does nothing; concatenation joins two valid runs; wrapping adds a matching push and pop around a valid inner run. That establishes exact correspondence, not just a few example strings.

Keep: Aₚᵩ is a name for balanced work between states. Four states give sixteen such names because both endpoints matter.

One connected check: In Aₚᵩ→aAᵣₛb, which two transitions determine p,r,s,q, and why must their stack symbols agree?

models.title: PDA normalization: make completion safe before converting
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF page 1: overall conversion specification
  • PDF pages 2–6: unsafe cleanup and supplied counterexample
  • PDF pages 7–8: isolated cleanup and unread-input protection
  • PDF page 9: one push or pop normalization
  • PDF pages 10–11: regular subset and non-CFL boundary

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The hidden issue: accepting state does not mean the stack is empty

Our general PDA accepts when a run consumes all input and finishes in an accepting state. It may still have stack contents. But the PDA→CFG construction summarizes balanced empty-to-empty runs. We therefore need an equivalent PDA that finishes with an empty stack at one designated accepting state.

This is a change of representation, not permission to change which strings accept. A cleanup gadget is correct only if it cannot help the original machine do extra input processing that used to be impossible.

Cleanup sounds harmless until the machine dumps its stack and strolls back into ordinary computation with evidence erased. That can accept new strings and fuck up the language. We need a one-way exit into cleanup. The source counterexample shows exactly what goes wrong when that boundary is missing.

Round 1 — Why “just pop the leftovers” can break the language · pages 1–6

The tempting cleanup edit adds pop-anything loops directly to each old accepting state. The slide gives a counterexample because that lets the machine clean the stack and then resume old computation. It may expose a symbol the original machine could never access at that point.

In the source example, ε moves push a and then b, producing top-left ba. The next real input a requires top a, but b blocks it, so the old machine does not accept a. With an added cleanup pop at an old accepting state, the machine can remove b, return to an original transition, consume a while popping a, and accept. The transformed machine has invented a new accepting behavior. Same intended goal, wrong implementation.

This is why correctness review must trace a counterexample, not merely admire that the diagram “clears the stack.” An added arrow changes the set of possible computations everywhere it can be taken.

Round 2 — Cleanup must be a one-way commitment · pages 7–8

Add a fresh start that pushes a fresh bottom marker $ before entering the old start. From every old accepting state, allow an ε move into one separate cleanup state q_pop. In q_pop, consume no input and pop ordinary stack symbols until $ is exposed; then pop $ and enter the unique new accept state. The old accepting states stop being accepting in the transformed machine.

There is no arrow from cleanup back into the old computation. A branch may enter cleanup while input remains, but it can never consume that remainder and therefore cannot accept the whole input. So we do not need a magical “input is finished” sensor. The no-return structure plus the acceptance definition enforces the condition.

If the old machine has a valid accepting run, enter cleanup afterward and finish. If the new machine accepts, its pre-cleanup part was a legal old run ending in an old accepting state after consuming all input. That proves equivalence in both directions.

Round 3 — Make every transition change stack height by exactly one · page 9

For a replace move a,b→c, first consume a and pop b into a fresh helper state; then consume ε and push c into the destination. For a no-change move a,ε→ε, first consume a and push a fresh dummy marker; then consume ε and pop that dummy into the destination. Each helper has only its designated outgoing continuation.

The dummy is temporary bookkeeping, not a terminal and not an original stack symbol with hidden meaning. Make it fresh so no original operation confuses it with its own markers. A push-only or pop-only move already has the required form. The splitting preserves consumed input and stack effect while making the balanced-trip grammar proof applicable.

Round 4 — Where the language families fit · pages 10–11

A DFA is simulated by a PDA that ignores its stack: on each symbol, make the DFA state update with no pop and no push. Since every PDA language is context-free, every regular language is context-free. The inclusion is strict because 0ⁿ1ⁿ is context-free and not regular. “More powerful” here means a larger family of recognizable languages, not automatically faster execution.

The final slide mentions non-context-free languages but omits their proof. A useful extra boundary example is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ:n≥0}. Its standard proof needs the context-free pumping lemma, a different theorem from the regular pumping lemma. It says sufficiently long members split as uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, |vy|>0, and uvⁱxyⁱz staying in the language for every i≥0.

For aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the short middle window vxy cannot reach all three blocks. Deleting v and y removes at least one symbol, affects at most two block types, and leaves at least one block's count p unchanged. The three counts cannot remain equal, contradicting the lemma. This is a supplementary application of that theorem, whose own parse-tree proof is outside these slides. A regular pumping argument alone would only show nonregularity, not non-context-freeness.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Why “just add pop loops” is broken

Suppose an old accepting state has stack ba$, top first, and a future input transition needs to pop a. In the original machine that transition is blocked by the top b. If we add arbitrary ε-pop loops directly to this state, it can discard b, expose a, and resume the original transition. We have handed the machine a new way to process unread input. Shit—that changes behavior before completion, not just afterward.

The deck illustrates precisely this danger: cleanup mixed into the old control can accept a string the original PDA rejects. A final-state label is not a magical barrier against later transitions.

The safe gadget is a one-way exit

Add a fresh bottom marker under the original stack contents. Add a fresh drain state. From each old accepting state, allow an ε handoff into this drain. There, pop original stack symbols using ε transitions. When the fresh bottom marker appears, pop it and enter the sole new accepting state.

There is no way back to the old machine and no input-consuming transition in the drain. If a branch guesses completion too early, unread input remains forever, so it cannot accept. If an old accepting run has actually consumed the whole input, it can safely drain and finish. Those two observations establish the language-preserving role of the gadget.

The marker must be fresh: an old computation must not confuse it with one of its legitimate stack symbols. It marks the baseline that the old machine cannot cross.

Normalize individual transitions too

The grammar construction wants each transition to perform exactly one push or one pop. For a transition that both pops b and pushes c, use a fresh intermediate state: first perform the pop (and any input consumption), then perform an ε push of c. The intermediate state has only the intended continuation, so no other old transition can interrupt the halfway state.

For a transition that changes state but neither pushes nor pops, insert a push of a fresh temporary symbol followed by its pop. This creates a balanced two-step version of the same action. Consume the input only once across the two steps.

Fresh states and symbols are not decoration. Reusing an old state could create extra exits; reusing a marker carelessly could allow a wrong pop to match.

How this closes the CFG/PDA connection

CFG→PDA stores pending derivation work. Normalized PDA→CFG summarizes balanced runs. Together they show that context-free languages are exactly the languages recognized by PDAs. A DFA can be simulated by a PDA that ignores its stack, so every regular language is context-free. The reverse inclusion fails: the stack can handle 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n, which the pumping argument ruled out for DFAs.

Keep: cleanup must be an irreversible commitment to stop reading. Normalize safely, then apply the balanced-run grammar recipe.

One connected check: Why is an early jump to the fresh drain harmless, while early popping at an old accepting state can be harmful?

the final slide mentions non-context-free languages but omits their proof. a useful extra boundary example is {aⁿbⁿcⁿ:n≥0}. its standard proof needs the **context-free pumping lemma**, a different theorem from the regular pumping lemma. it says sufficiently long members split as uvxyz with |vxy|≤p, |vy|>0, and uvⁱxyⁱz staying in the language for every i≥0.

for aᵖbᵖcᵖ, the short middle window vxy cannot reach all three blocks. deleting v and y removes at least one symbol, affects at most two block types, and leaves at least one block's count p unchanged. the three counts cannot remain equal, contradicting the lemma. this is a supplementary application of that theorem, whose own parse-tree proof is outside these slides. a regular pumping argument alone would only show nonregularity, not non-context-freeness.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## why “just add pop loops” is broken

suppose an old accepting state has stack `ba$`, top first, and a future input transition needs to pop `a`. in the original machine that transition is blocked by the top `b`. if we add arbitrary ε-pop loops directly to this state, it can discard `b`, expose `a`, and resume the original transition. we have handed the machine a new way to process unread input. shit—that changes behavior before completion, not just afterward.

the deck illustrates precisely this danger: cleanup mixed into the old control can accept a string the original pda rejects. a final-state label is not a magical barrier against later transitions.

## the safe gadget is a one-way exit

add a fresh bottom marker under the original stack contents. add a fresh **drain state**. from each old accepting state, allow an ε handoff into this drain. there, pop original stack symbols using ε transitions. when the fresh bottom marker appears, pop it and enter the sole new accepting state.

there is no way back to the old machine and no input-consuming transition in the drain. if a branch guesses completion too early, unread input remains forever, so it cannot accept. if an old accepting run has actually consumed the whole input, it can safely drain and finish. those two observations establish the language-preserving role of the gadget.

the marker must be fresh: an old computation must not confuse it with one of its legitimate stack symbols. it marks the baseline that the old machine cannot cross.

## normalize individual transitions too

the grammar construction wants each transition to perform exactly one push or one pop. for a transition that both pops b and pushes c, use a fresh intermediate state: first perform the pop (and any input consumption), then perform an ε push of c. the intermediate state has only the intended continuation, so no other old transition can interrupt the halfway state.

for a transition that changes state but neither pushes nor pops, insert a push of a fresh temporary symbol followed by its pop. this creates a balanced two-step version of the same action. consume the input only once across the two steps.

fresh states and symbols are not decoration. reusing an old state could create extra exits; reusing a marker carelessly could allow a wrong pop to match.

## how this closes the cfg/pda connection

cfg→pda stores pending derivation work. normalized pda→cfg summarizes balanced runs. together they show that context-free languages are exactly the languages recognized by pdas. a dfa can be simulated by a pda that ignores its stack, so every regular language is context-free. the reverse inclusion fails: the stack can handle \(0^n1^n\), which the pumping argument ruled out for dfas.

**keep:** cleanup must be an irreversible commitment to stop reading. normalize safely, then apply the balanced-run grammar recipe.

**one connected check:** why is an early jump to the fresh drain harmless, while early popping at an old accepting state can be harmful?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: determinism changes PDA language power
  • PDF pages 3–4: function output and competing enabled moves
  • PDF pages 5–6: acceptance, empty stack and epsilon loops

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

One table cell isn't the whole decision

For a DFA, the current state and next input symbol select exactly one move. For a PDA, a move may read input or ε, and may pop the top or ε. Several differently labeled transitions can therefore be enabled at the same situation. Determinism must rule out those competing actions, not merely forbid two answers in one cell.

Suppose the machine is in q, the next input is 0, and the stack top is X. It could potentially use any of these:

Transition lookup What it would do
δ(q,0,X) read the zero and pop X
δ(q,0,ε) read the zero without popping
δ(q,ε,X) pop X without reading
δ(q,ε,ε) move without reading or popping

If two are available, the machine has a choice right now. Different labels do not make that choice disappear.

Imagine two buttons available at once: read the next symbol, or take a free ε move. Each button may have only one destination, but you still have a choice between buttons. Determinism must eliminate that competition too. Counting destinations inside separate table cells does not settle which actions are simultaneously available.

Round 1 — Determinism means one enabled action, not one arrow per label · pages 1–4

An NFA's nondeterminism can be compiled into a finite checklist because its possible states come from a fixed finite set. A PDA's configurations include arbitrarily long stacks. The analogous collection need not fit into finitely many states with one deterministic stack. The theorem is that deterministic context-free languages form a proper subfamily of context-free languages; this observation motivates it but is not the full separation proof.

The DPDA transition output is one pair (next state, pushed symbol) or ∅ for undefined. It no longer returns an arbitrary set of pairs. But that alone does not prevent conflicting moves, because ε moves can compete with symbol-consuming moves.

For current state q, upcoming actual symbol a and actual top x, four table entries could apply: δ(q,a,x), δ(q,a,ε), δ(q,ε,x), δ(q,ε,ε). They correspond to inspect both; read input without inspecting stack; inspect stack without reading input; inspect neither. If two were available, the machine would still have a choice even though each individual cell contained one output.

The course uses an exactly-one-defined condition for every q,a,x with a∈Σ and x∈Γ. Other presentations use an at-most-one condition with partial transitions. For the exam, use this course's stated convention. Exactly one is stronger: a situation with all four entries empty needs completion, usually through rejection. Do not swap conventions halfway through a construction.

Round 2 — ε in a pop slot does not ask whether the stack is empty

This deserves its own sentence because it causes so much trouble: ε in the pop slot means no stack symbol is required or removed. That move can apply when the stack is nonempty too. Therefore it competes with an x-pop move when x is actually on top. Similarly, an ε-input move may be available while real input remains.

The four-way condition quantifies actual x∈Γ. An empty stack has no actual top x. Only no-pop alternatives can work there; a defined pop transition cannot conjure a symbol out of emptiness. Determinism does not mean every input must successfully finish.

Round 3 — Two ways the unique run can fail · pages 5–6

First source example: the only defined action is an ε-input move that pops 0. With input 0 and empty stack, it cannot execute because the required 0 is absent. No input gets consumed, and the run is stuck. That rejects the input.

Second example: the only available action consumes ε, pops nothing and pushes 1. It can repeat forever, producing 1,11,111,… on the stack while the input 0 never advances. There is a unique infinite run, but no accepting computation consuming the whole input. This also fails to accept.

For acceptance, retain the course's end-of-input accepting-state condition; for a nonempty input, reaching an accepting state before consuming all symbols is insufficient. A failed or looping path is not transformed into success by the label “deterministic.” Later, when discussing Turing machines, we will distinguish explicitly rejecting from looping. Keep that distinction separate from the language-level fact that both are nonacceptance.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Read the course definition precisely

This course's DPDA definition requires exactly one of those four entries to be nonempty, for every state q, input symbol a, and stack symbol x. Each nonempty entry returns one pair (next state, symbol to push) rather than a set of alternative pairs.

Some treatments use “at most one” and permit partial transitions. For these slides and exam questions, use the stated exactly-one convention. The next deck completes missing cases with rejecting behavior.

An entry equal to ∅ means there is no transition. A pair such as (r,ε) is an actual transition to r that pushes nothing. Those are very different: no action versus a legal action with no push.

Work one collision

Suppose δ(q,0,ε)=(r,X): read 0, push X. Also suppose δ(q,ε,X)=(s,ε): pop X without reading. When the next input is 0 and the current top is X, both can run. One consumes input and increases the stack; the other consumes nothing and decreases it. Each individual entry has one output, but the machine is nondeterministic.

To repair the design, the state must distinguish the phases in which those actions are allowed, or one of the conflicting moves must be removed while preserving the intended language. Writing the arrows farther apart on the page doesn't fix the collision.

Deterministic does not mean “will accept or reject quickly”

An ε cycle may keep running without consuming the next input symbol. A configuration may become stuck when the input or stack is empty and its required action is unavailable. The four-way condition is stated over actual alphabet symbols; ε is the no-consumption option, not a real member of the input alphabet.

Acceptance is still about a computation that has consumed the whole input and is in an accepting state. Visiting an accepting state while unread input remains isn't enough. This is unlike a Turing machine's accepting halt state, which will be introduced later.

The broader connection

Nondeterminism adds no language-recognition power to DFAs versus NFAs, but deterministic PDAs are more restricted than general PDAs. A stack does not make every midpoint guess deterministic. The absence of a visible separator can matter because the machine may not know when to stop pushing and start popping.

Keep: check the four entries together for every concrete situation. The source's definition controls the required completeness. Next we apply that test to the counted-block PDA.

One connected check: Why can an ε transition conflict with a 0 transition even though ε and 0 are different labels?

models.title: Completing a DPDA: make every required choice unambiguous
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: equal-block example and table format
  • PDF pages 3–5: four-way exclusions and rejection completion
  • PDF pages 6–8: later states and 011 empty-stack trace

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Start from the language, then audit the formal definition

The deck revisits the PDA for 0n1n0^n1^n0n1n. Its useful behavior is already clear: initialize a bottom marker, push zeros, pop for ones, and finish when the debt is paid. Now we ask a different question: does its transition table meet the course's strict DPDA definition for every state/input/top combination?

A familiar diagram can recognize the correct language yet fail that formal completeness requirement. This is why an exam may ask for a transition table, not just a plausible sketch.

We already know the intended workflow: push for zeros, pop for ones, finish when the debt is paid. Now make the table obey the course’s determinism rule in every situation, including bad inputs. Treat it like checking which buttons are enabled at once. A rejected input still needs coherent machine behavior.

Round 1 — The table is a conflict audit, not a wall of random ∅s · pages 1–3

The original 0ⁿ1ⁿ PDA has a natural deterministic phase structure: install $, push on zeros, pop on ones, then remove $. The task here is to express it under the course's formal exactly-one convention, including rejecting cases.

At q₁, δ(q₁,ε,ε)=(q₂,$) installs the marker regardless of the next input or existing top. Because it is the ignore-both move, every other competing entry in that row must be ∅. Otherwise the first action would be ambiguous. q₁ remains accepting for the empty string under the course's convention.

At q₂, δ(q₂,0,ε)=(q₂,0) reads zero and pushes zero without inspecting the stack. For either possible top, this move already handles next input 0. Therefore the 0-input/top-specific entries and competing ε-input moves must be empty. The zeros in the table header are literal input or stack symbols; ∅ in a cell means undefined action.

Round 2 — Why the rejecting state becomes necessary · pages 4–5

For next input 1 with top 0, define δ(q₂,1,0)=(q₃,ε): match a zero and switch to the one phase. Its competitors must be empty. Now inspect next input 1 with top $. None of the old successful moves applies: there is no zero to match.

Under an at-most-one definition you could leave that situation stuck. Under the course's exactly-one definition, fill it with δ(q₂,1,$)=(qᵣ,ε). qᵣ is a rejecting state. The slide abbreviates some cells as just qᵣ; the full formal output still needs the pair, including what is pushed. State labels alone are shorthand here, not a new transition type.

You can fill the table systematically: list each actual input/top combination; inspect its four candidate cells; keep the one intended move; force competitors empty; if none exists, supply a rejecting move consistent with all already-fixed cells. Check conflicts after every addition because one ε entry participates in several combinations.

Round 3 — The one phase forbids going back to zeros · pages 6–8

At q₃, another 1 with top 0 pops it. A zero while unmatched zeros remain goes to rejection because block order has already switched. When $ is exposed, δ(q₃,ε,$)=(q₄,ε) moves to the accepting endpoint and removes the marker. This ε move can occur even while unread input remains; the whole-input acceptance rule still applies.

Trace 011: q₁ installs $, q₂ reads 0 and pushes it, q₃ reads the first 1 and pops it, then removes $ and enters q₄. There is still one unread 1 and the stack is empty. The only entries that could operate without a top are δ(q₄,1,ε) and δ(q₄,ε,ε); both are empty. The run gets stuck and rejects.

“But q₄ is accepting!” Yes, for a completed input. It is not permission to throw away the final symbol. Also, the defined q₄ rejecting moves requiring an actual stack symbol cannot fire on an empty stack. This example ties together three separate conditions: correct state, all input consumed, and a genuinely enabled move when input remains.

The source's third-row intermediate displays are easier to read through these state meanings than by copying isolated shaded cells. The final behavior follows from the full transition condition. When a table entry is abbreviated, expand it to a complete (state,push) pair in your formal answer.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Initialization controls every other possibility

If q₁ has δ(q₁,ε,ε)=(q₂,$), that action is enabled without reading or popping. For any next input a and top x, it already occupies the one allowed choice among the four entries. Thus the other potentially competing entries from q₁ must be empty. The bottom marker is pushed once, then the machine changes phase.

In q₂, zeros are read and pushed. When reading a 1, the machine must have a zero marker to pop before entering q₃. If the top is $ instead, there is no owed zero to match; send that required case to rejecting behavior.

A rejecting completion is part of the machine

Use a rejecting state qᵣ for cases that must be defined but cannot lead to acceptance. Its subsequent actions must also obey the four-way condition and prevent a return to useful accepting computation. It is not enough to scribble “reject” in a table if the formal transition type expects a pair. The deck's shortened qᵣ entries stand for a specified pair such as (qᵣ,ε) where appropriate.

Adding reject behavior is safe because it handles situations in which the original partial construction had no successful accepting continuation. It should never steal a case needed by a valid string.

Trace the subtle 011 case

Read 0: one zero marker is pushed. Read the first 1: that marker is popped, leaving $ in q₃. The ε move on $ then enters q₄ and removes the marker. But one input 1 remains.

This is not acceptance. In the slide construction, the remaining situation has no legal way to consume that final symbol and finish successfully. Reaching q₄ didn't cause a TM-style halt that ignores unread input. The whole-input condition still applies.

Also notice the determinism constraint at q₃ with top $. The ε-pop action is already the enabled choice, so an input-consuming action that also competes there must not be added. Otherwise we would break determinism while trying to “complete” the table.

A reliable way to check your answer

For each state q, each actual input symbol a, and each actual stack symbol x, examine the four entries from the previous deck as one group. Count nonempty entries; under this course definition the count must be exactly one. Separately check that each output is one legal pair, that labels use the stated alphabets, and that the start/accepting states are identified.

Then trace ε, a valid nonempty example, too few ones, too many ones, and an out-of-order zero. Those traces catch different failures. They don't replace a general invariant: zeros create obligations, ones discharge them, and phase changes forbid later zeros.

Keep: determinism, completeness, and language correctness are three checks with different jobs. Next, Turing machines replace the stack's top-only access with a rewritable tape and movable head.

One connected check: Why can filling an empty table entry with a useful transition accidentally violate determinism even if that cell previously contained ∅?

sections.concepts: powers of two and repeated halving
actual diagram and reserved first zero

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: powers of two and repeated halving
  • PDF pages 4–5: actual diagram and reserved first zero
  • PDF pages 6–8: transition notation, states and invariant

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Read the language before reading the arrows

The deck's language is {02n:n≥0}\{0^{2^n}:n\ge0\}{02n:n≥0}. The number of zeros must be a power of two: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, … . This is not 02n0^{2n}02n, which describes even lengths. 000000 has even length six, but six is not a power of two. ε has length zero and is also excluded.

The numerical idea is simple: one is a power of two; a larger odd count isn't; a larger even count is a power of two exactly when its half is. So repeatedly halve an even count until either one remains or an odd count greater than one appears.

The tape is doing the counting for us. The finite controller only needs to remember “keep this one” versus “cross this one out.” So the trick isn't stuffing the number eight or eight billion into a state label; it's leaving the work distributed across the tape and shrinking it by a rule we can justify.

Crossing a zero out does not physically remove its tape cell. The notebook still contains the crossed-out mess, and the head still travels across it. This machine also reserves the first position. We have to distinguish what you literally see on tape from the count that this encoding represents.

Round 1 — We are testing the input's length, not its binary value · pages 1–3

The language {0^(2ⁿ):n≥0} contains strings with 1,2,4,8,… zeros. n is the exponent; 2ⁿ is the number of input symbols. Empty input is not included because 2ⁿ is never zero. A string 0000 represents length four, not the integer zero written four times.

A positive integer is a power of two exactly when repeatedly halving it reaches 1 without encountering an odd number greater than 1. For length 8: 8→4→2→1. For length 6: 6→3, then reject. Length 1 accepts immediately. That's the mathematical job the tape operations implement.

Crossed-out x symbols remain physically on the tape. “Remaining zeros” means unmarked zeros, not the total number of occupied tape cells. The head skips x without treating it as a new input zero. Forgetting that representation makes the source trace look like the tape length is mysteriously changing.

Round 2 — The first zero is reserved, so count it correctly · pages 4–5

The actual slide machine overwrites the first 0 with blank as a left marker. That reserved position represents the final one zero that would remain at the end. During the algorithm, the represented count is one plus the number of live zeros to its right.

For input 0000, after initialization the physical tape is ⊔000. That still represents four. One pass marks the first live zero and then alternates keeping/marking, producing ⊔x0x, representing two. The next pass gives ⊔xxx, representing one. A subsequent scan finds no live zero and accepts. The blank at the left is not evidence that the original input had an empty first symbol.

For 000, initialization leaves ⊔00. After marking the first live zero, there is an unmatched leftover zero when the scan ends. The represented count was three, which is odd and greater than one, so reject. The finite control's alternating states detect this parity.

Round 3 — Assign each state a purpose before tracing arrows · pages 6–8

q₁ establishes the left boundary and rejects an input that does not begin with 0. q₂ skips x looking for the next live zero; seeing right-end blank means only the reserved one remains, so accept. Finding a zero marks it and begins the pairing scan.

q₃ and q₄ alternate over live zeros, ignoring crossed-out x. Their phase tells whether the count has the required parity when the right blank arrives. q₅ returns left over 0 and x until the boundary blank, then moves right to q₂ for another pass. The state carries the phase; the tape carries which symbols remain live.

An edge labeled 0→R abbreviates 0→0,R: keep the symbol and move right. 0→x,R changes it. q_accept and q_reject have no executed outgoing rows. When you read a configuration like ⊔xq₃00, q₃ marks the control state and the scanned position, not a literal q₃ symbol on the tape.

Round 4 — Correctness and termination are separate promises

The invariant is that the tape encoding represents the current positive candidate count. A successful pass on an even count divides it by two; an odd count greater than one rejects; count one accepts. Powers of two repeatedly reach one; any other positive integer eventually reaches an odd factor greater than one. Each successful pass decreases the represented count, and each sweep crosses a finite used tape region. Therefore the machine halts on every input.

The numerical reasoning proves the algorithm. Matching each state/marking rule to that encoding explains why this particular diagram implements it. You need both layers; “it halves things” alone leaves the implementation unaccounted for.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

How a tape implements “halve the count”

Scan the live zeros and mark every other one. States alternate between “keep the next live zero” and “cross out the next live zero.” Marks are ignored on later passes; they are old work, not new zeros. The head returns to the left boundary to start another pass.

The state alternation records parity during one sweep. It does not store the whole count. The surviving unmarked cells carry the reduced count between sweeps. This is a recurring theme: use finite control for a small phase distinction, external memory for an unbounded amount.

Follow numbers first, then align with the actual diagram

For eight zeros, the conceptual counts go 8→4→2→1, so accept. For six, they go 6→3, so reject on the odd count greater than one. For one zero, accept without demanding an even count. That last exception matters: “reject all odd counts” would reject the successful stopping condition too.

The slide machine has a representation detail: it erases the first zero to make a left marker and treats that reserved contribution as part of the represented count. Consequently, the remaining visible live zeros represent the current count minus one. Don't stare at a row with three visible live zeros and conclude the represented count must be three; it may represent four under this convention.

In the diagram, q₂ begins a pass by marking the first remaining live zero, q₃ and q₄ alternate through subsequent live zeros, and q₅ returns left. The one-zero case is detected when the reserved initial zero has no remaining live partner. The conceptual halving test and the diagram are the same algorithm with different bookkeeping.

Here is the physical bookkeeping for input 0000, at successive pass boundaries:

Tape's used portion Live zeros after the left marker Represented count
⊔000 after initialization 3 4
⊔x0x after one halving pass 1 2
⊔xxx after the next pass 0 1

⊔ is the blank used as the left marker, and x means crossed out. On the final scan q₂ finds no remaining live zero and reaches accept. This table is the bridge between the arithmetic 4→2→1 and the marks actually visible in the slide trace.

Why rejection and halting follow

If an odd represented count greater than one appears, repeated exact division by two cannot lead to one without a fractional step. Reject. If an even represented count appears, halving preserves the property of being a power of two. Every successful nonfinal round strictly decreases a positive integer count, so it cannot continue forever. Each tape pass itself traverses only a finite used region.

That is the proof skeleton: a property preserved by a transformation, a failed condition causing rejection, and a decreasing measure causing termination. These are reusable tools, not facts unique to this TM.

How to read a dense transition diagram

Annotate each state with its phase before tracing. Record state, head position, and full changed tape—not just the input symbols consumed, because this machine revisits cells. When a trace seems to contradict the high-level plan, check the encoding convention before changing the mathematics.

Keep: powers of two are detected by repeated parity checks and halving; the tape stores the shrinking population through marks. Next we formalize a whole machine snapshot and distinguish recognition from guaranteed termination.

One connected check: Why is a single even-length check insufficient for this language, and why must length one be treated separately?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: configuration notation and local yields
  • PDF pages 4–5: recognizer versus decider
  • PDF pages 6–10: copy comparison state roles
  • PDF pages 11–12: multiplication and subroutines
  • PDF pages 13–14: pairwise distinct blocks and markers

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

A state name alone no longer describes the situation

For a DFA with fixed input position, the state was enough memory. For a TM, two visits to q can have different tape contents and head positions. A configuration must record all three: control state, tape, and head location. Otherwise a trace can silently lose the information that determines the next move.

The notation uqvu q vuqv writes the tape prefix u to the left of the head, inserts state q at the head position, and writes the scanned symbol as the first symbol of v. q is not a tape symbol; it is an annotation in the snapshot.

A state name alone is like saying “Marcus is checking” without saying what document is open or where he is pointing. A configuration supplies the whole situation: state, tape, head position. Then one transition changes that situation locally. We will unpack the compact notation into those three pieces.

Round 1 — A configuration is a screenshot of the whole machine · pages 1–5

uqv encodes tape contents uv, current state q, and the head scanning the first symbol of v. u and v are strings; q is inserted notation, not stored tape content. If v is empty in an abbreviated display, the head scans the next blank.

For ua qᵢ bv, the scanned symbol is b, while a is immediately to its left. If δ(qᵢ,b)=(qⱼ,c,L), write c where b was and move left: u qⱼ acv. For a right move, obtain uac qⱼ v. Separate the write action from the head movement; doing only one produces the wrong configuration.

A finite sequence of legal configurations from q₀w to an accepting configuration proves that M accepts w. A recognizer must eventually accept members, but on nonmembers it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input, accepting members and rejecting nonmembers. “Hasn't accepted yet” cannot tell you whether a recognizer will reject later or run forever.

Round 2 — The copy-checker's two leftward phases are different jobs · pages 6–10

For w#w, q₁ selects and marks the next left-half bit. The 0 branch uses q₂ then q₄ to cross the separator and demand a matching right-half 0. The 1 branch uses q₃ then q₅ and demands 1. The state remembers which bit was selected while the head travels.

After marking the right bit, q₆ travels left through the right half toward #. q₇ then travels through the remaining unmarked left bits until finding the marked left prefix, and moves right to the next work position. They cannot be merged: x means “keep going left” in the right half, but “turn around here” at the left prefix boundary. Same scanned symbol, different phase, different action.

For 01#01, the completed marking rounds are 01#01 → x1#x1 → xx#xx. q₈ verifies there are only x's in the remainder of the right half, then accepts at blank. Missing rejecting edges in the slide diagram are shorthand for rejection, not permission to improvise a transition.

Round 3 — Multiplication is repeated complete matching · pages 11–12

The source language is {aⁱbʲcᵏ:ij=k, i,j,k≥1}. First check nonempty blocks in that exact order. For each a, traverse all b's and cancel one previously uncancelled c per b. Restore the b markers after that round so the next a can use the full b count again. Mark that a as completed.

For aabbcccc, two a-rounds each cancel two c's, totaling four. For aabbccc, the second round runs out of c's; reject. For aabbccccc, all rounds finish but one c remains; reject. Empty blocks reject because the source specifies positive exponents.

A subroutine is a previously explained finite-state/tape procedure used as part of a larger machine, such as returning to a marker or matching a selected symbol. A high-level description is justified when these operations are implementable with the allowed head moves and finite work alphabet. It cannot hide an impossible instruction such as “instantly know whether this computation will ever stop.”

Round 4 — Pairwise means every different pair, not just neighbors · pages 13–14

The distinct-block language requires xᵢ≠xⱼ whenever i≠j. Adjacent comparisons alone miss duplicates in positions 1 and 3. Mark the two selected separators, compare their following blocks, restore temporary work, and advance through pairs (1,2),(1,3),…,(2,3),… . There are ℓ(ℓ−1)/2 pairs for ℓ blocks.

Blocks may be empty because each xᵢ belongs to {0,1}*. Two empty blocks are duplicates. Their delimiters still identify their positions. Correctness: reject when a checked pair is equal; accept only after every pair was checked and found different. Termination: finitely many pairs, finite-length comparisons, and a pair index that advances. The proof must account for both exhaustive coverage and finite progress.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Decode one transition completely

Suppose a configuration is a q bc: the tape contains abc, the head reads b, and the state is q. If δ(q,b)=(r,x,R), the new configuration is ax r c. The b was overwritten by x; the head moved to c; the state became r.

If instead δ(q,b)=(r,x,L), the result is r axc: the head now reads the a to the left. The entire tape is still axc; only the placement of the state annotation differs. At the left boundary there is no earlier cell to move into, so that case follows the boundary rule separately.

This is why copying only the state sequence is not a full TM trace. You need the tape edits and head movement too.

Three possible outcomes, not two

A TM may accept, reject, or keep running forever. A recognizer for L must accept every member and must never accept a nonmember. On a nonmember it may reject or loop. A decider must halt on every input, accepting members and rejecting nonmembers.

Every decider is a recognizer. Calling a recognizer “an algorithm that answers yes or no” overstates its guarantee: on some no-instances it may never answer. You cannot turn it into a decider by getting impatient after a million steps; a genuine accepting run might take a million and one.

Read the deck's constructions as phase programs

The w#w machine alternates marking, crossing, comparing, and returning. Its return states need different jobs on the two sides of #; reaching a marked symbol on the right is not the same as reaching the last processed symbol on the left. State meanings explain why several apparently similar left-moving states exist.

The slide language is aibjcka^ib^jc^kaibjck with ij=k and i,j,k≥1: all three blocks must be nonempty. Reuse the comparison routine on a whole list

Pages 13–14 ask that the binary blocks in #x₁#x₂…#xₗ all differ. Compare every pair, not only neighbors. models.title: Multiple tapes: give each part of the job its own workspace
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: stay-put simulation
  • PDF page 3: k-tape simultaneous transition type
  • PDF pages 4–7: even-length duplication phases
  • PDF pages 8–9: accepted and rejected traces

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The mental model: several work surfaces, one finite controller

A multitape TM has several tapes, each with its own head. It can keep the input on one tape and scratch work on another. This can make a program much easier to describe. It does not mean separate independent machines are voting on an answer: one control state selects a joint transition from the symbols currently under all heads.

For k tapes, a transition reads a k-tuple of symbols and returns a new state, k replacement symbols, and k movement choices. A tuple is ordered. The first entry belongs to tape 1, the second to tape 2, and so on. Swapping the entries can change the computation.

Give the worker a second notebook and copying becomes a lot less annoying. That convenience can save movement, but it does not automatically mean new problems become solvable. The claim is that one tape can simulate the extra notebooks. First understand the convenient algorithm; then we price and build its simulation.

Round 1 — More convenient machinery need not recognize more languages · pages 1–3

Equivalent computational power means the same languages can be recognized or decided. It does not mean equal speed, equal number of states or equally pleasant diagrams. A multitape machine is a convenient workbench; a later simulation shows one tape can do its work with extra bookkeeping.

A stay-put instruction writes a symbol but leaves the head in place. To simulate it using only L/R, write and move right into a fresh helper state, then preserve whichever symbol is there and move left into the intended destination state. Right then left works even at the tape's left boundary. Left then right would fail there because the first left move gets clamped in place.

For k tapes, δ receives the current state and k scanned symbols. It returns one next state, k symbols to write and k head directions. Γᵏ means an ordered k-tuple of tape symbols; {L,S,R}ᵏ means one direction choice per tape. The transition reads the old scanned symbols together, then performs the indicated updates. It does not read tape 2 only after already modifying tape 1.

Round 2 — This example produces output as well as accepting · pages 4–7

The input promise is w=0^(2n) with n≥1: a positive even number of zeros. The job is to produce ww on tape 1, doubling the input string. This is not the power-of-two language from the previous one-tape example. 000000 is permitted here because its length six is even.

The machine reserves a blank boundary on tape 2, copies the input zeros there, returns the second head toward the beginning while checking parity, and then copies the stored zeros onto the end of tape 1. Tape 1 retains the original half; tape 2 preserves a copy of what must be appended.

The parity check occurs during the return phase q₂↔q₃. The first head zigzags near tape 1's right end while the second head moves left across the copied zeros. Reaching tape 2's boundary in the required state confirms evenness. q₄ then appends the copy. Changing which phase checks parity would describe a different implementation, even if it could solve the same abstract job.

Round 3 — Trace the resources, not just a list of state names · pages 8–9

For input 0000, tape 2 eventually holds its reserved blank followed by four zeros. The return scan confirms even length, and the append phase produces eight zeros on tape 1. For 000, the parity phase reaches the boundary in the wrong state, so reject instead of treating a six-zero output as successful completion.

Empty input and a single zero reject under n≥1. The output requirement alone is insufficient: a machine that doubles every unary input would fail the specified domain check. Formal construction questions often bundle validation and transformation; state both obligations before drawing arrows.

The transition table must also cover unexpected scanned-symbol combinations. With two tapes, a row indexed by state q can have pairs (0,0),(0,⊔),(⊔,0),(⊔,⊔), plus any additional tape symbols. The slide sends unspecified cases to rejection. One two-tape arrow label represents both tape actions together, not two nondeterministic choices.

The proof separates three invariants: copy phase preserves a faithful second copy; return phase correctly tracks parity; append phase transfers exactly that copy once. Each sweep traverses a finite region and each phase advances toward completion. That's how the polished final tape earns the claim that the algorithm actually worked.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

One step uses one shared snapshot

Suppose two heads currently read (0, blank). A transition may write (x,0) and move (R,R). Both decisions are based on the original pair. Do not write x on tape 1 and then use some half-updated situation to choose tape 2's action. The transition is one joint instruction.

A stay-put movement S is a convenient extension. It can be simulated in a left/right-only model using a right move followed by a left move, with an intermediate state preserving the required control information. The order matters at the left boundary: left then right would not restore the original position there.

The slide example: even positive unary input

The deck works with input 02n0^{2n}02n, n≥1, and constructs a machine that doubles it. This is an even-positive-length requirement, not the earlier powers-of-two language 02n0^{2^n}02n. 000000 meets the input pattern here even though its length is not a power of two.

The machine uses the second tape as stored work, a boundary marker to find the beginning again, and control states to check parity while returning across the stored copy after copying. Once this check verifies the required form, the stored copy can be used in producing the doubled output. For four input zeros, the required result is eight zeros. A correct trace must show where each head sits during copying, resetting, and extending the output, not just write “4 becomes 8.”

The useful separation is: tape contents store the actual block; a small state distinction tracks odd/even position; a marker gives a reliable return point. Each part solves a different bookkeeping problem.

What an exam trace should record

Write one row per joint step: current state, each tape's contents with its head marked, and the transition used. Preserve unchanged cells. A blank symbol in the read tuple is a condition on that tape's scanned cell; it isn't permission to ignore that tape.

When designing rather than tracing, first assign a purpose to each tape and each phase. Only then translate phases into transitions. Otherwise you end up memorizing a pile of arrows with no way to reconstruct them under exam pressure.

The next question is about power

Extra workspace organization might look like a stronger model. The next deck shows how one tape can encode all the tapes and head positions, then simulate their joint steps. That establishes equal computability. It does not promise equal running time; organizing work differently can save a lot of movement.

Keep: multiple tapes are several ordered workspaces controlled by one joint rule. Snapshot first, simultaneous updates second.

One connected check: Why must a simulation remember all the scanned symbols before it starts applying the simulated writes?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: encoded virtual tapes and head markers
  • PDF page 4: simulation sweeps and extension
  • PDF page 5: carry-state shifting and correctness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The job: replace convenient hardware with an encoding

A multitape machine has k tapes and k head positions. A single tape can store their finite used contents as separated blocks, for example #block₁#block₂#…#blockₖ#. Use a marked version of a symbol to indicate each simulated head's position. The delimiter and marked symbols are extra members of the simulator's finite tape alphabet.

The representation must retain both the data and the head locations. Merely joining the tape contents loses which cell each simulated head reads next. That's the same lesson as configurations: an encoding has to preserve everything needed to determine the next step.

Put pictures of several notebooks into one long file, with separators between them. Mark one virtual cursor in each picture. The real head scans that file and updates the pictures. That is the simulation: several imagined heads represented by data, maintained by one actual moving head.

Round 1 — One tape holds a serialized picture of all the tapes · pages 1–3

Imagine putting several short documents into one file separated by dividers. A delimiter # separates virtual tape regions. A dotted version of a symbol marks each virtual head. The encoding in the slide stores three tape contents in sequence, with exactly one head mark per region.

A dotted 0 is a distinct tape symbol whose meaning is “this cell contains 0 and its virtual head is here.” It does not change the simulated data value to some mysterious number. If the original alphabet is finite, adding one marked copy of each symbol and finitely many separators still gives a finite alphabet.

The simulator has one physical head. The other head positions are data recorded on its tape. This distinction is the entire trick: it represents the multitape configuration rather than physically possessing those extra heads.

Round 2 — One virtual step takes several physical sweeps · page 4

First scan the encoding to collect the symbols under the k marked heads. Since k and Γ are fixed for this machine, there are only finitely many possible scanned-symbol tuples; the finite control can remember which tuple it saw. Apply the simulated transition rule to determine the new state, writes and directions.

Then sweep through the regions to rewrite the marked cells and move each marker one position. Preserve separators and all untouched simulated cells. The simulator may use intermediate marker types to distinguish old and updated head positions, so it does not accidentally perform the same virtual update twice.

If a virtual head moves beyond the represented right end, extend that region with a blank cell. That may require shifting later regions right. The original tape is infinite, so extra physical space exists; the simulation still performs a finite number of operations for this one step.

Round 3 — How can finite control move an arbitrarily long suffix? · page 5

The control need not remember the whole suffix. It carries just one displaced symbol at a time. To open a cell, replace its current symbol with the desired new one and remember the displaced symbol in the state. Move right, write the carried symbol, remember what was displaced there, and repeat. When the end of the finite represented region is reached, write the final carried symbol into spare space.

For the slide's binary shifting illustration, states q₀ and q₁ mean “carrying 0” and “carrying 1.” For a larger finite alphabet, use one carrying state per symbol, including separators and head-marked symbols. The carrying state stores a symbol value, not an unbounded string. That is why the construction remains a finite-state controller.

A delimiter marks region structure; a blank can be legitimate simulated tape content. A robust full encoding keeps track of the represented region's end so shifting does not confuse an internal simulated blank with the end of all data.

Round 4 — What the simulation proof must preserve

After each completed simulated step, the encoding must describe exactly the original machine's state, every represented tape symbol and every virtual head position. Initially we can construct the encoding from the input and blank auxiliary tapes. Each sweep implements the corresponding old transition, so induction preserves the representation.

If the multitape machine accepts or rejects, the simulator eventually reaches that corresponding halting state. If it runs forever, the simulator keeps producing faithful steps. models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: set-valued transitions and existential acceptance
  • PDF pages 3–5: contains-aab branching example
  • PDF pages 6–7: composite witnesses and bounded guessing

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

What branches now?

An NTM can have several legal actions for the same state and scanned symbol. Each action creates a possible next configuration: state, tape contents, and head position. As choices accumulate, the computation forms a tree. Branches are alternative histories, not multiple heads sharing one mutable tape.

A string accepts if at least one branch reaches accept after finitely many steps. A rejecting branch alone doesn't settle the input. A branch that loops also doesn't accept. The whole existential claim is: is there a finite successful computation somewhere in the tree?

A branch gets its own whole notebook, not just a different mood in the same state. One branch can overwrite a cell while another keeps it unchanged. Acceptance asks whether any legal branch succeeds. There is no probability threshold, and we cannot steal a useful tape mark from a different branch.

Round 1 — Each branch gets its own whole machine configuration · pages 1–2

An NTM transition returns a set of triples (state, write symbol, direction). Starting from the same state and scanned symbol, different branches may write different data and move in different directions. Each branch therefore needs its own state, tape contents and head position. You cannot merge branches just because their state names match.

Acceptance is existential: if one finite branch reaches q_accept, the input is accepted. Another branch rejecting or running forever does not cancel that success. If no branch accepts, the recognizer does not accept; a simulation may reject after exhausting a finite tree or continue forever when the search remains infinite.

This is mathematical branching, not a probabilistic choice with a success percentage. The definition asks whether an accepting branch exists. How to systematically simulate that existence on a deterministic machine is the next deck's problem.

Round 2 — Guess a place where aab starts · pages 3–5

The NTM scans right over a and b. Whenever it sees a, it may continue scanning or guess that this is the first a of an aab occurrence. The checking branch then demands another a and then b. On success it immediately accepts, even if more input remains, because finding that substring already proves the language condition.

For baaba, a branch guesses the second position, checks a then b, and accepts. A wrong guess later may reject; irrelevant. For ababa, every attempted aab check fails, and the continuing scan eventually reaches blank and rejects. All branches in this simple example move right through finite input and halt.

Notice a model difference: an NFA must consume the entire input to accept, so its substring-finding accept state needs loops for the remaining suffix. A TM may halt as soon as the fact “contains aab” has been established. The target language is the same; the acceptance mechanisms differ.

Round 3 — A witness is a proposed explanation we can check · pages 6–7

The unary compositeness language contains 0ⁿ when n is composite. Composite means n=pq with integers p,q≥2; allowing 1 as a factor would falsely call every positive number composite. Lengths 0 and 1 are not composite, and primes have no permitted factor pair.

The NTM guesses candidate p and q, then checks the multiplication relation using finite tape routines. To make every branch halt, bound the guesses by the input length n. One implementation nondeterministically decides when to stop constructing a candidate, but rejects if the candidate exceeds n. Merely saying “stop at any time” without a bound could introduce an infinite never-stop branch.

For n=6, a branch choosing p=2,q=3 succeeds. A branch choosing 2 and 2 fails. For n=5, every bounded candidate fails. A deterministic machine could enumerate the same finite candidate pairs sequentially; nondeterminism does not make an undecidable problem decidable here.

The slide asks why sequentially trying every pair sounds deterministic. Because it is. The nondeterministic description instead branches over possible witnesses and verifies each branch's candidate. These two descriptions can recognize the same language while distributing the search differently. Later complexity theory distinguishes the length of one branch from the cost of exploring the entire tree.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

A pattern example makes the guessing concrete

To recognize strings containing aab, one branch can keep scanning while another guesses “the occurrence starts here.” The checking branch then demands a, a, b in sequence. A wrong guess fails locally; a correct occurrence supplies a successful branch. This is the NFA idea with TM configurations behind it.

The word “guess” is mathematical shorthand for allowing all permitted choices as branches. It is not a probability claim and not a promise that a real computer luckily picks the right one.

A more useful guess: a factorization witness

For unary compositeness, input 0ⁿ represents the integer n. Guess integers p and q with 2≤p,q≤n−1, then verify pq=n. For n=6, the branch choosing p=2,q=3 succeeds. Guesses such as 2 and 2 fail their multiplication check. For a prime input, no legal pair succeeds.

The range bound matters. If the machine generates arbitrarily long guesses with no stopping bound, some branches may guess forever. For an NTM decider, every branch must halt. Bounding the guesses and using terminating arithmetic checks gives that guarantee. Acceptance can be existential while termination is required branch by branch.

Why tracing just the states is especially wrong here

Two branches may reach the same control state with different guessed factors on tape. Their later verification differs. You cannot merge them merely because both circles are named q. An NFA's finite state-set method does not directly apply to TMs: tape configurations can be arbitrarily large and there can be infinitely many of them.

A trace tree should show enough of each configuration to distinguish the guesses or edits. When proving correctness, identify what an accepting branch certifies: here, two nontrivial integer factors whose product is exactly the input number.

The obvious simulation idea has a trap

A deterministic simulator might try the first branch to completion, then the second. But the first can loop forever while the second accepts in ten steps. Waiting for completion would miss an available yes-answer. We need a fair schedule that never lets one infinite branch hog all the attention. That's why the next deck uses breadth-first exploration.

Keep: nondeterminism means existence of a successful branch; a branch carries a full configuration; a decider must halt on every branch.

One connected check: If one branch rejects, one loops, and one accepts after twenty steps, what determines the NTM's acceptance—and why would depth-first simulation be dangerous?
