models.title: Fair simulation: don't let one endless branch hide a short success

sections.concepts: three tapes, path addresses and invalid paths

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: deterministic simulation and breadth-first fairness
  • PDF pages 4–7: three tapes, path addresses and invalid paths
  • PDF pages 8–9: all-branches halting and finite-tree argument

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The problem is scheduling, not lucky guessing

To simulate an NTM deterministically, we must eventually inspect every finite candidate computation. A depth-first strategy can get trapped following an infinite branch. Breadth-first search explores all branches to depth 0, then 1, then 2, and so on. A successful branch of depth d is eventually inspected because only finitely many nodes occur at each earlier depth.

The finite branching condition matters: the transition table supplies finitely many choices per step. Without it, “finish this level before the next” might itself require infinite work.

One branch can wander forever while a successful branch sits two steps away. A simulator that follows the wanderer forever is doing a lousy search. Breadth-first exploration shares attention by depth. Every finite successful path eventually gets its turn. That fairness is the mechanism, not an optional implementation flourish.

Round 1 — Don't let one infinite branch hog the whole damn search · pages 1–3

Depth-first search follows one branch deeply before returning to alternatives. If that branch loops forever, the simulator never visits a short accepting branch next door. Therefore a naive depth-first simulation is not a correct recognizer for an arbitrary NTM.

Breadth-first search examines depth 0, then depth 1, then depth 2, and so on. Every finite accepting computation lies at some finite depth, so it will eventually be reached. This property is fairness: no finite branch prefix is permanently starved by another branch's endless work.

The maximum branching factor b is finite because the NTM has finitely many states and tape symbols, each transition offering finitely many choices. The number of nodes at each fixed depth is finite even though the whole tree may be infinite. That lets each breadth-first layer finish.

Round 2 — The three tapes have three distinct jobs · pages 4–7

Tape 1 preserves the original input. Tape 2 holds a fresh simulation of one branch. Tape 3 holds its address, a finite sequence of branch-choice indices. Address 231 means take child 2, then child 3, then child 1; it is not input data or a tape location.

Enumerate addresses in increasing length: empty address, 1,2,…,b, then 11,12,…,bb, and so on. For each address, reset tape 2 from the original input and follow at most that many choices. If an indicated child does not exist, discard the invalid address. If an accepting state appears, accept immediately. Resetting prevents mutations from one simulated branch contaminating the next.

An infinite branch cannot trap this procedure because each candidate address has finite length. The simulator examines a finite prefix and moves on. If no branch accepts and the tree is infinite, continuing forever is allowed for a recognizer. The construction promises discovery of every finite accepting branch, not a decision about absent acceptance in all cases.

A three-tape deterministic TM can perform these operations; the prior multitape theorem then converts it to one tape. Combining simulations is valid because each component has an explicit finite encoding and transition procedure.

Round 3 — “Every branch halts” needs one more argument · pages 8–9

An NTM decider halts on every branch for every input. To conclude that a deterministic breadth-first simulation halts too, we need its computation tree for each fixed input to be finite.

Here is the missing bridge. If a finitely branching rooted tree had infinitely many nodes, at least one child of the root would have infinitely many descendants; finitely many finite descendant sets cannot cover an infinite set. Choose such a child, then repeat the same argument below it. This constructs an infinite branch. Therefore, if no infinite branch exists and branching is finite, the tree must be finite. This is the relevant form of König's lemma.

The simulator should track the live frontier and reject when it becomes empty, after finding no acceptance. Blindly enumerating every imaginable address forever would not by itself detect that the real tree ended. Breadth-first frontier exhaustion supplies the terminating rejection procedure.

Thus deterministic and nondeterministic machines decide the same languages as well as recognize the same languages. The statement is about solvability. Exploring exponentially many branches may be far slower than following one branch, which is exactly why nondeterministic time becomes a separate topic later.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

How the three-tape simulation organizes the work

One tape preserves the original input. Another simulates a candidate branch's working tape. A third records an address: a finite sequence of transition-choice numbers. If at most three choices are available, addresses begin 1,2,3,11,12,13,21,… in length order.

To inspect address 213, reset the work tape to the input, choose option 2 on the first step, option 1 on the second, and option 3 on the third. If a requested option doesn't exist, discard that candidate. If accept is reached along the replay, accept. Then move on to the next address. No single replay is allowed to run past the address's finite length.

These addresses describe choices, not tape cell positions. Replaying from the original input prevents edits from one branch contaminating another.

Why every accepting branch is eventually found

Suppose the NTM accepts in d steps along choices c₁…c_d. There are finitely many shorter addresses and finitely many addresses of length d before that one. Each replay takes finitely many steps. Eventually the simulator replays the successful sequence and accepts.

If the NTM never accepts, the simulator never invents acceptance: every replay uses actual legal transitions. It may search forever. That is acceptable when simulating a recognizer, whose no-instances need not halt.

What changes for a decider?

If every NTM branch halts on a fixed input, and branching is finite, the whole computation tree is finite. The reason is subtler than “each branch is finite, so there are finitely many branches.” If a finitely branching tree had nodes at arbitrarily large depths, one child of the root would have arbitrarily deep descendants; then one child of that child would too; continuing would construct an infinite branch. That contradicts the all-branches-halt assumption.

A breadth-first simulator can therefore maintain the live frontier and reject when no live configuration remains and none accepted. It must actually detect exhaustion; endlessly enumerating meaningless longer addresses without checking completion would not itself be a decider.

What the theorem does and doesn't establish

Deterministic and nondeterministic TMs recognize the same languages and decide the same languages. This is about eventual answerability. The deterministic search may explore exponentially many branches before finding a witness. The later complexity decks ask whether this cost can always be avoided efficiently—an entirely different question.

Keep: bounded-depth replay gives every finite branch a turn. Fairness preserves recognition; finite-tree exhaustion supplies rejection for deciders.

One connected check: Why does replaying only a finite prefix of each branch avoid the failure of depth-first search?

to inspect address 213, reset the work tape to the input, choose option 2 on the first step, option 1 on the second, and option 3 on the third. if a requested option doesn't exist, discard that candidate. if accept is reached along the replay, accept. then move on to the next address. no single replay is allowed to run past the address's finite length.

these addresses describe **choices**, not tape cell positions. replaying from the original input prevents edits from one branch contaminating another.

## why every accepting branch is eventually found

suppose the ntm accepts in d steps along choices c₁…c_d. there are finitely many shorter addresses and finitely many addresses of length d before that one. each replay takes finitely many steps. eventually the simulator replays the successful sequence and accepts.

if the ntm never accepts, the simulator never invents acceptance: every replay uses actual legal transitions. it may search forever. that is acceptable when simulating a recognizer, whose no-instances need not halt.

## what changes for a decider?

if every ntm branch halts on a fixed input, and branching is finite, the whole computation tree is finite. the reason is subtler than “each branch is finite, so there are finitely many branches.” if a finitely branching tree had nodes at arbitrarily large depths, one child of the root would have arbitrarily deep descendants; then one child of that child would too; continuing would construct an infinite branch. that contradicts the all-branches-halt assumption.

a breadth-first simulator can therefore maintain the live frontier and reject when no live configuration remains and none accepted. it must actually detect exhaustion; endlessly enumerating meaningless longer addresses without checking completion would not itself be a decider.

## what the theorem does and doesn't establish

deterministic and nondeterministic tms recognize the same languages and decide the same languages. this is about eventual answerability. the deterministic search may explore exponentially many branches before finding a witness. the later complexity decks ask whether this cost can always be avoided efficiently—an entirely different question.

**keep:** bounded-depth replay gives every finite branch a turn. fairness preserves recognition; finite-tree exhaustion supplies rejection for deciders.

**one connected check:** why does replaying only a finite prefix of each branch avoid the failure of depth-first search?

models.title: Algorithms and the Church–Turing thesis: what counts as an effective method?

sections.concepts: integer roots, recognition and finite bounds

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–4: algorithm formalization and Church–Turing thesis
  • PDF pages 5–8: integer roots, recognition and finite bounds
  • PDF pages 9–10: description levels
  • PDF pages 11–13: connected-graph algorithm and encoding

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The whole-course question gets bigger

We've shown that several formal machine designs have the same computability power. Now connect them to the informal word algorithm: a finite, mechanical procedure whose individual steps can be carried out effectively. The Church–Turing thesis says that effectively computable procedures are captured by Turing machines.

This is a thesis linking an informal notion to a formal model, not a theorem proved by manipulating two formal definitions. Equivalence between one-tape and multitape TMs is a theorem; the claim that the model captures every effective method has a different logical status.

Searching for a witness is like checking lockers for a missing key. Finding it settles yes. Checking a million empty lockers does not settle no when infinitely many remain. A proved finite search bound changes the job completely: exhaust that bounded region and you can finally justify rejection.

Round 1 — “Find an algorithm” needs a definition of what counts · pages 1–4

Hilbert's tenth problem asks for a method that takes an integer-coefficient polynomial and decides whether some integer assignment makes it zero. An integer root is such an assignment; with several variables it is a tuple of integers. A polynomial is a finite sum of coefficient-times-variable-power terms.

The source example 6x³yz²+3xy²−x³−10 becomes zero at x=5,y=3,z=0: the first term is 0, the second 135, the third −125, and the last −10. Checking one proposed assignment is finite arithmetic. Deciding that no assignment exists is the harder issue.

The Church–Turing thesis identifies effectively executable algorithms with Turing-computable procedures. Because “effectively executable” began as an informal concept, this is not a theorem comparing two independently formalized mathematical definitions. The slide calls it a definition; thesis emphasizes the proposed identification supported by equivalent computational models. It is not a theorem that every physical phenomenon can be simulated efficiently.

Round 2 — Search can recognize without deciding · pages 5–8

For one variable, try 0,1,−1,2,−2,… . If evaluation gives zero, accept. Every integer eventually gets tried, so a root will eventually be found. Without an additional stopping rule, a rootless polynomial makes this search continue forever.

A proven finite root bound changes the job. If every root lies in [−B,B], test only those finitely many integers and reject after they all fail. For the source's 4x³−2x²+x−7, its stated bound gives B=4×7/4=7. Use the absolute value of the leading coefficient when writing a general positive bound; a negative leading coefficient cannot give a negative search radius. Treat the zero polynomial and nonzero constants separately.

Why can a one-variable bound work? Far enough from zero, the highest-degree term dominates the sum of lower-degree terms, so the polynomial cannot cancel to zero. If degree is d, there are k nonzero terms, maximum coefficient magnitude c_max and leading magnitude |c_d|, then for |x|>max(1,k c_max/|c_d|), the leading magnitude exceeds the total lower-degree magnitude. This gives a sufficient finite radius, even if not the tightest one.

The general multivariable problem is undecidable. The slide's “bounds are not possible” should be read as absence of a general computable search bound sufficient for deciding all inputs, not a claim that every particular polynomial lacks bounded solutions. That impossibility is a deep result cited by the deck, not proved by the little enumeration example.

Round 3 — Three levels of describing the same algorithm · pages 9–10

High-level: say what logical operations are performed, such as compare every pair. Implementation-level: explain tape marking, scans, stored phase and restoration. Formal-level: provide states and transitions. A high-level description is acceptable when its operations are known to be implementable and the required level permits it. The lower layers still exist; we are using justified subroutines rather than pretending the details don't matter.

Round 4 — Connectivity is reachability from one chosen node · pages 11–13

An undirected graph is connected when every vertex can be reached from every other through edges. Choose one vertex, mark it, then repeatedly mark any vertex adjacent to a marked one. Stop when a complete pass marks no new vertex. Accept if every vertex is marked; otherwise reject.

Why correct? Every newly marked vertex has a path from the chosen start, extending the path to its marked neighbor. Conversely, if a reachable vertex remained unmarked at the fixed point, take a path to it and the first unmarked vertex on that path; its predecessor is marked, so it should have been marked too. Contradiction. Termination follows because each productive pass adds a vertex and the graph is finite.

⟨G⟩ means an encoding of graph G as a string. Validate that encoding before graph reasoning: node identifiers are distinct and edge endpoints refer to listed nodes. The displayed tuple/list format is one representation, not the graph itself. Mathematical objects become TM inputs only after such a finite encoding is specified.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Searching for an integer root: yes can be easier than no

Given a polynomial with integer coefficients, try integer inputs and evaluate it. For one variable, test 0,1,−1,2,−2,… . If an integer root exists, this enumeration eventually finds it. If none exists, an unbounded search alone runs forever. It is a recognizer-style strategy for the yes-instances, not automatically a decider.

For a univariate polynomial of positive degree with nonzero leading coefficient, a computable bound on root magnitude turns this into a finite search. Once every integer within a valid bound has been checked, there are no other possible integer roots to miss. For the slide example 4x3−2x2+x−74x^3-2x^2+x-74x3−2x2+x−7, a bound such as |x|≤7 suffices. Constant and zero polynomials are handled separately rather than dividing by a nonexistent leading term.

The critical extra ingredient is the stopping certificate supplied by the bound. “I haven't found a root yet” is not the same information as “I've exhausted every possible root.”

Why the multivariable result is deeper

For polynomial equations in several integer variables, enumerating all integer tuples still recognizes existence of a solution. Hilbert's tenth problem asked for a general deciding procedure. The negative result says no such algorithm exists for all instances. This does not follow just from the fact that our current brute-force search may loop; a bad algorithm doesn't prove all algorithms impossible. An impossibility theorem needs a reduction or other general argument.

Three levels of describing a TM

A formal description lists states and transitions. An implementation-level description explains tape layouts, head movements, and marking. A high-level description uses algorithmic steps such as “search the finite graph,” while making those steps effective and termination clear.

For graph connectivity, begin with one marked vertex, repeatedly mark neighbors of marked vertices, and stop when a whole pass adds nothing. A finite graph has only finitely many vertices to add. Accept if all are marked. The algorithm's monotone progress explains termination; the reachability invariant explains correctness.

An input encoding, written with angle brackets such as ⟨G⟩, turns an abstract object into a finite string. Invalid encodings must have specified treatment. The machine reads symbols, not a Platonic graph floating in the void.

Keep: distinguish an effective procedure, a formal simulation theorem, and the Church–Turing thesis. Existence search needs a separate reason to stop on no-instances. Next, we ask which questions about encoded machines are decidable.

One connected check: What extra fact turns the univariate integer-root enumeration into a decider, and why does “it worked on many examples” not provide that fact?

models.title: Deciding questions about automata: inspect the finite object

sections.concepts: encoded DFA acceptance and total simulation

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–4: encoded DFA acceptance and total simulation
  • PDF pages 5–6: finite NFA/RE conversions
  • PDF pages 7–9: emptiness and reachability
  • PDF pages 10–12: equivalence via symmetric difference

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The shift: the input can be a machine description

Until now, a machine usually received a word such as 0011. It can also receive an encoding of another machine, perhaps together with a word. ⟨B,w⟩\langle B,w\rangle⟨B,w⟩ means a finite string describing the pair “machine B and input w.” Angle brackets are encoding notation, not a transition or a set.

For ADFAA_{DFA}ADFA​, the question is whether the encoded DFA B accepts w. A decider checks the encoding, simulates one transition per input symbol, then checks whether the final state is accepting. There are |w| input symbols, so this simulation finishes. Empty w simply asks whether the start state accepts.

The input can be a description of another machine. Think of an inspector reading a device’s wiring diagram. The inspector is one machine; the described device is another. “Accept” means the inspector answered its own question correctly, which might be “does this device accept nothing?” Keep those two jobs separate.

Round 1 — The input now contains a machine description · pages 1–4

A_DFA={⟨B,w⟩:B is a DFA accepting w}. Read the subscript as the kind of machine being inspected. The outer decider is a TM; its input contains a finite encoding of another machine B and a string w. B is data for this run. It is not the outer decider itself.

Validate the encoding: finite state and alphabet lists, a designated start, accepting states from the state set, exactly one destination for each state/symbol pair, and input w over the declared alphabet. Then simulate B one input symbol at a time. After exactly |w| updates, inspect its state and return accept or reject accordingly. Every table lookup and every input step is finite, so this is a decider.

An input such as ⟨B,w⟩ is one encoded string; the angle brackets mean “description of these objects,” not literal mathematical objects somehow stuffed onto a tape. Invalid encodings can be rejected by convention, making the algorithm defined on all input strings.

Round 2 — Finite conversion plus a decider gives a decider · pages 5–6

For A_NFA, convert the supplied NFA into its subset DFA and use the previous decider. For A_REX, convert the regular expression into an NFA, then a DFA, then simulate. Each conversion terminates because the source structure is finite and the construction creates finitely many objects.

Exponential size is still finite. Decidability asks whether the algorithm always finishes, not whether it is fast enough to enjoy using. Later complexity theory measures the cost that this argument intentionally leaves open.

Round 3 — Emptiness reverses the final answer you're tempted to give · pages 7–9

E_DFA asks whether the machine accepts nothing. Mark the start state, then mark destinations of arrows leaving marked states until a full pass changes nothing. A marked state is exactly a reachable state. At most |Q| states can be newly marked, so the process stops.

If an accepting state is reachable, some input spells a path to it, so the language is nonempty and the emptiness decider must reject. If no accepting state is reachable, accept the emptiness question. The outer machine's acceptance answers the problem statement; it does not imitate the inner DFA's acceptance blindly.

If the start itself accepts, ε witnesses nonemptiness immediately. An accepting circle disconnected from the start does not count. The printed reachability example can be read by its actual edge relation; the invariant, rather than the typography of an intermediate mark list, determines the marked set.

Round 4 — Compare infinite languages by searching for disagreement · pages 10–12

To decide whether L(A)=L(B), build a product DFA C that accepts exactly when one machine accepts and the other rejects. Its accepting pairs satisfy XOR. The language is the symmetric difference:

(L(A)∩L(B)‾)∪(L(A)‾∩L(B)).(L(A)\cap\overline{L(B)})\cup(\overline{L(A)}\cap L(B)).(L(A)∩L(B)​)∪(L(A)​∩L(B)).

A bar means complement relative to the common alphabet's Σ*: all strings not in that language. The complements are easy for complete DFAs: swap accepting/nonaccepting states. If alphabets differ, extend to a common alphabet with rejecting sink behavior first.

Now languages agree exactly when C has no accepted disagreement witness. Run the emptiness decider on C. We did not enumerate infinitely many strings; we explored finitely many pairs of states that summarize all possible prefixes. This is the payoff of the finite-state mental model: an infinite language question can collapse to a finite graph question.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Reuse conversions when they come with termination

For NFA acceptance, convert to a DFA or directly update the finite candidate-state set while reading w. For regular-expression acceptance, compile the expression to an NFA, then use the NFA procedure. These are finite constructions. This is an early example of solving one problem by translating it into another already-solved problem.

The important claim is not “it feels computable.” We can identify each finite step and why the process ends.

Emptiness is not an infinite list of membership tests

EDFAE_{DFA}EDFA​ asks whether a DFA's language is empty. Trying ε, then all length-one strings, then all length-two strings will find a member if one exists, but may search forever if the language is empty. A decider needs a way to certify that no word works.

Treat the DFA as a finite directed graph. Mark the start. Repeatedly mark every state reachable by one outgoing arrow from a marked state. Stop when no new state is marked. If any accepting state is marked, a path to it spells an accepted string; otherwise none is reachable and the language is empty.

There are finitely many states, so marks can be added only finitely many times. A start state that already accepts makes the language nonempty via ε. That's an easy boundary case to miss if you only inspect arrows.

Equivalence becomes a search for disagreement

EQDFAEQ_{DFA}EQDFA​ asks whether two DFAs accept exactly the same strings. Build a product machine that tracks both states. Make a pair accepting exactly when one component accepts and the other rejects. This is exclusive-or, not union and not intersection.

For each input w, the product's final pair records both original verdicts. Thus its language consists exactly of disagreement witnesses. If that language is empty, the machines agree on every string; if nonempty, a member proves they differ. Run the finite emptiness algorithm on the product.

A product accepting when both components accept would answer a different question: whether they share a member. Machines may share many members and still disagree elsewhere.

The reusable reasoning pattern

Membership used a bounded run on one supplied word. Emptiness used reachability over a finite graph. Equivalence converted universal agreement into absence of a counterexample. These are three different reasons termination is available. Learn the reason, not just the conclusion “decidable.”

Keep: machine descriptions are finite inputs; finite graph structure can settle infinitely many possible words at once. Next, CFGs need different finite summaries because their derivations can grow without bound.

One connected check: Why does checking accepted strings one by one fail to decide DFA emptiness, while marking finitely many states succeeds?

sections.concepts: PDA looping, CFL decidability and hierarchy

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: bounded CNF membership search
  • PDF pages 3–5: productive-variable emptiness fixed point
  • PDF page 6: CFG equivalence and closure limitation
  • PDF pages 7–10: PDA looping, CFL decidability and hierarchy

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The obstacle: a grammar can keep expanding forever

Given a grammar G and a string w, blindly enumerate derivations. A left-recursive rule can keep producing longer sentential forms without finishing. Even if w is not generated, that search may never run out of work. To decide membership, we need a justified finite boundary.

CNF provides one. For a nonempty target of length n, each parse tree has n terminal-producing leaves and n−1 binary splits. Therefore a successful derivation uses exactly 2n−1 rule applications. With finitely many productions, there are finitely many derivations of that length to inspect. ε is handled separately using the protected start's ε rule.

Randomly trying grammar rewrites can get stuck in pointless delegation forever. CNF gives us a size budget for a successful derivation of a specified string length. Now the search has an actual fence around it. We can inspect every candidate inside that fence and justify both yes and no answers.

Round 1 — CNF finally pays rent · pages 1–2

Naively enumerating arbitrary grammar derivations is dangerous: A→B→A can repeat forever without printing anything. CNF removes those arbitrary unit/ε detours for nonempty derivations. If a generated string has n≥1 terminals, its parse tree has n terminal-producing nodes and n−1 binary-splitting nodes, totaling 2n−1 production applications.

Why n−1 splits? Start with one pending leaf. Each binary split increases the number of pending leaves by one. To end with n leaves requires n−1 increases. Each final leaf then prints one terminal. This is the structural reason for the bound, not an unexplained number to memorize.

Convert G to CNF, then enumerate leftmost derivations of exactly 2n−1 steps and compare outputs to w. Fixing leftmost expansion removes the additional choice of which variable occurrence to expand. If there are q productions, at most q choices per step gives a finite upper bound q^(2n−1); incompatible choices can be discarded. Handle w=ε separately by checking whether the start is nullable or has the allowed ε rule.

This algorithm may be wildly inefficient, but it always finishes. Its purpose here is decidability. The later dynamic-programming algorithm improves the runtime.

Round 2 — Productive means “can finish some terminal string” · pages 3–5

For grammar emptiness, mark terminals as already finished. Mark a variable A when some rule A→U₁…Uₖ has every right-side symbol marked. Then A can finish by following that rule and finishing each child. An ε rule has no unfinished children, so it marks its left variable immediately.

Repeat until no new variable is marked. The set only grows, and there are finitely many variables. A cycle A→B,B→A without any terminal-producing exit never gets marked: passing work around forever is not completing it.

If the start is unmarked, no complete output exists, so accept the emptiness question. If marked, reject emptiness. Soundness follows from the completed derivations behind marks. Completeness follows upward from any finite terminal parse tree: its leaves are marked, then their parents, eventually its root.

Round 3 — One failed method is not an impossibility proof · page 6

DFA equivalence used intersection and complement to build a disagreement language. CFLs are not closed under arbitrary intersection or complement, so the same construction is unavailable. That alone does not prove CFG equivalence undecidable; it only blocks this proof method. A separate reduction establishes the impossibility result in later theory.

Intersection with a regular language is a different statement and is closed for CFLs. “Not closed under intersection” means two arbitrary CFL operands can leave the family. Keep the operand conditions, or a memorized slogan will lead you into the wrong argument.

Round 4 — A PDA recognizer may loop even though its language is decidable · pages 7–10

A PDA can make infinitely many ε pushes without consuming the next symbol. Simulating it directly therefore may fail to give a halting decision algorithm. The language's decidability does not require every machine recognizing it to halt; it requires at least one decider.

Given a fixed CFL, choose a CFG for it and run the bounded membership procedure above on each input. This produces the needed decider. PDA→CFG conversion is finite, so a supplied PDA's membership can be decided by that route too.

The hierarchy is regular ⊊ context-free ⊊ decidable ⊊ Turing-recognizable. Each inclusion means every language in the inner family belongs to the outer; strictness means some outer languages are missing inside. Examples include equal blocks for the first separation and acceptance problems for the last. A language family classifies accepted sets, while a particular machine may have extra unnecessary loops or cumbersome implementation.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Work the size argument rather than memorize 2n−1

A binary split increases the number of pending leaves by one: replace one variable by two. Starting from one variable, it takes n−1 splits to create n final positions. Each position then uses one terminal rule, contributing n more applications. Total: (n−1)+n.

For a three-symbol word, the tree uses two binary splits and three terminal productions: five applications. The shape can vary, and there may be many candidate trees, but none needs an arbitrarily long chain of unit or ε productions because CNF removed those ordinary rules.

The resulting exhaustive algorithm may be slow. “Finite” establishes decidability, not polynomial efficiency. A later deck states the stronger fact that CFL membership has polynomial-time algorithms.

Emptiness uses a different summary: can this variable finish?

For ECFGE_{CFG}ECFG​, mark variables capable of producing terminal-only strings. Initially mark variables with terminal-only right-hand sides, including ε. Then mark A if a rule A→α has every variable in α already marked. Terminals in α are already finished output. Repeat to a fixed point.

If the start is marked, some completed word can be generated. If it isn't, the language is empty. For A→BC, B→b, C→c, B and C become marked first, then A. For A→B, B→A with no finishing production, neither ever becomes productive. A cycle alone does not manufacture output.

Why is the test complete? Any finite parse tree has productive terminal leaves, then productive parents, working upward. Why is it sound? Each new mark is justified by combining actual terminal derivations for the rule's children. Finitely many variables guarantee termination.

Why DFA equivalence doesn't transfer automatically

For DFAs, disagreement was represented by complement, intersection, and union constructions. Context-free languages are not generally closed under complement or intersection, so that route is unavailable for arbitrary CFGs. The deck states that CFG equivalence is undecidable. Failure of this one construction is not itself a proof of undecidability; the impossibility claim needs a separate theorem.

This also explains why a PDA with ε loops can recognize a decidable language. We need not use its possibly nonterminating branches as our deciding algorithm. Convert to a CFG and use a terminating membership procedure.

Keep: bound successful derivation size for membership; compute productivity for emptiness. Different questions may need different finite summaries.

One connected check: Why does a cycle A→B→A not make A productive unless some reachable rule can actually finish in terminals?

models.title: Counting programs and languages: infinity has different sizes
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: acceptance versus halting
  • PDF pages 3–8: injection, surjection, bijection and countability
  • PDF pages 9–10: rational enumeration
  • PDF pages 11–12: real diagonalization and decimal ambiguity

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The question: could every language have a program?

A language is a set of finite strings. A TM is a finite description. Even before constructing a specific impossible problem, we can compare how many descriptions and how many languages there are. If there are more languages than programs, some languages have no recognizing program at all.

“Both collections are infinite” does not settle the comparison. Infinite sets can have different cardinalities—different sizes in the sense of whether their elements can be paired one-to-one.

“I have not seen it accept yet” could mean rejection, or a loop, or acceptance much later. That is the nasty part. The problem asks for a checker that handles every supplied program and input, always halts itself, and gets the answer right. We need to understand that promise before attacking it.

Round 1 — Acceptance and halting are related, but ain't identical · pages 1–2

A_TM asks whether M accepts w. HALT_TM asks whether M halts on w, either accepting or rejecting. The deck informally calls its A_TM discussion the halting problem; keep the displayed acceptance definition precise. A machine that immediately rejects halts, but does not accept.

A_TM is recognizable: simulate M on w and accept if it accepts. If M rejects, reject; if M loops, the simulation loops. The missing ability is a universally terminating no-answer for all nonaccepting computations. A long runtime is not evidence of an infinite loop, and a finite timeout cannot decide this for arbitrary programs.

Round 2 — Infinite size is measured by pairing, not by how crowded a list looks · pages 3–8

A function is injective, or one-to-one, when different inputs have different outputs. It is surjective, or onto, when every codomain element is hit. A bijection has both properties, pairing the sets without collisions or leftovers.

For f(x)=x² on real inputs, outputs never go below zero. With codomain all reals it is not onto; with codomain nonnegative reals it is onto. It is not one-to-one in either version because x and −x share a square. By contrast x³ is a bijection from reals to reals.

The map n→2n pairs positive integers with positive even integers. An infinite proper subset can therefore have the same cardinality as its parent. Cardinality means size in this pairing sense. The sets are not equal as collections—1 belongs to one but not the other—even though their cardinalities agree. The slide's wording “two sets are equal if paired” concerns size, not membership equality.

A set is countable if finite or bijective with the natural numbers. Informally, its members can be placed in a list where every member eventually appears. The list may never end, but no particular member is postponed forever.

Round 3 — Why row-by-row enumeration fails for fractions · pages 9–10

Put positive fractions m/n in a grid. Reading the first infinite row completely would never reach the second row. Instead traverse finite diagonals of increasing m+n. Every positive pair lies on some finite diagonal, so every fraction appears eventually. Skip repetitions such as 2/2 after 1/1 has appeared; reduced fractions give unique representatives.

To include all rational numbers rather than only the positive ones, add 0 and interleave positive and negative fractions. This illustrates the difference between an infinite search that is fair and one that starves later possibilities—the same issue as NTM branch simulation.

Round 4 — Construct a number that dodges every proposed row · pages 11–12

Assume a list r₁,r₂,… contains all reals in (0,1). Construct x one decimal place at a time. At position n, choose digit 1 if rₙ's nth digit is not 1, otherwise choose 2. Then x differs from rₙ at digit n for every n. Digits only 1 and 2 avoid the 0.999…=1.000… representation ambiguity.

Since x is a real in (0,1), the allegedly complete list must contain it at some row k. But its kth digit differs from row k. Contradiction. We did not need to locate a missing number before seeing the list; the construction works against any proposed complete list.

The diagonal uses one carefully chosen disagreement per row. It does not claim x differs from every row at every digit. That distinction is what makes the construction possible and sufficient.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Countable means listable, not finite

A set is countably infinite when its elements can be listed as first, second, third, and so on without missing any. All finite strings over a finite alphabet can be listed by increasing length, and within each length in a fixed order. Every particular string eventually appears.

TM descriptions are some of those finite strings. We can enumerate candidate encodings and discard malformed ones. Thus there are only countably many TMs. Program length has no fixed maximum, but every individual program is finite.

A bijection pairs each element on one side with exactly one on the other, using every element of both. Equal cardinality does not mean the sets contain the same objects. Integers and finite machine encodings are not literally the same set.

Diagonalization shows that some collections cannot be listed

Suppose someone lists infinite binary sequences as rows. Build a new sequence whose nth bit differs from the nth bit of row n. It differs from row 1 in position 1, row 2 in position 2, and so on. Therefore it is absent from the supposedly complete list.

The construction defeats every row for a specific reason, not by vaguely saying “there must be another one.” In the real-number version, choosing safe decimal digits avoids the ambiguity of two decimal representations such as a trailing sequence of 9s. The logical engine is the same: disagreement on the diagonal.

Connect the counting argument to languages

List all finite input strings as s₁,s₂,s₃,… . A language determines an infinite membership sequence: bit i is 1 if sᵢ belongs, 0 otherwise. Conversely, each such sequence defines a language. Since these infinite sequences cannot all be listed, neither can all languages.

Countably many programs cannot cover uncountably many languages. Some languages are not even recognizable. This is an existence result; it does not yet tell us a particular familiar language with no algorithm.

Keep the named problems distinct

ATMA_{TM}ATM​ consists of pairs ⟨M,w⟩ where M accepts w. HALTTMHALT_{TM}HALTTM​ asks whether M halts on w, either accepting or rejecting. These are different languages, although both are undecidable. If M rejects w, that is a no-instance of acceptance and a yes-instance of halting.

The next deck gives an explicit contradiction for A_TM, then uses recognizability and complement to sharpen the picture. Counting proves there are impossible tasks; diagonal self-reference identifies one.

Keep: finite programs are listable; arbitrary languages correspond to unlistable infinite bit sequences. “Infinite” alone is not a size comparison.

One connected check: For a machine that halts and rejects w, how do its A_TM and HALT_TM membership answers differ?

models.title: The acceptance contradiction: build a program that flips its own predicted answer

sections.concepts: countably many programs and uncountably many languages

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: countably many programs and uncountably many languages
  • PDF pages 4–8: self-reference contradiction and diagonal view
  • PDF pages 9–12: co-recognition and dovetailing theorem

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Assume the impossible helper precisely

Suppose a decider H answers whether any encoded machine M accepts any input w. H always halts. On a yes-instance it says yes; on a no-instance it says no. “No” includes both M rejecting and M looping forever. H would have to settle both cases correctly.

We are assuming this helper exists to derive a contradiction. We are not claiming we can already implement it, and we are not waiting for a looping machine to finish.

Suppose a perfect predictor tells a program what it will do. Build the program to do the opposite of that prediction when inspecting its own description. Now follow both possible predictions. Each breaks the predictor’s promise. The contradiction needs that exact construction; self-reference alone is not some magic spell.

Round 1 — There are more languages than programs · pages 1–3

List finite binary strings by increasing length, then lexicographic order within a length: ε,0,1,00,01,… . Every finite string appears at a finite position. TM descriptions are finite strings, so there are only countably many machines, even though there are infinitely many.

A language is an arbitrary subset of that string list. Its characteristic sequence writes 1 at position i when string i belongs, otherwise 0. For the language of strings starting with 0, the opening bits are 010110011… under the slide's enumeration. This sequence is infinite because it answers membership for every possible finite input.

Infinite binary sequences are uncountable by diagonal bit-flipping. Each corresponds to one language, so there are uncountably many languages. Each machine recognizes one language, though several machines may recognize the same one. Countably many machines cannot cover the uncountable collection. Thus some languages are not even Turing-recognizable. This counting argument proves existence; it does not yet identify a specific example.

Round 2 — The hypothetical perfect checker gets asked about itself · pages 4–8

Assume H decides A_TM, so H always halts and answers whether a supplied M accepts its supplied input. Construct D on input ⟨M⟩: run H on ⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩, then output the opposite result. D can do this because machine descriptions are ordinary finite strings and H is assumed total.

Now feed D its own description. If H predicts D accepts ⟨D⟩, D rejects. If H predicts D does not accept ⟨D⟩, D accepts. Either answer contradicts H's promised correctness. Therefore H cannot exist.

The no-case for an arbitrary M is “M does not accept,” including rejection or looping. The slide sometimes writes “rejects” where that broader condition is needed. D itself always halts under the assumption that H is a decider, so its self-case has no third looping escape route.

In the diagonal table, row i records what Mᵢ does on each machine description. D differs from row i at its diagonal input ⟨Mᵢ⟩. If D appeared as a row, its own diagonal cell would have to disagree with itself. This is the program version of constructing a missing decimal, with total H supplying the hypothetical answers.

Round 3 — Why swapping accept and reject does not complement a recognizer · pages 9–12

A recognizer may loop on a nonmember. Swapping its two halting labels leaves that loop unchanged, but the input should now be accepted by a recognizer for the complement. So the swap works for deciders, where every run reaches a halt, but not for arbitrary recognizers.

Co-recognizable means the complement has a recognizer. The theorem is: A is decidable iff both A and its complement are recognizable. Forward: a decider recognizes A, and swapping its answers gives a decider—and therefore recognizer—for the complement.

Reverse: run the two recognizers with dovetailing, one step of the first, then one step of the second, repeatedly. If the A-recognizer accepts, accept. If the complement-recognizer accepts, reject. Every input belongs to exactly one side, so one of those accepting events eventually happens. A rejection by one recognizer is not needed as the decisive signal; its behavior on nonmembers may include looping.

Since A_TM is recognizable but undecidable, its complement cannot also be recognizable, or the theorem would produce a decider. This provides the explicit nonrecognizable language that the earlier counting proof did not name.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the challenger D

On input ⟨M⟩, D asks H about ⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩\langle M,\langle M\rangle\rangle⟨M,⟨M⟩⟩: does M accept its own description? If H says yes, D rejects. If H says no, D accepts. Because the assumed H always halts, D also halts.

A machine description can be input data just like any other string. M is a machine; ⟨M⟩ is its encoded description. Feeding code to a program is not mystical self-awareness—it's ordinary data processing.

H is the supposed perfect predictor; D is the deliberately contrary program. D doesn't have to be clever. Its entire move is “whatever H predicts about acceptance, do the opposite.” The contradiction arrives only when the predictor is asked about that very contrary program on its own code. Keep those roles fixed before substituting D for M.

Now give D its own description

Ask what D does on ⟨D⟩.

If H predicts “D accepts ⟨D⟩,” D follows its rule and rejects. The prediction is wrong.

If H predicts “D does not accept ⟨D⟩,” D follows its rule and accepts. Again the prediction is wrong.

These two cases exhaust H's possible answers. Therefore the assumed universal acceptance decider cannot exist. The contradiction is not “D loops somehow.” D was defined to halt using H; it is the correctness of H that becomes impossible.

Recognition still exists

A universal simulator can recognize A_TM: decode M and w, simulate M on w, and accept if M accepts. If M rejects, reject; if M loops, the simulation may loop. This satisfies recognition but not decision. Undecidable does not mean no useful yes-verifier or simulator exists.

Why complements expose the missing guarantee

The complement of a language contains exactly the input strings outside it, within the fixed encoding universe. If both L and its complement have recognizers, run the two recognizers in alternating steps on the same input. Exactly one side contains that input, so its recognizer eventually accepts. If L's recognizer accepts, answer yes; if the complement's accepts, answer no. This always terminates and decides L.

For A_TM, a recognizer exists but a decider does not. Therefore its complement cannot also be recognizable. This is a logical consequence of the parallel-recognizer construction.

Why not simply swap accept and reject in an A_TM recognizer? Because loops remain loops. A no-instance that used to loop doesn't become an accepted complement member. Swapping halting verdicts works for deciders, which have no third outcome to worry about.

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: direction of algorithmic reduction
  • PDF pages 4–7: emptiness reduction, hardcoding and nonacceptance

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The direction is the whole game

To prove a new problem B undecidable, start with a known undecidable problem A. Show how a solver for B would let you decide A. In words: hard input in, translate it, call the supposed B solver, translate its answer back. If that worked, it would contradict A's known impossibility.

The arrow goes from the known hard problem toward the target problem. Showing that B can be solved using an A oracle says little about B's impossibility; easy problems can also wastefully call a hard oracle.

You are building an adapter: plug the old impossible question into the proposed new solver, then translate its answer back. If that adapter worked, the new solver would solve the old impossible job. So the new solver cannot exist. The damn direction matters; an adapter pointed backward proves something else.

Round 1 — Borrow a solver for B to solve A · pages 1–3

“A reduces to B” means a procedure for B would let us solve A through an effective construction and finite surrounding computation. The direction is easy to reverse by accident. To prove a new target B hard, start with an already hard problem A and show how a B-solver would solve it.

Think of a socket adapter: you already know the task requiring plug A is impossible to power with the available universal setup. If a purported B outlet plus a finite adapter would power A, that B outlet cannot exist under the assumptions either. The analogy represents dependency; the actual proof must specify the adapter algorithm and its answer correspondence.

The logical form is B decidable ⇒ A decidable. Its contrapositive is A undecidable ⇒ B undecidable. A reduction from an easy A to B proves no hardness for B. A reduction that itself calls an undecidable oracle without justification is not a valid finite adapter.

Round 2 — Turn one acceptance question into an emptiness question · pages 4–7

Given ⟨M,w⟩, construct the description of a new machine M₁. On its own input x, M₁ rejects if x≠w. If x=w, it simulates M on w and accepts if M accepts. The fixed w is stored in M₁'s program description.

We can write this description in finite time without discovering whether M will accept. That's crucial. Constructing a simulator is not the same as running the simulated computation to completion. The reduction creates code; the hypothetical emptiness decider must inspect its language behavior.

There are two language cases. If M accepts w, M₁ accepts exactly w, so L(M₁)={w}. If M does not accept w—whether it rejects or loops—M₁ accepts no input, so L(M₁)=∅. A looping run on x=w contributes no accepted member. This repairs the slide's occasional shorthand “rejects” in the no-case.

Assume R decides E_TM, the set of TM descriptions whose language is empty. Run R on ⟨M₁⟩. If R says empty, reject the original acceptance question. If R says nonempty, accept it. R always halts by assumption, and constructing M₁ is finite, so the resulting outer procedure would decide A_TM. Contradiction.

Round 3 — Audit the proof by asking what each machine receives

M is the original machine; w is its fixed test input. M₁ is the constructed machine; x is its arbitrary future input. R is the hypothetical emptiness decider; it receives the description ⟨M₁⟩, not x. S, the outer decider we derive for contradiction, receives ⟨M,w⟩.

These are different levels. If you silently replace x with w everywhere, you can lose the proof that all other inputs are rejected and therefore fail to characterize L(M₁). If you run M inside S before calling R, S may loop and the contradiction collapses.

The result also does not say every particular TM has an unknowable language. Many individual machines are trivially empty or nonempty. It rules out one algorithm that correctly decides emptiness for every encoded TM.

The construction maps acceptance to nonemptiness, so the final Boolean answer is flipped. When later distinguishing many-one reductions from more general decision-procedure reductions, preserve that polarity explicitly instead of claiming a yes-preserving mapping to E_TM without the flip.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

The deck's target: is a TM's language empty?

ETM={⟨M⟩:L(M)=∅}E_{TM}=\{\langle M\rangle:L(M)=\emptyset\}ETM​={⟨M⟩:L(M)=∅}. This asks whether M accepts no input at all. A machine that loops on every input has an empty accepted language. “Empty” refers to the set of accepted strings, not whether the program runs or the tape starts blank.

Assume a decider R for E_TM exists. Given an acceptance instance ⟨M,w⟩, construct a new machine M₁:

  1. On input x, if x≠w, reject.
  2. If x=w, simulate M on w.
  3. Accept if that simulation accepts; if it rejects, reject; if it loops, keep simulating.

M and w are hardcoded into M₁'s description. Constructing that description is finite; we do not need to run M first to decide which code to write.

The wrapper is a booby-trapped test case for the supposed emptiness checker: the single candidate w gets through only if the embedded simulation accepts. Every other candidate is rejected at the door. That is the mechanism linking one execution question to a property of an entire language. The code is easy to write; knowing which behavior eventually happens is the hard part the hypothetical checker would have to solve.

Work both cases before deciding the answer flip

If M accepts w, M₁ accepts exactly w, so L(M1)={w}L(M_1)=\{w\}L(M1​)={w}, which is nonempty—even if w happens to be ε.

If M does not accept w, M₁ accepts nothing, so L(M1)=∅L(M_1)=\emptysetL(M1​)=∅. For x≠w it rejects immediately; for x=w it rejects or loops. Neither outcome is acceptance.

Thus R's “empty” answer means the original acceptance answer is no; R's “nonempty” answer means yes. We flip R's emptiness verdict to decide A_TM, a contradiction.

Why this isn't circular

M₁ may loop. That's allowed: R was assumed to decide a property of any encoded TM, including looping ones. Our overall hypothetical A_TM decider does not execute M₁ to completion; it gives M₁'s finite description to R, which is assumed to halt.

The reduction itself must be effective and terminating. Writing a wrapper program around ⟨M,w⟩ satisfies that. “Wait to see whether M accepts, then output one of two machines” would not: it might wait forever and fail to produce the transformed instance.

What a rigorous reduction answer contains

Name the assumed target decider, define the constructed machine for every input, analyze the source yes-case and no-case, show how the target answer yields the source answer, and explain why the construction and oracle use would terminate. The two-case table is the bridge between intuition and proof.

Keep: you don't solve the hard instance while constructing the wrapper. You encode its eventual behavior into a property the hypothetical solver is supposed to decide.

One connected check: Why does M looping on w still make M₁'s language empty rather than leave the mathematical set L(M₁) “unknown”?

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–4: regularity property switch
  • PDF pages 5–6: equivalence to a fixed empty-language machine

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The mental model: a behavioral switch

A reduction can construct a TM whose accepted language has one form if M accepts w and another form if M does not. Then a hypothetical property checker distinguishes the cases. The wrapper is fixed code; the language it ends up recognizing depends on the embedded simulation's behavior.

The target here is REGULARTMREGULAR_{TM}REGULARTM​: given a TM description, decide whether its accepted language is regular. The input is not a DFA with visibly finite-state behavior. It's an arbitrary TM, and the question is whether some DFA recognizes the same language.

Turn the unknown computation into a switch. In one case the constructed machine accepts a familiar regular language; in the other it accepts a known nonregular language. A perfect regularity checker would reveal which case happened. The construction must set up that switch without secretly solving the unknown computation first.

Round 1 — Make the unknown behavior control a visible language property · pages 1–4

REGULAR_TM asks whether the language accepted by a supplied TM is regular. It does not ask whether the TM's diagram looks like a DFA or whether it uses its tape. A cumbersome TM can recognize a simple regular language.

Given ⟨M,w⟩, build M₂ on input x. First decide whether x has form 0ⁿ1ⁿ. If so, accept immediately. Otherwise simulate M on the fixed w and accept if M accepts. The first branch is decidable because we already know a matching algorithm for equal ordered blocks.

If M accepts w, every x accepts: members of 0ⁿ1ⁿ use the first branch, all other binary strings eventually use the simulation branch. Therefore L(M₂)={0,1}*, which is regular. If M does not accept w, only the first branch contributes accepted strings, so L(M₂)={0ⁿ1ⁿ:n≥0}, which is nonregular. Again, “does not accept” includes looping; the proof must not assume M always halts.

A hypothetical regularity decider for ⟨M₂⟩ would therefore answer whether M accepts w. The outer reduction only constructs M₂ and calls that total decider. It never waits for M itself to finish. That gives the contradiction with A_TM's undecidability.

Round 2 — Why the order of the two branches matters

If M₂ first simulated M on w and only afterward checked x's equal-block form, then a looping M would prevent even valid 0ⁿ1ⁿ strings from being accepted. The baseline nonregular language would disappear, and the intended two-case analysis would be wrong.

The unconditional baseline branch must happen before the potentially nonterminating simulation, or be fairly interleaved with it. Here doing the easy decidable baseline test first is sufficient. The mechanism is a property switch: unknown acceptance toggles the language from a known nonregular set to a known regular set.

You need to prove both language identities, not merely exhibit one accepted string in each case. Regularity concerns the entire accepted set. The same reduction design pattern later works for many other nontrivial language properties, though each theorem has its own hypotheses.

Round 3 — Equivalence can hide emptiness as a special case · pages 5–6

EQ_TM asks whether two TMs accept exactly the same language. Choose a fixed machine Z that rejects every input, so L(Z)=∅. Then L(M)=L(Z) exactly when L(M)=∅.

If R decided EQ_TM, an emptiness decider could take ⟨M⟩, construct ⟨M,Z⟩, run R and return its answer. This construction preserves yes/no directly; no flip is needed. Since E_TM was just proved undecidable, EQ_TM is undecidable too.

Notice the economy: the second reduction starts from E_TM because equality with an empty-language reference makes the connection immediate. You do not have to reduce from A_TM every time. Choose a previously established hard problem whose question aligns cleanly with the target.

The general proof checklist is source problem, hypothetical target decider, finite construction, exact yes/no relationship, termination of the outer procedure, and contradiction. A paragraph that merely says “similar to the previous proof” omits the actual adapter; spell out the machine behavior that makes the relationship true.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Build the two cases into one machine

Given ⟨M,w⟩, construct M₂. On input x:

  1. If x is in K={0n1n:n≥0}K=\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}K={0n1n:n≥0}, accept immediately. K has a terminating membership test, even though it is not regular.
  2. Otherwise simulate M on w, accepting x if that simulation accepts.

If M rejects w, M₂ may reject on that second branch; if M loops, M₂ loops there. Either way, those x's are not accepted.

Identify the two languages exactly

If M accepts w, every x in K is accepted by step 1 and every x outside K is eventually accepted by step 2. Thus L(M2)=Σ∗L(M_2)=\Sigma^*L(M2​)=Σ∗, which is regular.

If M does not accept w, only step 1 contributes accepted strings. Thus L(M2)=KL(M_2)=KL(M2​)=K, which is nonregular by the pumping proof.

A REGULAR_TM decider would therefore answer yes exactly when M accepts w. That would decide A_TM, contradiction. This time the answer is not flipped. Decide the direction from the case analysis, not from a memorized rule that “reductions negate the answer.”

Why the nonregular base language is doing real work

K supplies a known no-instance of the target property, while Σ* supplies a known yes-instance. The simulation switches between them. If both cases produced regular languages, the target checker could not reveal the source answer. If the wrapper accepted extra strings in the no-case, you would need to re-prove the resulting language nonregular; hand-waving about “mostly K” is not enough.

Also distinguish “nonregular” from “undecidable.” K is nonregular but decidable. That is why step 1 can be an ordinary finite algorithm. The target property of arbitrary TM languages is the undecidable task.

Equivalence gives another route

EQTMEQ_{TM}EQTM​ asks whether two TMs accept the same language. Compare an arbitrary M against a fixed machine that rejects every input. Their languages are equal exactly when L(M) is empty. So an equivalence decider would give an emptiness decider, which the previous deck ruled out.

Again, the reduction handles accepted languages, not identical running times or identical step-by-step behavior. Two machines can recognize the same language while one rejects a nonmember and the other loops on it.

Keep: construct a clear property switch; prove exactly what language appears in both cases; then read off the contradiction.

One connected check: Why is it valid for the wrapper to decide membership in a nonregular language K, and why would that not be valid if K had no decider?

the unconditional baseline branch must happen before the potentially nonterminating simulation, or be fairly interleaved with it. here doing the easy decidable baseline test first is sufficient. the mechanism is a **property switch**: unknown acceptance toggles the language from a known nonregular set to a known regular set.

you need to prove both language identities, not merely exhibit one accepted string in each case. regularity concerns the entire accepted set. the same reduction design pattern later works for many other nontrivial language properties, though each theorem has its own hypotheses.

## round 3 — equivalence can hide emptiness as a special case · pages 5–6

eq_tm asks whether two tms accept exactly the same language. choose a fixed machine z that rejects every input, so l(z)=∅. then l(m)=l(z) exactly when l(m)=∅.

if r decided eq_tm, an emptiness decider could take ⟨m⟩, construct ⟨m,z⟩, run r and return its answer. this construction preserves yes/no directly; no flip is needed. since e_tm was just proved undecidable, eq_tm is undecidable too.

notice the economy: the second reduction starts from e_tm because equality with an empty-language reference makes the connection immediate. you do not have to reduce from a_tm every time. choose a previously established hard problem whose question aligns cleanly with the target.

the general proof checklist is source problem, hypothetical target decider, finite construction, exact yes/no relationship, termination of the outer procedure, and contradiction. a paragraph that merely says “similar to the previous proof” omits the actual adapter; spell out the machine behavior that makes the relationship true.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## build the two cases into one machine

given ⟨m,w⟩, construct m₂. on input x:

1. if x is in \(k=\{0^n1^n:n\ge0\}\), accept immediately. k has a terminating membership test, even though it is not regular.
2. otherwise simulate m on w, accepting x if that simulation accepts.

if m rejects w, m₂ may reject on that second branch; if m loops, m₂ loops there. either way, those x's are not accepted.

## identify the two languages exactly

if m accepts w, every x in k is accepted by step 1 and every x outside k is eventually accepted by step 2. thus \(l(m_2)=\sigma^*\), which is regular.

if m does not accept w, only step 1 contributes accepted strings. thus \(l(m_2)=k\), which is nonregular by the pumping proof.

a regular_tm decider would therefore answer yes exactly when m accepts w. that would decide a_tm, contradiction. this time the answer is not flipped. decide the direction from the case analysis, not from a memorized rule that “reductions negate the answer.”

## why the nonregular base language is doing real work

k supplies a known no-instance of the target property, while σ* supplies a known yes-instance. the simulation switches between them. if both cases produced regular languages, the target checker could not reveal the source answer. if the wrapper accepted extra strings in the no-case, you would need to re-prove the resulting language nonregular; hand-waving about “mostly k” is not enough.

also distinguish “nonregular” from “undecidable.” k is nonregular but decidable. that is why step 1 can be an ordinary finite algorithm. the target property of arbitrary tm languages is the undecidable task.

## equivalence gives another route

\(eq_{tm}\) asks whether two tms accept the same language. compare an arbitrary m against a fixed machine that rejects every input. their languages are equal exactly when l(m) is empty. so an equivalence decider would give an emptiness decider, which the previous deck ruled out.

again, the reduction handles accepted languages, not identical running times or identical step-by-step behavior. two machines can recognize the same language while one rejects a nonmember and the other loops on it.

**keep:** construct a clear property switch; prove exactly what language appears in both cases; then read off the contradiction.

**one connected check:** why is it valid for the wrapper to decide membership in a nonregular language k, and why would that not be valid if k had no decider?

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: finite accepting histories and validation
  • PDF pages 4–7: LBA memory bound and end markers
  • PDF pages 8–10: configuration counting and membership decision

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Replace “run the machine” with “inspect a claimed run”

A computation history is a finite sequence of configurations C₁,C₂,…,Cₘ. It claims that C₁ is the starting snapshot, each next snapshot follows legally from the previous one, and Cₘ is an accepting or rejecting halt. It's a transcript of the computation, with tape and head information included.

Checking such a supplied transcript is different from waiting for a machine to produce one. A looping computation has arbitrarily long finite prefixes, but no completed accepting or rejecting history. A finite checker can reject an invalid claimed history without resolving whether some other, longer accepting one exists.

A program can leave a receipt listing every configuration it visited. Checking a supplied receipt is local: right start, legal neighboring steps, right finish. Finding out whether any successful receipt exists is a different job. Keep the finite audit separate from the potentially unbounded search for something to audit.

Round 1 — A history is a receipt for a completed computation · pages 1–3

A computation history lists configurations C₁,…,Cℓ. To be an accepting history, it must start at the correct input configuration, end in an accepting configuration, and make one legal transition between every neighboring pair. A rejecting history ends in rejection instead.

These histories are finite by definition. A looping computation has arbitrarily long finite prefixes but no completed accepting/rejecting history. A deterministic machine has at most one complete halting computation on a fixed input; an NTM may have several because different choices produce different runs.

Think of auditing a transaction log: the first balance must be right, each update must follow the rules, and the final status must meet the required outcome. A plausible final line alone cannot certify a valid history. The analogy concerns local consistency and endpoints, not financial semantics.

Checking a supplied finite receipt can be manageable even when deciding whether any successful receipt exists is impossible. The next deck exploits that distinction in reductions.

Round 2 — Linear bounded means memory grows with this input · pages 4–7

An LBA is a TM constrained to a tape region whose size is bounded by a constant times the input length. The slide's exact-window version uses the input cells themselves, with end markers preventing escape. It is not a finite automaton: input length n can be arbitrarily large, so its available memory is not one fixed constant for all inputs.

The markers may not be overwritten, and the head may not move beyond them. A constant-factor larger workspace can be encoded using multiple tracks per cell, enlarging the finite tape alphabet. That is why common linear-space variants have equivalent language power. A finite alphabet can encode a fixed number of tracks, not an input-dependent unbounded number.

The slide lists finite-automaton and grammar decision tasks as examples that fit this kind of bounded storage; it does not derive those implementations here. Do not confuse “the algorithm terminates” with “it uses only linear space.” The latter needs its own storage accounting.

Round 3 — Count complete configurations, not just control states · pages 8–9

For q states, n available head positions and g tape symbols, there are at most q·n·gⁿ configurations. The three factors represent state choice, head-position choice and all n-cell tape contents. gⁿ arises because each cell independently has g options. Protected-marker conventions may forbid some combinations, so this is a sufficient upper bound even when not every combination is legal.

For illustration, q=3,n=2,g=2 gives 3×2×4=24 possibilities. Revisiting the same state alone does not force a loop: tape or head position may differ. Revisiting the same entire configuration in a deterministic machine forces identical future behavior.

Round 4 — A finite configuration graph gives a halting algorithm · page 10

For a deterministic LBA on a fixed input, simulate until it accepts, rejects, or repeats a complete configuration. Repetition means a loop, so reject the acceptance question. Equivalently, use the configuration bound to know when repetition must have occurred. Handle empty input separately according to the machine's boundary convention rather than substituting n=0 blindly into a zero bound.

For a nondeterministic LBA, one repeated configuration on one branch is not enough to reject everything. Explore the finite configuration graph with a visited set and accept iff an accepting configuration is reachable. The graph is finite for this fixed input, so the search terminates.

Thus A_LBA is decidable. The input length supplies the finite bound. Asking whether the same LBA accepts some input of any length removes that fixed n, which is why the emptiness problem in the next deck can be undecidable without contradicting this result.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Three checks make the claim precise

First verify that C₁ is the actual start configuration for the specified input. Then check every adjacent pair: did exactly the allowed write, head movement, and state change occur, with other cells unchanged? Finally check the required terminal condition, such as an accepting halt state in Cₘ.

A string with the right first and last states can still contain a fake middle step. Conversely, a sequence of locally legal steps beginning from the wrong input proves nothing about the intended instance. All three clauses matter.

This is another proof pattern: a long global claim can have a finite certificate with many small consistency checks. Later, NP uses polynomially bounded certificates; here the history can be arbitrarily long.

Bounded tape makes the configuration space finite

A linear bounded automaton, LBA, is a TM whose available tape is bounded by the input length under the course model. It may revisit and rewrite those cells, but it cannot keep expanding its workspace beyond the allotted region.

For n available cells, q control states, and g tape symbols, there are at most q n gnq\,n\,g^nqngn configurations: q state choices, n head positions, and g choices independently for each cell. The exact boundary convention can change a constant factor; finiteness is the key. Fix the input before counting—n is not one constant for all possible inputs.

Why membership becomes decidable

For a deterministic LBA, if the same complete configuration repeats before halting, future behavior repeats too, so it will loop. Simulate until accept, reject, or a repeated configuration. Finite configuration space guarantees one of these outcomes.

For a nondeterministic LBA, searching one path is insufficient. Explore the finite directed graph of configurations and ask whether an accepting configuration is reachable. Keep a visited set to avoid revisiting loops forever. This is the DFA reachability idea applied to a much larger finite graph.

The limit of this result

We have a bound for one fixed input length. It does not automatically settle whether an LBA accepts some input of any length. That problem ranges over unbounded n, so no single finite configuration graph covers all candidates. The next deck uses computation histories to show why this distinction matters.

Keep: a finite claimed run can be verified; bounded space gives finitely many configurations per input; membership and emptiness quantify over different things.

One connected check: Why does the bound qngⁿ decide one-input acceptance without supplying a bound on the shortest accepted input of an arbitrary LBA?
