models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–6: history-checking LBA and emptiness reduction
  • PDF pages 7–10: CFG universality and bad-history complement
  • PDF pages 11–13: PDA witness check and alternating reversal

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The apparent paradox

LBA membership is decidable: for one supplied input, search a finite configuration graph. Yet LBA emptiness is undecidable: there is no general algorithm deciding whether it accepts any input. The difference is the quantifier. “Check this candidate” does not give a finite stopping rule for “no candidate of any length works.”

Given ⟨M,w⟩, construct an LBA B whose input is a claimed accepting computation history of M on w. B checks its formatting, correct start, legal adjacent steps, and accepting final configuration. It uses the candidate's own length as bounded workspace. It does not simulate M forever hoping that a history eventually appears.

The checker receives the entire proposed history as its input. That long receipt supplies the space for its own audit. So a bounded-tape machine can check a huge computation history without simulating that whole computation on the tiny original input. The input changed; that is where the workspace comes from.

Round 1 — Give the bounded machine a long enough receipt · pages 1–6

Given ⟨M,w⟩, build an LBA B that accepts exactly encoded accepting histories of M on w. Its input x is a proposed history, not the original w. x may be enormously longer than w, and B's available workspace scales with |x|. That resolves the apparent contradiction: B does not simulate an arbitrary unbounded computation using only |w| cells; it audits a history already supplied as input.

The history format is #C₁#C₂#…#Cℓ#. Validate separators, configuration syntax, exactly one state/head marker per configuration, the correct initial configuration for w, an accepting last configuration, and every adjacent transition. Neighboring configurations agree away from the old/new head neighborhood; a legal TM step changes only the scanned symbol, state and head position. Marking and zigzag comparison can check those local conditions inside a linear-sized work representation.

If extra constant-factor workspace is convenient, use fixed tracks or a padded input convention as the slide suggests. The encoding must be specified consistently. It cannot quietly demand an input-dependent superlinear amount of new tape while still claiming an LBA.

If M accepts w, at least one finite accepting history exists, so L(B) is nonempty. If M does not accept w, including looping, no such history exists and L(B)=∅. A hypothetical E_LBA decider would answer emptiness, and flipping its answer would decide A_TM. The finite construction of B hardcodes M and w; it does not first wait for the history to exist.

Round 2 — For CFG universality, accept every bad receipt · pages 7–10

ALL_CFG asks whether L(G)=Σ*. The reduction wants G to generate every string except valid accepting histories of M on w, using a carefully chosen history encoding. If M never accepts, no excluded history exists and G generates everything. If M accepts, at least one history is excluded and the grammar is not universal.

A history is valid when its format is correct AND its start is correct AND its end accepts AND every neighboring pair is legal. Negating that conjunction gives an OR: malformed format, wrong start, wrong end, or at least one invalid adjacent step. This is De Morgan's law. The “at least one” is what makes a nondeterministic witness-of-error checker useful.

An error detector can choose which defect to demonstrate. If one actual defect exists, a branch can find it. On a completely valid history, no branch may falsely claim a defect. This is existential acceptance applied to invalidity, not a magical PDA that verifies an arbitrary full TM computation.

Round 3 — Reverse alternating configurations so the stack lines up · pages 11–13

A stack pops its stored block backward. If neighboring configurations were both written left-to-right, pushing the first and popping while reading the second would compare opposite ends. Encode instead

#C1#C2R#C3#C4R#⋯ .\#C_1\#C_2^R\#C_3\#C_4^R\#\cdots.#C1​#C2R​#C3​#C4R​#⋯.

R denotes reversal. For an odd/even neighboring pair, pushing Cᵢ lets the PDA compare with the reversed next configuration from right to left. For an even/odd pair, pushing Cᵢᴿ makes popping present Cᵢ forward, matching the next forward block. Finite control remembers parity and the constant-sized local transition neighborhood.

The PDA guesses an adjacent pair, stores one block, and checks the next for a mismatch outside the permitted local update or an incorrect local update itself. It also checks unequal lengths or boundary conventions consistently with the encoding. The start/end/format error branches need only finite-state checks for the fixed M,w and regular configuration syntax. Converting this PDA to a CFG gives G.

The construction is subtle: it recognizes the union of error witnesses. It does not use a false claim that CFLs are closed under complement. The complement-like language is built directly through a PDA capable of finding one defect. A universality decider for that G would then decide the original acceptance question, giving the contradiction.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Analyze the two cases

If M accepts w, its finite accepting run can be written as a history. That string passes B's checks, so L(B) is nonempty.

If M does not accept w, no valid accepting history exists. Every candidate fails at least one check, so L(B) is empty.

A decider for LBA emptiness would distinguish these cases and decide A_TM, contradiction. Each individual history check terminates, yet the existence question over histories of unbounded length remains undecidable. No contradiction at all once the two questions are separated.

Why reversed configurations show up in the CFG argument

For the CFG universality problem ALLCFGALL_{CFG}ALLCFG​, the construction uses a PDA for bad histories. A bad history has some defect: malformed syntax, wrong start, wrong finish, or an illegal adjacent step. Nondeterminism can guess a defect to check. Acceptance means at least one real defect is found.

To compare neighboring configurations using a stack, encode alternating configurations in reverse order. Pushing one configuration and reading the reversed next one brings corresponding positions together under last-in-first-out access. Without that reversal, the stack would present the first configuration backward while the next arrived forward, and the local comparison would not line up.

The PDA needs to verify a local illegal transition, including unchanged regions and the small region affected by the head. This is a construction argument; the phrase “just check the pair” stands for specific stack work, not an unlimited random-access comparison.

Why “bad histories” produces universality

If M never accepts w, every string is either malformed or fails to describe a valid accepting history. The bad-history language is then all strings over the encoding alphabet, Σ*.

If M accepts w, at least one valid accepting history exists. That string has no defect, so it is excluded. The bad-history language is not universal.

Convert the PDA to a CFG. A hypothetical CFG-universality decider would reveal whether M accepts w by checking whether the resulting grammar generates all strings. The construction must include malformed strings among the bad ones; otherwise the no-acceptance case might still omit them and fail to be Σ*.

How the earlier topics cooperate

The proof uses configurations from TM theory, stack reversal from PDA design, PDA→CFG equivalence, and the two-case structure of reductions. This is why disconnected formula memorization collapses here: the pieces have jobs in one larger argument.

Keep: a finite checker can verify candidates while existence over unbounded candidates remains hard. Bad-certificate recognition turns a missing valid history into universality.

One connected check: Why must the bad-history PDA accept malformed encodings as well as well-formed histories with an illegal step?

Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck

  • PDF pages 4–8: Big-O quantifiers, proof and negation
  • PDF pages 9–11: logarithms and base change
  • PDF pages 12–15: sum rules, exponential notation and constants

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The question changes from “can it finish?” to “how much work?”

A decider halts on every input, but its running time may grow wildly with input length. Complexity studies that growth. Let n be the length of the encoded input, and T(n) the worst number of steps among inputs of that length. We want useful comparisons without listing every constant setup cost.

f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n))f(n)=O(g(n)) says that beyond some threshold n₀, f stays below a constant multiple c of g. Formally, there exist c>0 and n₀ such that f(n)≤c g(n)f(n)\le c\,g(n)f(n)≤cg(n) for every n≥n₀, for the nonnegative functions under discussion.

The constants must be fixed across all sufficiently large n. You don't get to choose a new c for each n; that would make the claim almost meaningless.

Aight, now we stop asking “can it finish?” and ask “how does the bill grow?” Count steps against input length, then look at the eventual growth. A fixed multiplier can absorb some overhead. It cannot grow whenever the input gets inconvenient. That fixed-versus-growing distinction is the whole damn point.

Round 1 — “Eventually finishes” and “finishes this century” are different jobs · pages 1–3

A decider always halts. Complexity asks how its resource use grows with input length. Let T(w) be the number of transitions on one input w; worst-case time f(n) is the maximum T(w) over inputs of length n. Average-case time would require a probability distribution over inputs; “average” is not defined by wishful thinking.

n counts encoded input symbols, not necessarily the numeric value represented by them. A binary integer of value about 2ⁿ needs about n bits. This distinction later separates polynomial time from algorithms that are fast only in the numeric value.

The one-tape equal-block procedure repeatedly crosses the input to match a zero and a one. To analyze it, count rounds and cost per round. State diagrams show behavior; runtime analysis accounts for how often that behavior repeats.

Round 2 — Big-O is an eventual ceiling with a fixed multiplier · pages 4–8

For eventually nonnegative functions, f(n)=O(g(n)) means there exist constants c>0 and n₀ such that for every n≥n₀, f(n)≤c g(n). c is a fixed scaling allowance; n₀ lets us ignore a finite initial region. Neither may keep changing with n after the proof chooses them.

For 6n³+5, choose c=7,n₀=2. Since n³≥8 there, 5≤n³, giving 6n³+5≤7n³. It is also O(n⁴), a looser ceiling. Big-O does not claim a tight equality or fastest possible algorithm. The equals sign in f=O(g) is conventional membership shorthand: f belongs to the collection of functions eventually bounded by a constant multiple of g.

To prove it is not O(n²), take any proposed c,n₀ and choose an integer n≥n₀ with n>c. Then 6n³+5>c n². You have defeated every possible fixed ceiling, not merely shown one numerical counterexample. The negation is ∀c>0,∀n₀,∃n≥n₀ with f(n)>c g(n). Quantifiers are doing the same careful work they did in pumping proofs.

Round 3 — A logarithm counts how many multiplicative growth steps · pages 9–11

log₂n is the exponent needed to make 2 to that power equal n. For powers of two, it counts repeated halving steps back to 1. The base-change identity log_b n=log₂n/log₂b holds for fixed b>1. Changing between such fixed bases changes only a constant factor, so O(n log n) does not need a specified base.

For 3n log₂n+5n log₂log₂n, use n≥2 so the nested logarithm is defined. Then log₂n≤n, and taking log₂ gives log₂log₂n≤log₂n. Thus the expression is at most 8n log₂n. The slide's n≥1 wording overlooks the undefined log₂log₂1; choosing a valid eventual threshold repairs that without changing the asymptotic result.

Round 4 — Add costs and keep the actual quantifier obligations · pages 12–15

If f≤c₁n² after n₁ and g≤c₂n after n₂, take n₀=max(n₁,n₂,1). Then f+g≤c₁n²+c₂n≤(c₁+c₂)n². Both bounds are now simultaneously valid. That's the proof behind O(n²)+O(n)=O(n²).

O(1) means bounded by a constant independent of n, not exactly one operation. 2^{O(n)} means bounded by 2^{cn} eventually for some fixed c; the O occurs in the exponent. It is different from O(2ⁿ): 4ⁿ=2^{2n} belongs to 2^{O(n)} but is not O(2ⁿ). A finite initial collection of exceptions can be covered by enlarging a constant, provided the function is finite on those inputs.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Work a bound from the definition

Take f(n)=6n³+5. For n≥2, 5≤n³, so 6n3+5≤7n36n^3+5\le7n^36n3+5≤7n3. Choose c=7 and n₀=2. That proves f=O(n³). The lower-order extra 5 is absorbed into a fixed multiplier once n is large enough.

Why isn't f=O(n²)? If 6n3+5≤cn26n^3+5\le cn^26n3+5≤cn2 eventually held, dividing by n² would give 6n+5/n2≤c6n+5/n^2\le c6n+5/n2≤c. But 6n exceeds any fixed c when n is large enough. No fixed constant can contain that growth.

O(n³) is an upper bound, not necessarily a tight one. The same f is also O(n⁴). A statement can be correct and still less informative. Do not read the equals sign in f=O(g) as ordinary equality of two numerical functions; it is conventional membership-in-a-growth-class notation.

How bounds combine

For sequential phases, add costs. If one is at most c₁g(n) after n₁ and another at most c₂g(n) after n₂, their sum is at most (c₁+c₂)g(n) after max(n₁,n₂). The maximum threshold ensures both bounds are valid at once.

For a nested loop, count how often the inner work runs and its cost each time. n passes each taking O(n) steps give O(n²). But check whether the pass length shrinks; mindlessly multiplying every visible loop by n can miss a stronger bound.

Input representation is part of the problem

An integer N written in binary takes about log₂N bits; unary 0ᴺ takes N symbols. An algorithm using N iterations is linear in unary length but exponential in the binary length. Saying “linear in the number” without specifying encoding can hide the entire difficulty.

Also distinguish 2O(n)2^{O(n)}2O(n) from O(2n)O(2^n)O(2n). The former allows an unspecified constant multiplier in the exponent, such as 2^{3n}; the latter permits only a fixed multiplier outside 2ⁿ. Those are not interchangeable.

Keep: Big O is a quantified eventual upper bound on growth. Name the input-size measure and machine model before counting steps.

One connected check: In the proof that 6n³+5 is O(n³), what jobs do c=7 and n₀=2 each perform?

models.title: Little o and algorithm cost: distinguish smaller growth from the same scale
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–4: little-o and quantifier order
  • PDF pages 5–7: quadratic matching and TIME class
  • PDF pages 8–11: halving algorithm and scan cost
  • PDF page 12: two-tape linear algorithm

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

“At most a constant multiple” versus “eventually a tiny fraction”

Big O allows comparable growth: 6n³ is O(n³). Little o is stronger. f(n)=o(g(n))f(n)=o(g(n))f(n)=o(g(n)) means that for every positive constant c, f(n)≤c g(n) eventually. The threshold may depend on c. When the ratio is defined appropriately, this is equivalent to f(n)/g(n)→0.

For √n versus n, the ratio is 1/√n, which tends to zero. Thus √n=o(n). For 6n³ versus n³, the ratio is always 6, so it is not little o. It cannot eventually fit below 0.01 times n³. The difference is the order of the quantifiers: some fixed multiplier versus every arbitrarily small multiplier.

Throwing half the live items away sounds cheap until you notice they still occupy crossed-out tape cells. Your head keeps walking over them. Count rounds and price each real scan separately. If you charge only for the remaining live symbols, you are giving the machine a shortcut it does not have.

Round 1 — Little-o means the ratio actually dies away · pages 1–4

Big-O permits some fixed multiplier c. Little-o must eventually fit beneath every positive multiplier, however tiny. Formally f=o(g) means f(n)/g(n)→0, assuming g is eventually positive and the relevant functions are nonnegative.

For √n versus n, the ratio is 1/√n. Given any c>0, choose n₀>1/c²; afterward the ratio is below c. For n versus n, the ratio is always 1, so choosing c=1/2 defeats little-o. Thus n=O(n) but n≠o(n). “Smaller” means asymptotically negligible relative to g, not merely f(n)<g(n) for some inputs.

The threshold may depend on c. That is what ∀c∃n₀ allows. One threshold that works for all positive c simultaneously would be a much stronger and generally wrong requirement.

Round 2 — Count the scans, including returns · pages 5–7

For the basic 0ᵏ1ᵏ algorithm on total input length n, format checking and returning left each cost O(n). Each round matches one zero and one one and may scan O(n) cells. At most n/2 matching rounds yield O(n²), plus linear final checking. This proves an upper bound for this algorithm, not a lower bound for all algorithms.

TIME(t(n)) is the family of languages decided by some deterministic TM in O(t(n)) time under the stated model. A language may belong to several nested TIME classes. Giving a faster algorithm improves the known upper bound; it does not erase the existence of the slower one.

Round 3 — Halve the two counts while checking the discarded bits · pages 8–11

After validating 01, repeatedly compare the parity of the live zero count and live one count, then replace each by its floor-half by crossing off alternating symbols in each block. Equal parities are equivalent to an even total count. If parities differ, reject. If both counts reach zero, accept.

Why does this detect inequality? For counts a,b, matching parity says their lowest binary digits agree. Floor-halving discards that digit. Repeating compares every remaining binary digit. If a=b, every comparison agrees; if a≠b, some digit eventually differs. This supplies the reasoning behind the slide's repeated even-total check.

For counts 5,5: 5,5→2,2→1,1→0,0, accept. For 4,2: both initially even, but halving gives 2,1; total is odd, reject. Checking parity only once would miss this case.

There are O(log n) rounds because the live counts halve. Each sweep still crosses a physical region of length O(n): crossed-out symbols occupy cells. Therefore total time is O(n log n), not a geometric-sum O(n). Physically compacting the surviving symbols has a cost too; a naive one-tape repeated-copy procedure can be quadratic. Don't price an expensive rearrangement at zero.

The source cites a lower-bound theorem: a language decided in o(n log n) on this deterministic one-tape model is regular. Since equal blocks are not regular, that rules out such a faster bound here. The theorem itself is not proved in the deck; its model assumptions matter.

Round 4 — Two tapes change the movement cost · page 12

Copy zeros onto tape 2 while scanning the initial zero block. Then match each one against one stored zero, moving the heads locally. Reject extra ones or leftover zeros; reject bad block order. Only a fixed number of linear passes is needed, so time is O(n). Same decidable language, different machine model, different efficient implementation. Computational power and runtime are separate comparisons.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Return to a familiar language and count actual work

To decide {0k1k:k≥0}\{0^k1^k:k\ge0\}{0k1k:k≥0} on a single tape, first check block order. A straightforward machine crosses off one zero and one one per round, repeatedly traveling across a region of length O(n). There are O(n) rounds, so the time is O(n²).

The reason isn't just “two loops.” It is the combination of how many obligations are discharged per round and how far the head travels to discharge them. Tape movement is part of the cost.

Why repeated halving can improve the bound

Instead of matching one pair at a time, compare the parity of the two remaining counts, then retain roughly half of each for another round. Equal counts have equal low-order binary bits; after removing that bit by halving, their quotients must still match. If parities differ in some round, reject. Boundary cases with no surviving symbols must be handled explicitly.

The number of rounds is O(log n), since each successful round roughly halves the live populations. But the old crossed-out cells still occupy physical tape positions. A pass may still travel across O(n) cells even when few live symbols remain. Therefore the time is O(n log n), not automatically O(n) from imagining the tape physically shrinks.

That distinction—logical population versus physical span—is exactly the kind of detail that separates a plausible story from a correct time analysis.

Multiple tapes can change the movement cost

With a second tape, copy the first block and compare it against the second in coordinated scans. Each relevant symbol needs only a constant amount of local work, so a linear-time method is possible on that model. This does not contradict the one-tape analysis: the storage layout and allowed head movements changed.

The language is the same, the yes/no condition is the same, and computability power is the same. The number of physical steps can differ. Complexity claims must name the model under which they are measured.

How to structure a time proof

Identify the input length n. Divide the algorithm into phases. For each phase, bound the number of repetitions and the cost per repetition, including resets and scans over marked cells. Sum the bounds, then simplify using Big O. If claiming little o, show the ratio or quantify over every positive multiplier; an ordinary upper bound is insufficient.

Keep: little o means vanishing relative growth. For algorithms, count physical work, not just useful-looking edits.

One connected check: Why can halving the number of live symbols leave the cost of one tape sweep proportional to the original input length?

models.title: Simulation cost: equal computability can come with a quadratic bill

sections.concepts: power versus runtime and theorem assumptions

models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: power versus runtime and theorem assumptions
  • PDF pages 3–4: encoded span and per-step simulation
  • PDF page 5: total bound and polynomial robustness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Revisit the one-tape encoding with a stopwatch

We already know one tape can represent k tapes using separated blocks and marked head positions. Now ask how much time that simulation takes. Suppose the multitape machine runs in t(n) steps on inputs of length n, with t(n)≥n and fixed k.

In t steps, each head can visit only O(t) cells, and the original input occupies at most t cells under the assumption. With a fixed number of tapes, the entire encoded configuration therefore has length O(t). This is a bound on how far the simulator may need to scan.

We already built an interpreter for several virtual tapes on one tape. Now audit its bill: how long is the encoded workspace, how many scans per simulated step, how many steps total? The theorem comes from multiplying those costs with the machine’s fixed number of tapes kept fixed.

Round 1 — The old simulation proves possibility; now price the work · pages 1–2

The theorem says a k-tape TM running in t(n)≥n time can be simulated by a one-tape TM in O(t(n)²) time. k is fixed for the source machine; it is not an extra parameter growing with the input. This is an upper bound on one general simulation, not a claim that every multitape computation inherently needs that much time on one tape.

The condition t(n)≥n ensures the input length is covered by the runtime bound. More generally the represented span is controlled by n+t(n); using t(n)≥n simplifies that to O(t(n)). Conditions written before a theorem usually pay for some later step like this.

Round 2 — How long can the encoded tapes get? · pages 3–4

In t steps, a head can move at most t cells from its initial position. Each step writes only one cell per tape. Including the original input, the used span of each tape is O(n+t), hence O(t). With fixed k tapes, the combined delimiter/head-marker encoding has length O(kt)=O(t).

One simulated step scans that encoding to find all marked head symbols, computes the source transition in finite control, and scans to update writes and head marks. If a region must grow, shifting the remaining encoding costs O(t) too. A fixed number of such scans and shifts remains O(t).

The simulator may carry a displaced symbol in its state during a shift, as explained in the earlier conversion. It does not need an unbounded state set because the source alphabet and number of tapes are fixed. The tape stores the growing data; finite control stores a fixed-sized local tuple.

There are at most t source transitions. Each costs at most C·t simulator transitions for some machine-dependent constant C, after accounting for initialization and encoding. Thus total ≤C·t² plus lower-order setup costs, giving O(t²).

The proof uses specific local tape operations and a fixed finite encoding. If you add an operation that solves an arbitrary hard problem in one step, this simulation theorem no longer justifies treating it as free.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

One simulated step is not one real step

The simulator must sweep to find the marked symbols, remember their tuple, apply the joint transition, move markers, and sometimes insert a blank cell by shifting later data. Each such phase costs O(t) on a representation of length O(t). A fixed number of phases still costs O(t).

A constant number of extra tapes may alter the exponent or practical speed without turning a polynomial computation into an exponential one under this simulation.

By contrast, nondeterministic simulation will involve a tree of alternative configurations, not merely one encoded configuration. The next deck counts how many branches must be explored. Different source of overhead, different bound.

models.title: Nondeterministic time: depth is cheap to define, the whole tree is costly to search
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF page 1: longest-branch time and finite branching
  • PDF pages 2–4: breadth-first simulation costs
  • PDF pages 5–6: exponential algebra and one-tape overhead

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Name what “time” measures before counting

For a nondeterministic decider, time t(n) is the maximum number of steps along any branch on inputs of length n. It measures the longest branch, not the total number of nodes across the computation tree. Every branch must halt within that bound.

If each step has at most b choices, with b a constant determined by the machine, there can be roughly b^d paths of length d. A depth-t tree can therefore contain exponentially many candidates even though each individual branch is short.

A nondeterministic tree can have short branches and a shitload of branches. Those are different costs. The NTM time bound measures the longest branch; a deterministic search pays to explore alternatives. First count possible branches, then include what it costs to represent and inspect them.

Round 1 — Nondeterministic time measures one branch, not the whole tree · page 1

For an NTM decider, t(n) bounds the number of transitions on every branch for every input of length n. The maximum includes rejecting branches. A machine with one fast accepting branch and another infinite branch is not a polynomial-time NTM decider under this definition.

Let b be a fixed upper bound on the number of transition choices from any local situation. A computation tree of depth t has at most 1+b+…+bᵗ nodes. For b≥2, this is O(bᵗ). If b=1, the machine is deterministic and the tree is a single path; we can still use the looser exponential upper bound by taking max(2,b).

Nondeterministic “parallel” language is a way to describe existential branches, not a promise of exponentially many physical processors running for free. Deterministic simulation must account for exploring the choices.

Round 2 — Pay for each branch address you inspect · pages 2–4

Use the three-tape breadth-first simulator: original input, current branch simulation, branch address. Each address has length at most t. Resetting/copying the input costs O(n), which is O(t) because t≥n. Following that address costs O(t), and updating/enumerating its next address costs O(t).

Invalid addresses can stop early; they do not exceed the bound. Keeping the bound for all possible addresses is safe even if many do not correspond to real nodes. If an accepting configuration is found, accept. When every relevant branch is exhausted without acceptance, reject. The NTM's all-branches time bound makes this finite.

Thus a direct multitape simulation costs O(bᵗ·t). The factor t is real bookkeeping work; we do not omit it and hope the exponential hides the explanation.

Round 3 — Why that product becomes 2^{O(t)} · pages 5–6

Rewrite bᵗt as 2^{t log₂b+log₂t}. Since b is fixed, log₂b is a constant. For t≥1, log₂t≤t. Therefore the exponent is at most (log₂b+1)t, giving 2^{O(t)}.

Now convert the three-tape simulator into one tape using the previous quadratic-overhead theorem. If the multitape bound is at most 2^{ct}, its square is 2^{2ct}. Doubling a fixed constant in the exponent still fits 2^{O(t)}. This is why the final single-tape statement has the same broad exponential form.

Do not confuse 2^{O(t)} with O(2ᵗ). The former allows any fixed constant multiple of t in the exponent; the latter only allows a fixed multiplier outside 2ᵗ. That distinction was introduced in Big-O 1 and is doing useful work here.

Round 4 — What the theorem does and does not settle

For a polynomial-time NTM, this general simulation gives a deterministic exponential-time upper bound. It does not prove exponential time is necessary for that language. A clever deterministic algorithm might avoid enumerating the full tree.

That gap leads to P versus NP: can every polynomially bounded nondeterministic search be replaced by some polynomial deterministic method, perhaps one quite different from brute-force simulation? An expensive generic simulation cannot answer no. To establish a lower bound, we would have to rule out all faster algorithms, not merely analyze this particular one.

The transferable proof pattern is explicit: count candidates, bound work per candidate, multiply, and then account for model-conversion overhead. Each layer needs a bound before the final asymptotic shorthand is justified.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

See the difference on a small tree

With two choices per step and depth three, there can be eight length-three choice sequences: 111,112,121,122,211,212,221,222. Each branch takes three steps. A deterministic simulator that explores all choices may need to inspect all eight branches before concluding that none accepts.

Growing depth from three to thirty doesn't merely multiply the candidate count by ten. It can multiply it from 2³ to 2³⁰. That's the source of the exponential cost; no individual transition became expensive.

Derive the simulation bound

Enumerate candidate choice sequences up to length t, replay each for at most O(t) steps on a multitape simulator, and check whether any accepts. The number of candidates is bounded by a constant-base exponential in t. Multiplying by a polynomial factor such as t still gives 2O(t)2^{O(t)}2O(t).

If b=1 there is no branching and the search is much cheaper, but the exponential expression remains a valid general upper bound. Converting the resulting deterministic multitape simulation to one tape squares its running time. Squaring 2ct2^{ct}2ct gives 22ct2^{2ct}22ct, still 2O(t)2^{O(t)}2O(t). The constant in the exponent changes; the broad form does not.

What this says about power and efficiency

Nondeterministic and deterministic TMs decide the same languages because the finite tree can be searched. But the straightforward deterministic simulation may be exponentially slower than the longest nondeterministic branch. Whether every polynomial-time nondeterministic decision problem has some polynomial-time deterministic method is the P versus NP question—not settled by this expensive simulation.

An exponential simulation proves an upper bound that is sufficient for decidability. It does not prove that an exponential slowdown is unavoidable. Again: “our method costs this much” and “every possible method must cost this much” are different claims.

Connect this to a guessed solution

A nondeterministic branch can guess a short candidate and verify it. The branch length includes both guessing and checking. A deterministic exhaustive search may try every candidate. Later, the certificate definition of NP packages exactly this distinction: a supplied candidate can be easy to check even when finding one efficiently is not known.

Keep: nondeterministic time measures branch depth; deterministic search may pay for the whole tree. Do not silently substitute one quantity for the other.

One connected check: Why does a polynomial bound on each branch fail, by itself, to give a polynomial bound on the number of branches?

models.title: P: algorithms whose work is polynomial in the encoded input length
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–2: P and polynomial/exponential scaling
  • PDF pages 3–5: PATH reachability algorithm
  • PDF pages 6–11: gcd invariant and bit complexity
  • PDF page 12: CFL dynamic programming supplement

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

The definition is a growth guarantee, not a compliment

P is the class of languages decided by deterministic TMs in polynomial time: for some fixed exponent k, running time is O(nᵏ), where n is input length. The machine must halt on every input and answer correctly. “Polynomial” does not mean instantly practical; n¹⁰⁰ is polynomial and can be absurdly large.

The value of the class is robustness: standard deterministic model changes have polynomial overhead, and useful efficient algorithms often fall inside it. It gives a precise mathematical boundary to investigate, not a guarantee about your laptop's response time.

The good algorithms stop paying for the same work repeatedly. Reachability marks what is already discovered. Euclid preserves the common divisors while shrinking the numbers. Parsing saves answers for substrings. We will identify that reusable fact, show why the updates preserve it, and count the resulting work.

Round 1 — Polynomial is a mathematical class, not a stopwatch guarantee · pages 1–2

P contains languages decided by deterministic TMs in O(nᵏ) time for some fixed k. The union over k means the exponent may differ between languages/algorithms, but it cannot grow with n within one claimed polynomial bound. n³ is polynomial; nⁿ is not.

At n=1000, n³ is 10⁹ while 2ⁿ is about 10³⁰¹. That illustrates the growth gap. Nevertheless a polynomial with a huge exponent or constant can be impractical, and an exponential algorithm may work on small inputs. P captures a robust theoretical notion of efficient solvability, not a universal practical cutoff.

Round 2 — PATH avoids enumerating paths · pages 3–5

PATH asks whether a directed graph contains a route from s to t. A route with repeated vertices can have its cycles removed, so a reachable target has a simple path using at most m vertices. Brute-force enumeration of candidate vertex sequences is finite but exponential.

Instead mark s, repeatedly scan edges and mark b whenever an edge a→b has marked a, then stop when no new vertex is marked. At most m productive passes occur. A simple directed graph has at most m² edges, and each marking/check can be implemented in polynomial time in the graph encoding. Thus total time is polynomial.

Correctness uses the reachability invariant from earlier decks: every mark has a path justification, and at a fixed point no reachable vertex can remain unmarked. Complexity adds a new obligation: bound passes and cost per pass. A correct decider without that accounting has not yet proved membership in P.

Round 3 — Euclid preserves the common divisors · pages 6–11

The greatest common divisor gcd(x,y) is the largest positive integer dividing both. Two positive integers are relatively prime iff their gcd is 1. The update is (x,y)→(y,x mod y), continuing until y=0, then returning x.

Why preserve gcd? Write x=qy+r. Any common divisor of x and y divides r=x−qy. Conversely, any common divisor of y and r divides x=qy+r. The common-divisor sets are identical, hence their largest member is identical. At y=0, every divisor of x also divides 0, so gcd(x,0)=x.

Trace (24,18)→(18,6)→(6,0), returning 6. If x<y initially, the first remainder is x and the swap fixes their order. For x>y>0, x mod y<x/2 or at most x/2 by splitting into y≤x/2 and y>x/2. Across successive iterations the positive operands shrink rapidly, giving O(log x+log y) iterations.

Those logarithms are proportional to binary input length. Long division/remainder on n-bit numbers uses polynomially many bit operations; swapping stored values is polynomial too. Therefore the whole algorithm is polynomial in encoded length, not merely in the enormous numeric values.

Round 4 — The omitted CFL-in-P proof: reuse solved substrings · page 12

For a fixed CNF grammar and input w of length n, let T[i,j] be the set of variables that generate substring wᵢ…wⱼ. Initialize length-one intervals from rules A→wᵢ. For longer intervals, consider each split k and each rule A→BC; put A in T[i,j] when B∈T[i,k] and C∈T[k+1,j]. Process shorter intervals before longer ones. Accept iff the start variable belongs to T[1,n]; handle ε separately.

There are O(n²) intervals and O(n) splits per interval, with finitely many grammar rules to check. This gives O(|R|n³) rule checks. The invariant follows the binary root split of a CNF parse tree. Dynamic programming means storing answers to repeated smaller subproblems so they are not recomputed exponentially. This is a supplementary proof of the theorem the slide states without proof.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

PATH: search the graph without enumerating all paths

Given a directed graph G and vertices s,t, ask whether a path from s to t exists. Mark s. Repeatedly inspect outgoing edges from marked vertices and mark their destinations. Stop when t is marked or no new vertex can be marked.

On a graph s→u→t with an extra cycle u→s, marking still progresses safely: revisiting s doesn't create an endless search. A vertex needs to be newly marked only once. At most the number of vertices can be added, and each pass inspects finitely many encoded edges, giving a polynomial bound.

Correctness comes from two directions: each marked vertex has a path from s; every reachable vertex is eventually marked by following a path's edges. Termination comes from finitely many new marks. Enumerating every possible path would waste work on repetitions and cycles.

Euclid: use a preserved relation and a decreasing quantity

To compute gcd(a,b), repeatedly replace (a,b) by (b, a mod b) until b=0. The greatest common divisor stays the same because a divisor divides both a and b exactly when it divides both b and the remainder a−qb.

For 18 and 24: (18,24)→(24,18)→(18,6)→(6,0), so the gcd is 6. The remainder is smaller than the divisor, ensuring progress. More sharply, the relevant magnitude shrinks by at least a factor of two within a bounded number of iterations, giving logarithmically many rounds in the numerical magnitude.

The numbers are binary encoded. Their bit length is logarithmic in their value, so a rigorous polynomial-time claim also counts the bit cost of division/remainder operations. Treating arbitrary-size arithmetic as one free step would hide work.

A familiar language class returns

The deck states that every context-free language is in P. Earlier, CNF gave a finite exhaustive membership algorithm via 2n−1 derivation steps. That particular enumeration can be exponential; it established decidability, not the stronger polynomial result. Polynomial parsing uses shared subproblems instead of separately trying every tree.

This distinction is useful everywhere: a language may admit a slow algorithm and also a fast one. Complexity classes assert the existence of a suitably bounded algorithm, not that every algorithm for the problem is efficient.

Keep: find a reusable summary—reachable vertices, a gcd invariant, shared parsing subproblems—and prove both correctness and a bound in encoded input length.

One connected check: Why does “at most N iterations” fail to establish polynomial time when the integer N is supplied in binary?

## the definition is a growth guarantee, not a compliment

p is the class of languages decided by deterministic tms in polynomial time: for some fixed exponent k, running time is o(nᵏ), where n is input length. the machine must halt on every input and answer correctly. “polynomial” does not mean instantly practical; n¹⁰⁰ is polynomial and can be absurdly large.

the value of the class is robustness: standard deterministic model changes have polynomial overhead, and useful efficient algorithms often fall inside it. it gives a precise mathematical boundary to investigate, not a guarantee about your laptop's response time.

the good algorithms stop paying for the same work repeatedly. reachability marks what is already discovered. euclid preserves the common divisors while shrinking the numbers. parsing saves answers for substrings. we will identify that reusable fact, show why the updates preserve it, and count the resulting work.

## round 1 — polynomial is a mathematical class, not a stopwatch guarantee · pages 1–2

p contains languages decided by deterministic tms in o(nᵏ) time for some fixed k. the union over k means the exponent may differ between languages/algorithms, but it cannot grow with n within one claimed polynomial bound. n³ is polynomial; nⁿ is not.

at n=1000, n³ is 10⁹ while 2ⁿ is about 10³⁰¹. that illustrates the growth gap. nevertheless a polynomial with a huge exponent or constant can be impractical, and an exponential algorithm may work on small inputs. p captures a robust theoretical notion of efficient solvability, not a universal practical cutoff.

## round 2 — path avoids enumerating paths · pages 3–5

path asks whether a directed graph contains a route from s to t. a route with repeated vertices can have its cycles removed, so a reachable target has a simple path using at most m vertices. brute-force enumeration of candidate vertex sequences is finite but exponential.

instead mark s, repeatedly scan edges and mark b whenever an edge a→b has marked a, then stop when no new vertex is marked. at most m productive passes occur. a simple directed graph has at most m² edges, and each marking/check can be implemented in polynomial time in the graph encoding. thus total time is polynomial.

correctness uses the reachability invariant from earlier decks: every mark has a path justification, and at a fixed point no reachable vertex can remain unmarked. complexity adds a new obligation: bound passes and cost per pass. a correct decider without that accounting has not yet proved membership in p.

why preserve gcd? write x=qy+r. any common divisor of x and y divides r=x−qy. conversely, any common divisor of y and r divides x=qy+r. the common-divisor sets are identical, hence their largest member is identical. at y=0, every divisor of x also divides 0, so gcd(x,0)=x.

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

given a directed graph g and vertices s,t, ask whether a path from s to t exists. mark s. repeatedly inspect outgoing edges from marked vertices and mark their destinations. stop when t is marked or no new vertex can be marked.

models.title: NP: a yes-answer has a short certificate that can be checked quickly
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: Hamiltonian path and verification
  • PDF pages 4–5: composite witnesses and no-certificates caveat
  • PDF pages 6–9: verifier, certificate bounds and NP
  • PDF page 10: bounded nondeterministic path algorithm

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Start with checking, not with a mysterious acronym

Suppose someone hands you a proposed Hamiltonian path in a graph: an ordered list of vertices. You can check that it starts and ends where required, visits every vertex exactly once, and uses an actual graph edge between each adjacent pair. The list may have been hard to find, but checking a supplied list is a concrete finite job.

A certificate is that extra proposed evidence. A verifier is a deterministic algorithm that checks the original input together with the certificate. NP consists of decision languages where yes-instances have certificates of polynomially bounded length that can be verified in polynomial time.

For no-instances, every permitted certificate must fail. A verifier that accepts some bogus witness would certify the wrong language.

Think “show me the route and I'll check it.” The certificate supplies the route; the verifier checks the graph's actual edges and the once-per-vertex requirement. It doesn't trust the person who supplied it. A pretty-looking list gets no free pass. This is the concrete meaning of verification before the acronym starts sounding like wizard shit.

A certificate is somebody handing you a proposed reason for yes: “here, this route visits every vertex once.” You still inspect the whole claim. A plausible-looking route with a repeated vertex is bullshit evidence. Fast checking means every required condition is checked within the time bound, not that we trust the suggestion.

Round 1 — A proposed solution can be easier to check than to discover · pages 1–3

A Hamiltonian path visits every graph vertex exactly once. HAMPATH additionally specifies start s and end t. It differs from ordinary PATH, which only asks for some route and need not visit every vertex.

Given a candidate list p₁,…,pₘ, check it contains exactly the graph's m vertices, with no duplicates; starts at s and ends at t; and every consecutive pair is a directed edge. A claimed route that skips one vertex is not a Hamiltonian witness. A list of m distinct valid vertices already covers all m vertices, but validity of each listed identifier must be checked too.

Verification is like checking a supplied route itinerary against a map. The itinerary saves you the search for which route to try; it does not let you skip checking the actual constraints. An invalid certificate must never convince the verifier of a false yes-answer.

Round 2 — The certificate is extra input, with a bounded size · pages 6–9

A verifier V checks an instance w together with a proposed certificate c. The language satisfies w∈A iff there exists a c making V accept ⟨w,c⟩. For yes-instances, at least one valid certificate exists. For no-instances, every certificate must fail. The verifier does not need to accept all certificates for a yes-instance.

For NP, certificate length is bounded by a polynomial in |w| and verification takes polynomial time in |w| under that bound. Making the bound explicit prevents smuggling an exponentially long search transcript into “easy verification.” An arbitrary useless suffix can be ignored in some machine conventions; the clean definition restricts the certificate actually used to polynomial length.

NP stands for nondeterministic polynomial time, not “non-polynomial.” P⊆NP: a polynomial decider can serve as a verifier that ignores the certificate. Membership in NP does not establish that a problem is hard or outside P.

NTIME(t(n)) bounds the longest branch of a nondeterministic decider by O(t(n)). The equality NP=∪ₖNTIME(nᵏ) is proved in the next deck; here the verifier definition gives the first mental model.

Round 3 — Do not overclaim from the compositeness example · pages 4–5

For integer x, a certificate p can be a nontrivial divisor: check 1<p<x and x mod p=0. Or provide p,q≥2 and check pq=x. These are polynomial-time arithmetic checks in bit length.

The slide uses compositeness to illustrate easy verification, but compositeness is also known to be in P through polynomial-time primality testing. Its witness example does not establish a search-versus-decision separation or an example outside P. The earlier guide links the primary AKS result.

For the complement of HAMPATH, one failed proposed route is not a certificate that no Hamiltonian route exists. That explains why the obvious yes-certificate does not automatically work for no-instances. It does not prove that no polynomial no-certificate system exists; making that stronger claim would run into unresolved complexity questions.

Round 4 — Guess finitely, then verify every condition · page 10

An NTM guesses a list of m vertex identifiers, with bounded encoding length, then runs the checks above. Guessing is a sequence of branching choices, each branch selecting one candidate list. Every branch halts after polynomial work, accepting exactly when its list is valid.

If a Hamiltonian path exists, one branch guesses it. If none exists, every guessed list fails at least one check. The number of branches may be huge, but nondeterministic time measures the longest branch. Deterministic enumeration would have to pay for exploring the list space unless another algorithm avoids that search. The distinction is a definition, not a claim that real hardware gets those branches for free.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Work the HAMPATH certificate

For a graph with vertices {s,a,b,t}, a candidate [s,b,a,t] claims a path using all four exactly once. Check its endpoints, count and uniqueness of vertices, and edges s→b, b→a, a→t. If any edge is missing, reject this certificate. That does not by itself prove the graph has no Hamiltonian path; another ordering may work.

The certificate length grows with the graph encoding size. Trying all vertex orderings may take huge time, but the verifier processes one supplied ordering. Keep the quantifiers straight: some certificate for a yes-instance; no certificate for a no-instance.

NP does not mean “non-polynomial”

The name refers to nondeterministic polynomial time, which the next deck connects to certificates. Problems already in P are also in NP: a verifier can simply run the polynomial decider and ignore the certificate. Therefore membership in NP does not establish hardness or rule out an efficient deterministic algorithm.

The deck uses compositeness as a verification example. A nontrivial factor certifies that an integer is composite: check the factor bounds and divisibility. But compositeness is also in P, because primality has an unconditional deterministic polynomial-time algorithm. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena paper establishes that prime/composite decision result. Finding a full factorization is a different task; don't slide from one claim to the other.

What about certifying a no-answer?

A Hamiltonian path is a compact witness that a path exists. The absence of one particular candidate is not a witness that no candidate exists. The complement class coNP concerns languages whose no-answers, viewed as yes-answers to the complement, have polynomial certificates.

It is not established that NP and coNP differ. So say “we have this yes-certificate” rather than “there can never be a short no-certificate.” A lack of a known method is not an impossibility theorem.

Connect to earlier proof practice

An ambiguity witness gave one string and two derivations. A computation history gave a finite run. A counterexample refuted a universal claim. These are all evidence objects, but NP adds quantitative requirements: certificate length and verification time must be polynomial in the original input length.

Keep: NP is about polynomially checkable yes-evidence. It includes easy problems and does not itself mean NP-complete.

One connected check: Why does rejecting [s,b,a,t] fail to decide that a graph has no Hamiltonian path?

models.title: Verifiers and guessing machines: two descriptions of the same resource
models.html:
Follow the source pages · concepts in this deck
  • PDF pages 1–3: verifier/NTM equivalence with both directions
  • PDF pages 4–6: subset-sum certificates and multiplicity
  • PDF pages 7–8: P versus NP and completeness

Page map for this explanation; supplementary examples and source corrections are identified in the prose. Reading coverage does not establish mastery.

Turn a certificate verifier into a nondeterministic machine

If a language has polynomially bounded certificates and a polynomial-time verifier, an NTM can guess a certificate of the allowed length, then run the verifier. A yes-instance has at least one successful guessed certificate, so at least one branch accepts. A no-instance has none, so every branch rejects.

The guess must be bounded. “Guess any finite string” with no length limit could produce arbitrarily long or nonterminating branches, destroying the polynomial-time guarantee. Guessing itself consumes time; it isn't free magic.

A short certificate is a script telling the verifier which successful possibility to inspect. An accepting branch is that same script played out as choices. The bound matters: unlimited guessing can wander forever and wreck the time promise. We will connect the two descriptions one direction at a time.

Round 1 — A certificate and an accepting branch encode the same witness · pages 1–3

Suppose V verifies a language in polynomial time with polynomially bounded certificates. An NTM guesses a certificate of at most that bounded length, then runs V. Every branch terminates in polynomial time. If w belongs, some certificate makes a branch accept; if not, every branch rejects.

The length bound must be enforced during guessing. “Guess any finite string, then verify” would allow arbitrarily long branches and would not establish a polynomial bound. Include a counter or a fixed polynomial-sized guessing workspace.

Conversely, suppose an NTM decides the language in p(n) time on every branch. A certificate can list the branch choices for a proposed accepting run. The branching factor is fixed, so each choice uses only a constant number of bits and the certificate has O(p(n)) length. A deterministic verifier simulates those choices, rejects nonexistent transitions or malformed certificates, and accepts only if the recorded branch legally reaches acceptance within the bound.

This proves both directions. The certificate need not magically contain the correct answer; it contains a checkable reason. “Some accepting branch” corresponds exactly to “some accepted certificate.”

Round 2 — A subset chooses occurrences, not unlimited copies · pages 4–6

SUBSET-SUM gives numbers x₁,…,xₖ and target t, asking whether some selection sums to t. The slide permits repeated values in the input, such as two occurrences of 11. Treat the input as an indexed list or multiset: each occurrence can be chosen at most once.

A safe certificate is a k-bit mask. Bit i=1 means include occurrence xᵢ; bit i=0 means omit it. For {4,11,16,21,27} and target 25, mask 10010 chooses 4 and 21. Verify mask length and bits, sum selected values using binary arithmetic, and compare with t.

The slide's bare check “each cᵢ belongs to s” is not sufficient when the certificate lists values. With input list [4,11] and target 8, certificate [4,4] passes value-membership and sum checks but illegally reuses the only 4. A mask or distinct valid indices enforces multiplicity. If the input really contained [4,4,11], selecting both 4 occurrences would be legal.

The certificate size is at most polynomial in the input length; it need not be strictly shorter than the input, contrary to a loose slide inequality. Summing k binary integers increases bit length by at most a logarithmic factor in k, so verification remains polynomial. Guess-and-verify proves membership in NP, not by itself NP-completeness.

Round 3 — The open question is whether finding can always be as efficient as checking · pages 7–8

P has polynomial deterministic decision algorithms. NP has polynomially checkable, polynomial-sized yes-certificates. We know P⊆NP; whether equality holds remains open. “Most people believe unequal” is an opinion about the conjecture, not evidence you may use as a theorem.

A language B is NP-hard when every language in NP reduces to B by a polynomial-time many-one reduction: a polynomially computed transformation f with x∈A iff f(x)∈B. It is NP-complete when it is NP-hard and also belongs to NP. These are two separate requirements.

If one NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, compose that algorithm with each polynomial reduction and every NP language would be in P. If one NP-complete problem were proved outside P, then P≠NP. A failed search for a fast algorithm, a slow brute-force method or a list of difficult instances does not prove that lower bound.

Reductions now have a polynomial-time requirement, stronger than the merely computable reductions used for undecidability. Same dependency idea, stricter cost constraint. That's the connection between the earlier impossibility proofs and this final complexity story.

Reconnect the pieces in the worked model

Now put the mechanism back together. The worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

Reverse the construction

If an NTM decides a language in polynomial time, an accepting branch has polynomially many steps. Record its transition choices as a certificate. A deterministic verifier follows those choices, checks that each is legal, and confirms an accepting halt within the bound.

Because the fixed machine has only finitely many choices per step, each choice needs only a constant number of bits. A polynomial number of choices gives a polynomial-size certificate. The verifier doesn't search all branches; the certificate identifies one candidate branch to check.

That proves the equivalence: polynomial nondeterministic time and polynomially verifiable certificates describe the same class NP.

SUBSET-SUM: make the witness concrete

The deck uses numbers such as {4,11,16,21,27} and a target. For target 25, selecting 4 and 21 works. A certificate can be a bit vector 10010, with one bit per listed entry: 1 means select that occurrence, 0 means skip it. Add the selected numbers and compare with the target.

The input is a list of entries; repeated equal values, if present, are distinct positions. You may use each occurrence at most once in ordinary SUBSET-SUM. A certificate that reuses one index repeatedly would be solving a different problem. Check certificate length, valid entries, and the sum.

Binary arithmetic takes time proportional to bit lengths, but summing at most the listed number of integers of bounded input size remains polynomial. Exhaustively trying every subset has 2ᵐ candidates for m entries. A fast verification procedure does not by itself provide a fast search over all candidates.

Where P versus NP actually stands

P asks for a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm. NP asks for polynomially checkable yes-certificates, equivalently polynomial-time nondeterministic decision. P⊆NP. Whether P=NP remains unresolved; the Clay Mathematics Institute lists P versus NP as unsolved (checked November 1, 2026).

NP-complete means a problem is in NP and every NP problem can be transformed into it by a polynomial-time reduction. It is a special kind of completeness, not a synonym for NP. If one NP-complete problem had a polynomial-time algorithm, all NP problems would. No known polynomial algorithm is not the same as a proof that none exists.

The course's final connection

We began by asking what a machine must remember. We moved to what it can compute at all, then what it can compute within a time budget. The same habits keep paying off: specify the object, preserve its meaning through a construction, prove both directions, and account for termination or cost separately.

Keep: bounded guesses are certificates; checking one branch differs from searching the whole tree; the major separation questions remain open.

One connected check: In the verifier-to-NTM construction, why are both the certificate-length bound and the verifier-time bound necessary?

the certificate size is at most polynomial in the input length; it need not be strictly shorter than the input, contrary to a loose slide inequality. summing k binary integers increases bit length by at most a logarithmic factor in k, so verification remains polynomial. guess-and-verify proves membership in np, not by itself np-completeness.

## round 3 — the open question is whether finding can always be as efficient as checking · pages 7–8

p has polynomial deterministic decision algorithms. np has polynomially checkable, polynomial-sized yes-certificates. we know p⊆np; whether equality holds remains open. “most people believe unequal” is an opinion about the conjecture, not evidence you may use as a theorem.

a language b is **np-hard** when every language in np reduces to b by a polynomial-time many-one reduction: a polynomially computed transformation f with x∈a iff f(x)∈b. it is **np-complete** when it is np-hard and also belongs to np. these are two separate requirements.

if one np-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, compose that algorithm with each polynomial reduction and every np language would be in p. if one np-complete problem were proved outside p, then p≠np. a failed search for a fast algorithm, a slow brute-force method or a list of difficult instances does not prove that lower bound.

reductions now have a **polynomial-time** requirement, stronger than the merely computable reductions used for undecidability. same dependency idea, stricter cost constraint. that's the connection between the earlier impossibility proofs and this final complexity story.

## reconnect the pieces in the worked model

now put the mechanism back together. the worked model below revisits the key example and compresses the reasoning into something you can reconstruct.

## reverse the construction

if an ntm decides a language in polynomial time, an accepting branch has polynomially many steps. record its transition choices as a certificate. a deterministic verifier follows those choices, checks that each is legal, and confirms an accepting halt within the bound.

because the fixed machine has only finitely many choices per step, each choice needs only a constant number of bits. a polynomial number of choices gives a polynomial-size certificate. the verifier doesn't search all branches; the certificate identifies one candidate branch to check.

that proves the equivalence: polynomial nondeterministic time and polynomially verifiable certificates describe the same class np.

## subset-sum: make the witness concrete

the deck uses numbers such as `{4,11,16,21,27}` and a target. for target 25, selecting 4 and 21 works. a certificate can be a bit vector `10010`, with one bit per listed entry: 1 means select that occurrence, 0 means skip it. add the selected numbers and compare with the target.

the input is a list of entries; repeated equal values, if present, are distinct positions. you may use each occurrence at most once in ordinary subset-sum. a certificate that reuses one index repeatedly would be solving a different problem. check certificate length, valid entries, and the sum.

binary arithmetic takes time proportional to bit lengths, but summing at most the listed number of integers of bounded input size remains polynomial. exhaustively trying every subset has 2ᵐ candidates for m entries. a fast verification procedure does not by itself provide a fast search over all candidates.

## where p versus np actually stands

p asks for a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm. np asks for polynomially checkable yes-certificates, equivalently polynomial-time nondeterministic decision. p⊆np. whether p=np remains unresolved; the [clay mathematics institute lists p versus np as unsolved](https://www.claymath.org/millennium/p-vs-np/) (checked november 1, 2026).

np-complete means a problem is in np and every np problem can be transformed into it by a polynomial-time reduction. it is a special kind of completeness, not a synonym for np. if one np-complete problem had a polynomial-time algorithm, all np problems would. no known polynomial algorithm is not the same as a proof that none exists.

## the course's final connection

we began by asking what a machine must remember. we moved to what it can compute at all, then what it can compute within a time budget. the same habits keep paying off: specify the object, preserve its meaning through a construction, prove both directions, and account for termination or cost separately.

**keep:** bounded guesses are certificates; checking one branch differs from searching the whole tree; the major separation questions remain open.

**one connected check:** in the verifier-to-ntm construction, why are both the certificate-length bound and the verifier-time bound necessary?

modelOverview:
Round zero — what the hell is this course trying to do?

Alright. Before another Greek letter lands on your screen, fix the job in your head: someone gives us a finite input, and we want to determine whether it follows a rule.

Take 0011. A rule might say: “zeros first, then exactly the same number of ones.” This input passes. 001 fails because one zero has no matching one. 0101 fails the order requirement even though the counts match. The rule has two conditions. Forget either and you solve a different problem.

A string is one input sequence. An alphabet is the set of symbols allowed in it. A language is the set of all strings satisfying the rule. The language is the target; a machine is our proposed checker. A machine can be designed incorrectly. Calling a circle “accept” doesn't make its decisions match the target by magic.

First build the machine in your head: what can it remember?

Imagine reading 000… and then receiving the first 1. The earlier zeros are behind you. To decide whether enough ones follow, something must preserve the number of unmatched zeros. That's the actual problem. The circles and arrows are our way of specifying the solution—or proving a proposed kind of solution cannot exist.

Model What survives from earlier input? What that buys us
DFA One of finitely many state labels A finite summary: odd/even, the last symbol, remainder modulo 3
NFA Several possible finite-state runs Convenient guesses; a DFA can track the set of possibilities
PDA A finite state and an arbitrarily growing stack Store one marker per unmatched obligation; discharge the newest one first
Turing machine A finite state, a writable tape, and a movable head Write down information, revisit it, change it and compare separated pieces

A stack is a pile whose top is the only accessible end. A tape is a row of cells you can revisit by moving a head. Those access rules matter as much as the amount of storage. “More memory” is too vague; ask what can be written, inspected, and retrieved next?

For 0011, a PDA pushes two markers while reading the zeros, then pops one per 1. State labels enforce “no zeros after ones.” The stack handles the count; the state handles the phase. That's how the parts cooperate.

Grammars approach the same target from the other direction

A checker receives a finished string. A grammar starts with an unfinished job and constructs a string using replacement rules.

Consider S → 0S1 | ε. S is the unfinished job. → means “may be replaced by.” The vertical bar separates choices. ε means produce no symbols.

S
0S1       add one zero before the unfinished job and one one after it
00S11     repeat that same wrapping move
0011      replace the remaining S by ε

Every wrapping adds a matched pair, and every zero is placed before the unfinished middle while every one is placed after it. The rule builds equality and order into the structure. The PDA's stored markers are another way to manage those unfinished obligations. Grammar ↔ PDA conversions make that connection exact.

CNF then changes the grammar's internal building blocks while preserving its finished strings. It is like reorganizing a recipe into smaller instructions: the meal must remain the same. We will explain exactly what corresponds, so the analogy doesn't have to carry the proof.

A proof is the explanation that survives every input

Watching 0011 work tells us about 0011. To justify the whole PDA, we need a statement that remains true throughout every run: during the matching phase, the stack has one marker for each earlier zero not yet matched by a one. That statement connects the changing machine to the fixed language rule.

To use it, check three things: it starts true; each allowed move preserves it; the final acceptance condition means the rule is satisfied. We also show every valid string has a successful run. This is the bridge from “I can follow the diagram” to “I can prove the diagram works.”

The pumping lemma goes the other way: finite memory forces some long runs to repeat a state, creating a reusable loop. If reusing that loop necessarily breaks the target language, no DFA could have been its correct checker. The loop is forced by the resource limit; the contradiction is between the checker's behavior and the target rule.

Where the later chapters go

Once a tape gives us a general model of an algorithm, we ask a bigger question: does any algorithm solve this problem and always finish? Decidability studies that. Reductions show that a solver for one problem would give a solver for another. Complexity then asks how the number of steps grows with input length. “A solution exists,” “it eventually finishes,” and “it finishes quickly” are three different claims.

Use the deck guides in course order or jump to the concept blocking you. Each names the question, builds the mechanism, runs a concrete example, unpacks the notation, and explains the connection forward. The later-chapter guides are available because this is a guide to every published deck; their presence does not make them confirmed Midterm 2 scope.

For your current CNF question, start with CNF 1: preserve the finished strings while changing the recipe. Work from the meaning of a variable that can finish empty. The deletion rules will then have a reason behind them.

How we are going to work through the details

Each deck now has connected rounds tied to its source pages. Start with the job, follow the actual mechanism, then decode the notation and the proof. An analogy gets a specific mapping: which part is the state, which part is stored data, which part is a legal operation. If the analogy stops matching the mathematics, the guide says where.

When a word like “nullable,” “invariant” or “certificate” appears, unpack what the object can actually do before treating the word as shorthand. Keep the source example fixed while learning its rules; a new example that reuses S or q₁ gets its conditions restated. Formal exam answers remain precise even when the explanation talks casually.

After one coherent worked example, try the connected check without copying the answer. In our chat, bring the first step that stops making sense; we stay there and repair the missing link. Reading a whole round is useful exposure. Explaining or solving a fresh case is the evidence that the model is becoming yours.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤5-state PDA for 0ᵐ1ᵐ⁺ⁿ0ⁿ, m,n≥1; satisfy normalization conditions already.
items.guide: Separate the first matched 0/1 block from the later matched 1/0 block. The middle phase can pop old zero markers then push markers for trailing zeros. Show the three preconditions.

items.prompt: Convert that PDA to CFG wrapped rules; give push/pop tables.
items.guide: Pair each push with every pop of the same stack symbol; include the bottom-marker pair. Only the wrapped family is requested.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤2-state PDA for 0ᵐ1ⁿ, m≥n≥0, with Γ={0}; give diagram and formal definition.
items.guide: Push on zeros; switch on the first one and pop on ones. Both ordinary phases accept because leftover zeros and ε are allowed.

items.prompt: Prove no one-state PDA with Γ={0} recognizes that language.
items.guide: Use acceptance of ε and 01, then replay an accepting 01 run to force acceptance of 0101. Explain why stack operations remain legal.

items.prompt: Construct a ≤3-state DPDA, including reject state; give δ.
items.guide: Remove choices, retain both accepting phases, reject zeros after ones, and check all four-way table conditions.

items.prompt: Simulate the supplied PDA on 000111 using a tree.
items.guide: Keep branches for the competing 1 transitions with different stack effects. A single path is explicitly insufficient.

items.prompt: Find a counterexample to that PDA for 0ᵐ1ⁿ, m≤n, and draw its tree.
items.guide: Check zero-only inputs and too few ones; acceptance in an ordinary state need not empty the stack. The paper supplies 0 and 001 as examples.

items.prompt: Repair the PDA using ≤4 states and one accept state; trace the counterexample.
items.guide: Use a bottom-marker check before final acceptance; preserve ε and strings containing only ones.

items.prompt: Convert S→A|0A, A→SAS|ε to CNF, showing all four stages.

items.prompt: Design a ≤9-state outside-in TM for w#wᴿ with restricted Γ; trace 01#10 and 010#0 fully.
items.guide: Remember the erased left bit in the state; find and erase the matching rightmost bit. Check # and exhaustion on both sides; count both halting states.

items.prompt: Use the prescribed inside-out TM strategy with ≤8 states and special initial-symbol marks; trace both strings.
items.guide: Use the left boundary marks to know when matching is complete; verify extra separators and the string #. Follow the specified strategy.

items.prompt: Give a ≤4-state two-tape TM for the same reversal language and trace both strings.
items.guide: Copy the left side to tape 2, then compare the right side while scanning that copy backwards. Show both head positions at each joint step.

items.prompt: Adapt the square-length pumping proof using i=3 and the lecture witness.
items.guide: With |y|=k, bound the new length p²+2k strictly between p² and (p+1)².

items.prompt: Can the same witness use i=0 if square lengths exclude n=0?

items.prompt: Give the full truth table for ¬(A∧B∧C) and (A∧B)⇒¬C.

items.prompt: Give a CFG for the same language with ≤5 rules and ≤3 variables.

items.prompt: Identify the language of the supplied PDA and explain it.

items.prompt: Normalize the PDA without changing Σ or Γ; construct all CFG rule families.
